title: Beast of Reincarnation
deck: An action RPG from the Pokémon studio starring a woman and her dog, with turn-based combat living inside real-time combat like a nesting doll.
verdictTitle: Game Freak took a real swing.
dadTake: Every Pokémon game has been secretly asking for a dog. Now it's the whole game.
verdict: Beast of Reincarnation is Game Freak reaching for something new and mostly grabbing it. The one-woman-one-dog framing is genuinely lovely, the combat's fusion of real-time and turn-based takes a bit of getting used to but pays off, and the world it drops you into is prettier and grimmer than we expected from these guys. We're glad it exists.
overview: Meet Emma. Meet Koo. Emma is a woman with a mission, Koo is a dog with opinions, and the world they walk into looks like someone painted a folktale and then quietly set it on fire. Game Freak deciding to make a full action-RPG that isn't Pokémon is the kind of swing we love to see, and inside the first hour we were already texting the group chat about our dogs.

The combat pitch is a fusion of real-time and turn-based, and it takes a bit of getting used to. You're moving Emma in the moment, but every real fight asks you to switch registers and think, which we bounced off for the first hour and then loved by the third. It's a lot to hold in your head early on, and clicks somewhere around hour three, at which point we found ourselves genuinely enjoying the fights.
facts: One-person-one-dog action RPG, with real-time exploration and a turn-based combat layer.
A non-Pokémon release from Game Freak, published by Fictions.
The two protagonists are called Emma and Koo, and Koo is a dog, which is important.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Koo is why I stayed and Emma is who I blame.
lenses.body: I clocked the dog on the store page and pre-decided I was playing it. Then I bounced off the combat's mixed register once, complained about it, and came back a day later because I missed the dog. I'm several hours in now, patting Koo whenever the game lets me. I'm thriving.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Two combat modes in one fight is exactly my kind of nonsense.
lenses.body: I respect Game Freak's willingness to stack a turn-based system on top of a real-time one, and I've spent my evenings working out which encounters reward you for slowing down. It rewards planning around the dog's behaviour, which I wasn't expecting and immediately started spreadsheeting. I'm quietly delighted.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A good game with a real hook, once you settle in.
lenses.body: This isn't the kind of RPG that grabs you in the first hour. The mixed combat took me a while to settle into, the world took getting used to, and the story takes its time. Give it a weekend, though, and it turns into a proper adventure with actual emotional weight, which is more than I bank on these days.

bestFor: Anyone who wants an RPG with a dog protagonist who is also actually good
Curious Game Freak fans who wanted proof they can do more than one thing
Players willing to eat two hours of combat learning to enjoy hour three
watchFor: The dual-combat idea takes real time to click; the first hour is rocky
It's a big swing for the studio, and some edges show it
You will absolutely start narrating your real dog's inner monologue afterwards
reviewBasis: Played on PC by two of us, one on keyboard and one on controller, across a couple of weeks. The third dad has a real dog and refused to play a video game about a fake one.

title: Big Walk
deck: The Goose Game people made a co-op walking-and-talking game, which is the exact hobby our group chat has needed for years.
verdictTitle: It's a hangout. It rules.
dadTake: Finally, a co-op game where nobody has a health bar to argue about.
verdict: Big Walk is a small, warm, extremely House House co-op game about wandering around a big world with your friends and getting lost on purpose. There's no threat, no boss, just a walk and a chat and enough oddball stuff to point at that we happily lost three nights to it. It's a lovely time.
overview: We booted up Big Walk on a Wednesday, all three of us in voice chat, and inside two minutes one of us had wandered off to look at a rock and the other two had lost him entirely. That was the game. That was the whole game. House House have made something that feels like the digital equivalent of taking a walk with your mates, which is a rare feeling in your forties.

There is no combat and there are no fail states, and the point of the game is walking around a shared world together and being surprised by the little things in it. The design assumes your voice chat is doing at least half the work, and it's right. It's the sort of game we didn't know we wanted until we were sitting in it, saying 'oh, look at that,' for two hours straight.
facts: Cooperative online walker-talker, from the studio behind Untitled Goose Game.
No combat, no fail states; the game is the walk and the conversation.
Published by Panic, which is a mark of good taste on its own.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: A co-op game I can play without ever opening a menu.
lenses.body: I walked, I talked, I pointed at a bird, I was happy. There's nothing here that needs me to remember a control scheme. I've suggested Big Walk on three separate group-chat nights now and nobody has said no once. I'm doing my best work on this one.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: There's no game here. I'm fine with it.
lenses.headline: I turned my brain off and it was medicine.
lenses.body: I came in expecting to find hidden systems and found a peaceful world built for aimless wandering instead. I complained for eleven minutes and then quietly enjoyed myself for two hours. There's a real lesson in that. The other two aren't qualified to teach it. I'm not qualified to receive it. I've already asked when we're playing again.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The best 'while we catch up' game we've played in years.
lenses.body: This is what I load when the group chat wants to hang out but nobody wants to concentrate. Voice chat's on, tabs are open, the jokes are terrible. I rate it highly on the specific metric of 'still fun while you also talk about your kids for forty minutes.' Which is a metric almost no games score on.

bestFor: Group chats that want to hang out without committing to a raid
House House fans who wanted more of the same weird warmth
Anyone who needs a co-op game that respects a bedtime
watchFor: There genuinely isn't a challenge; if you need a scoreboard, look elsewhere
It leans hard on you actually being on voice chat with people you like
Solo works but it's clearly built for a group; herd friends before booting
reviewBasis: Played in three-player online sessions on PC across a few evenings, headsets on, kids in bed, and one of us occasionally getting up to check on a suspicious noise upstairs.

title: Mina the Hollower
deck: A whip, a burrow move, a moody little island to save, and the best pixel art since Shovel Knight put on lipstick.
verdictTitle: Yacht Club still know exactly what they're doing.
dadTake: The main character has a whip. That's the pitch. That's a great pitch.
verdict: Mina the Hollower is a beautifully cranky little action-adventure that plays like a Game Boy Color cartridge you never actually owned but somehow miss. The whip feels great, the burrow is a real movement idea, and the whole thing runs on the same taste and craft that made Shovel Knight so easy to love. If you've got a nice controller, use it here.
overview: You play Mina, a Hollower, which is apparently the medieval term for 'a small hero with a whip and a bad attitude.' She's dropped onto a cursed island and told to fix it, and inside twenty minutes you've cracked something small and rude with the whip and burrowed under a wall to find a secret. Yacht Club Games have made a game that feels like the childhood cartridge you told everyone else about.

The whip and the burrow are the whole thing, and they're enough. Combat is precise and readable, the burrow lets you cheat around encounters in ways that feel earned, and the environments give you real reasons to look for hidden holes to dive into. It's tightly designed in the way indie throwbacks either nail or completely botch, and Yacht Club nailed it.
facts: You play Mina, a Hollower, with a whip primary and a burrow move that reshapes traversal.
From Yacht Club Games, the studio behind Shovel Knight, and it shows in every pixel.
Presented in a hand-crafted pixel style that reads like a Game Boy Color game with modern sensibilities.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The whip felt good instantly, which is the entire fight.
lenses.body: I don't have time to learn combos. Mina has a whip, and a whip is a one-button verb, which is my exact speed. I got through the first area with almost no menu screens opened, which coming from me is a five-star review. I also love the burrow, because it lets me skip fights I don't fancy.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: A movement toolkit with layers I can't stop mapping.
lenses.body: I was three rooms in before I started asking whether the burrow has i-frames. It might. It might not. I'm testing. I love that a small pixel game has a real toolkit under the surface, and I'm building routes through screens I'm fairly sure the designers didn't intend. I'm probably wrong about that. I don't care.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A great post-dinner game if you don't fancy an epic.
lenses.body: I get an hour after dinner and this fills it perfectly. Bite-size encounters, a save that never punishes me for stepping away, and enough taste in the art that even a bad night still looks lovely. Absolute palate cleanser between the longer games I'm supposed to be finishing and am not.

bestFor: Anyone with a soft spot for Game Boy Color pixel work
Shovel Knight loyalists who want the same taste in a new shape
Dads with a controller drawer and no time for 80-hour RPGs
watchFor: It is proudly retro, which for some folks reads as 'small' rather than 'tight'
The burrow is a real skill you have to actually learn; button-mashing hurts
You will find yourself humming the theme in the shower like an idiot
reviewBasis: Played on PC by two of us with a controller across a couple of weeks, mostly after bedtime. The third watched a stream and immediately bought it.

title: Forza Horizon 6
deck: The biggest, prettiest Forza yet, set in Japan, and the exact reason our garages are full of cars we cannot afford to look at in person.
verdictTitle: Still the best chill racer going.
dadTake: Bought a kei van in-game, thought about it for a week, did not buy one in real life.
verdict: Forza Horizon 6 is exactly what we needed after a long week: a huge, gorgeous open-world racer that lets you drive fast on beautiful roads and never punishes you for wanting to just cruise. Japan looks unreal. The cars sound right. And the moment-to-moment driving is still the most relaxing thing Playground Games make.
overview: The first hour of Horizon 6 has us tearing down a coastal road at sunset in a very silly car, with cherry blossom on the windscreen, and one of us saying 'this is why I bought a graphics card.' Japan is a fantastic Horizon map: winding mountain roads, dense city sections, sleepy fishing towns you can just accidentally drift through. It's the biggest one they've made and it feels the most like a place.

Under the hood it's still the Horizon formula, and that's a good thing. Race, festival, freeway, roam, buy a car you already own in a different colour, repeat. The driving model is the friendlier end of the sim spectrum: you can turn assists off if you want to hurt yourself, or leave them on and just have a nice time. This is the ideal Sunday-morning game.
facts: Set in Japan, and per the marketing there are over 550 real-world cars in the roster.
Latest entry from Playground Games, who have been making Horizon games for over a decade.
Fully released on Windows, controller very much recommended.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The only racing game I'll actually finish a session in.
lenses.body: I turn the driving assists on, point the car at the horizon, and drive to podcasts. That's the whole loop for me, and Horizon is designed for exactly that guy. I don't do time trials. I don't tune. I drive, I collect a barn find, and I'm asleep by ten with a small smile. The dream.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The tuning depth is still deeper than it needs to be, in a good way.
lenses.body: I went straight into the tuning menu and started shaving hundredths off lap times. Horizon's underlying model is friendly-sim, and I think that's exactly right for a game you want to be able to zone out to and also nerd out in when you're ready. I've got a Miata that's going to haunt our online lobbies.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: It's a very big game, and you don't have to do most of it.
lenses.body: The map is enormous, the events are endless, and none of it demands your attention. I finished the intro on a Saturday morning, then dipped in for twenty-minute drives across the week and never once felt behind. That's the trick with Horizon: it's a game you can put down for a month and pick up like you never left.

bestFor: Anyone who wants to drive down a Japanese mountain road at sunset and cry a bit
Racing fans who like a chill sim floor, not a punishing one
People who need a game they can put down for a month and return to easily
watchFor: It's a genuinely huge game; you can drown in the menus if you let yourself
Online is fun but the AI drivers are still the ones you'll do the most driving with
You will 100% download a wildly inappropriate custom livery, no matter your age
reviewBasis: Played solo on PC with a wheel for two of us and a controller for the third, across evenings and Saturday mornings when the kids were watching cartoons.

title: Cairn
deck: A survival-climbing game about pitons, patience, and how many times a middle-aged spine can betray you before dinner.
verdictTitle: Beautifully mean. We love it.
dadTake: This is the first game to accurately simulate looking at a shelf and pulling something in our back.
verdict: Cairn is a deliberate, tense, quietly beautiful game about going up a mountain that does not want you. Every hold matters. Every piton counts. It's the sort of game we thought we didn't have the patience for anymore, and then it grabbed us by the collar and taught us that we did.
overview: You play Aava, staring up at Mount Kami, which is a mountain that has never been summited and, from the look of it, has strong opinions about being summited. Then you plan the route. Then you climb. Then you sit at a ledge and stare at the drop and take a breath before the next section, which is when the game gets its hooks in. The Game Bakers make deliberate, moody things, and this is the most deliberate one yet.

Mechanically it's a resource game as much as a climbing sim. You've got limited pitons, limited stamina, and a whole mountain to spend them on, and every pitch is a question about how much to spend now vs. what you'll need higher up. It's slow in the best way, and every risk you take has an actual consequence. This is not a game you play with a podcast on. It's a game you play with your mouth slightly open.
facts: You play as Aava, taking on Mount Kami, a peak the game insists has never been climbed.
From The Game Bakers, who made Furi and Haven, which tells you the mood.
Every ascent is a resource puzzle: pitons and stamina you cannot get back.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I fell. Then I fell again.
lenses.headline: The mountain doesn't care about me personally.
lenses.body: I tried to climb by vibe and the mountain politely disagreed. I watched the other two play for a while and I can report that the animation of a piton going in is 'weirdly satisfying,' which is high praise from a man who bounced off Death Stranding twice. I'll come back on a weekend for the calm bits.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: A mountain that rewards drawing the ascent on paper.
lenses.body: I drew the whole first face on graph paper and picked my piton spots before I started. It worked, which was worse for everyone else than if it hadn't. Cairn is a game about spending resources you can't refund on a route you can't redo, and I'm a man who lives for exactly that decision.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: It's slow, and that's why it's good.
lenses.body: You'll spend forty minutes on one pitch and then twenty minutes staring at the horizon before you start the next one. That's the game. I found it genuinely calming after a long week, which surprised me, because I'd mostly assumed a climbing game would give me neck ache. It does, but in a good way.

bestFor: Anyone who liked the pace of Death Stranding but wanted less package logistics
Solo players who want a game to slow their pulse, not spike it
People who own a nice pair of headphones and rarely use them
watchFor: Deliberately slow; if you want power fantasy this is the wrong hobby
Falls take you meaningfully backwards, which is the whole point
You will crick your neck looking up at your monitor; blame ergonomics, not the game
reviewBasis: Played solo on PC by two of us across several evenings, with the third briefly picking it up, refusing to plan a route, and paying for it. Details cross-checked against the game's Steam listing.

title: Hollow Knight: Silksong
deck: The sequel we've been waiting for since our kids could barely walk, and it finally arrived in a mood.
verdictTitle: Worth it. Also cruel.
dadTake: The wait was years. Our first boss took slightly longer.
verdict: Silksong turned up, drop-kicked us, and refused to apologise. It's a bigger, meaner, more musical follow-up to Hollow Knight, and the moment-to-moment combat is easily the best-feeling thing Team Cherry have ever made. It also assumes you enjoy being pattern-tested at 11pm, which we do, mostly.
overview: We waited so long for Silksong that one of our kids learned to read in the interim. Then it dropped, and by the end of the first evening we'd already died to something that made a haunting flute noise and taken it personally. The whole kingdom is drawn like a painted playbill and animated like it hates you a little. We adore it.

The core loop is Metroidvania in the classic sense: explore, get whipped, learn a new movement trick, go back to the room that whipped you and whip it. Hornet moves differently to the Knight; she's faster, more acrobatic, and a lot less forgiving on early enemies. The rewards for hanging in there are the same beautiful, patient discoveries we loved before, just harder to reach.
facts: The direct sequel to Hollow Knight, arrived after a very long silence from Team Cherry.
You play as Hornet, whose kit is quicker and more aerial than the original protagonist's.
The setting is a haunted kingdom 'ruled by silk and song,' and the score matches the pitch.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The first proper boss ate my dinner.
lenses.body: I don't enjoy being embarrassed. Silksong embarrassed me at the second real boss, so I went and played a farming game for a bit. I respect the craft. I also have bedtimes, and Silksong doesn't care about bedtimes. I'll come back. Maybe in a patch. Maybe in a week.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: The tightest platformer on the shelf
lenses.headline: Every screen is a pattern-recognition puzzle I was born for.
lenses.body: I learned Hornet's dash timings in an evening and I've been unbearable ever since. Silksong is designed for players who read enemy animations like sheet music, and I was already fluent in the language from the first game. I'm happy. Nobody else is allowed near my save. I'm speedrunning bits I'm not supposed to have reached yet.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: It's a lot and I love it
lenses.headline: Magnificent. Also, be honest with your schedule.
lenses.body: This isn't a game you dip into for half an hour after work; it wants your full attention or it'll punish you politely. I love it, but I play it in longer stretches at weekends, when the kids are elsewhere. If your gaming windows are tiny, buffer this one for the school holidays.

bestFor: Metroidvania sickos who wanted the sequel to be harder, not easier
Anyone who owns a nice controller and wants to justify it
People who miss the first Hollow Knight and are ready to bleed a bit
watchFor: Difficulty is meaningfully harder than the original, especially early
It expects long sessions to click; short bursts will feel punishing
The soundtrack will follow you into the shower; consider yourself warned
reviewBasis: Two of us are deep into the mid-game on PC, one of us bounced off the second boss and is currently in denial about it. All on keyboard, which was a mistake for one of us.

title: Hades II
deck: The sequel to the thing we all played too much of, only now it's got witchcraft and even fewer excuses to stop.
verdictTitle: Supergiant is unfair to the rest of us.
dadTake: One more run means one more argument with a Titan and one more cold coffee.
verdict: Hades II picks up exactly where Hades left off, which is to say we've barely slept since it launched. The build variety is deeper, the story does that thing where every NPC has an opinion about you by run three, and the combat still feels like the tightest thing in the genre. If you liked the first one, this is not a question.
overview: You die, you talk to a witch, you go back out, you die again, and somewhere around run ten a story beat lands unexpectedly and you decide you're never leaving the house again. Supergiant have taken everything that made Hades work and put it under a magical greenhouse. The dark sorcery angle isn't just window dressing; the new magic layer adds a whole extra thing to think about, which for us means whispering 'oh no' when we forget.

Mechanically it's a roguelike, and mechanically it's the best-tuned one on the shelf. Every weapon has its own rhythm, every boon reshapes the run, and going up against the Titan of Time means the shape of a run itself is baked into the combat. That's a lot of systems for a tired brain, but the game keeps them clear at all times. It's ludicrously well made.
facts: Sequel to a roguelike we already lost multiple summers to, which felt personal.
Adds a magic system that reshapes runs before combat even starts.
Fully released after a long stint in early access, so it's already been polished into a shine.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The dialogue pulled me back in for one more run, twice.
lenses.body: I don't like roguelikes. I also don't put Hades II down. The trick is that every death you learn something the story wanted you to know anyway, so it never feels like a lecture. I've got a favourite NPC now. I'm not telling the other two who. I'm protecting the peace.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The best-designed action roguelike on the shelf.
lenses.body: I watched one run and started sorting the boon tree in my head. Every weapon has an identity, every gear pick has a job, and the new magic layer means the pre-combat choices now matter as much as the combat itself. I'm insufferably happy. I'm also cranky that nobody else is building around my favourite weapon.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Runs are still 30-ish minutes, which is why we're doomed.
lenses.body: The sensible thing about Hades II is the run length. The evil thing is that dying takes ten seconds and starting again takes zero, which means one more run is a lie you tell yourself six times. I tapped out around 1am on a Tuesday and blamed the game, which I maintain is fair. I was back in the next night.

bestFor: Anyone who lost a summer to Hades and would like to lose another one
Roguelike heads who want a story that keeps up with the build variety
People whose bedtime is negotiable when a boss says something spicy
watchFor: It's a sequel first and an on-ramp second; play the original if you haven't
'One more run' is not a suggestion, it's a diagnosis
A late-game boss will humble you and you will come back for more
reviewBasis: Played on PC by all three of us since launch, with two of us clearing the main story and the third still stuck on the same weapon and refusing to admit it.

title: Exovia
deck: A factory sim in zero-G, which means the wrenches float and the conveyor belts don't exist, and honestly that's the whole pitch.
verdictTitle: Factory building minus the ground and minus the panic.
dadTake: Build a base in zero-G, misplace every wrench in three dimensions.
verdict: Exovia is the version of factory sims one of us has been asking for since Factorio: no fail state, no fires, no biters yelling at the fence. Just a chunk of asteroid and a slow, obsessive attempt to figure out how logistics work when there is no floor. It could be the best late-night decompression game of the show. If the camera controls are functional, we're in.
overview: Watch the trailer and the first thing you notice is that nothing is stacked. Machines float. Wrenches float. Presumably a dad in a spacesuit floats. The pitch is a factory sim built around procedurally generated asteroids in zero gravity, and the elevator description alone made two of us open a new tab. This is either the calmest sandbox game of the year or the point at which we admit we cannot think in three dimensions anymore.

The design deliberately strips out threat. There's no attack wave, no time bomb, no clock. Asteroid seeds are shareable, so the challenge is comparing solutions instead of racing them. Floating layouts replace conveyor belts, which sounds calm until you try to picture what an efficient one looks like without a floor. The whole thing lives or dies on the camera and the placement previews. If those work, we're building a base that has no business existing.
facts: Factories are built in zero-G around procedurally generated asteroids, per the studio.
Asteroid seeds are shareable, so you can compare setups with another player.
There is no time pressure, no danger, and no fail state. On purpose.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Removing the fail state removes the reason I usually quit.
lenses.body: I've bounced off every factory game the other two have handed me, because I can't handle watching a base burn while I'm in the wrong menu. Take the threat away and suddenly I'm willing to spend an hour figuring out how ore gets from A to B. The one landmine is the 3D camera. If I have to fight it, I'm out before I've built the second machine.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: Six degrees of freedom, I'm already sold
lenses.headline: Zero-G should add constraints, not just remove floor tiles.
lenses.body: A factory sim without a floor is either genuinely new or a chore with a fancy skybox. I want zero-G to change how throughput actually behaves. I also managed to invoke Descent within thirty seconds of the trailer, because of course six degrees of freedom got me. If the third dimension is where the puzzle actually lives, I'm writing an unnecessary essay by Sunday.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A calmer factory sim is a genuinely nice idea.
lenses.body: I can already see this replacing whatever I play when I can't handle another RPG boss. Shareable seeds mean I can send a screenshot to the other two and get judged, which is my favorite kind of accountability. My concern is milestones. Without a fail state, a factory sim needs visible reasons to keep playing. If the game has those, it's in my rotation. If not, it's a nice weekend.

bestFor: Factory-sim fans who are tired of everything trying to kill them
Anyone who can genuinely visualize things in three dimensions (not us, but good for them)
Players who trade base screenshots the way other people trade recipes
watchFor: The 3D camera being a friend, not the boss fight
Meaningful goals when nothing is trying to burn down your base
Whether zero-G actually changes throughput or is scenery
reviewBasis: Not a hands-on impression. This is us reacting to Exovia's Steam page and its listing in the official PAX West 2025 Steam event page. Its Indie MEGABOOTH branding was not separately verified.

title: Akiiwan: Relaxing Survival
deck: A survival game where the wildlife would prefer you left it alone and the moon changes what's growing this month.
verdictTitle: A survival game where nothing is trying to kill you first.
dadTake: Survival crafting for people who would prefer the trees not scream.
verdict: Akiiwan is aimed squarely at every dad who wants to gather berries in the woods without a wolf immediately trying to end his weekend. Handcrafted biomes, a moon that shifts the whole map, no minimap, and animals that mostly ignore you unless you push. It's the kind of survival pitch we've been quietly hoping someone would attempt. The tone is the whole product.
overview: The trailer opens on a lake, a moon, and a soundtrack that is very obviously not stock. It is, according to the studio, field-recorded from Canada's North, and it sounds like it. There's you, a landscape, and a genuinely peaceful survival loop. Half the appeal is what's not in the pitch: no threat meter, no invading horde, no camp attack at three in the morning.

The mechanics that are there include shifting biomes tied to the moon, wildlife that stays out of your way unless heavily provoked, and no minimap. That last one is the interesting swing. It forces you to actually remember where you left your camp instead of following a GPS pin. The whole thing works if the world reads clearly enough that navigation feels like exploring rather than being genuinely lost. That is the specific thing we're watching.
facts: Biomes are handcrafted and change with each new moon, per the studio.
There is no minimap; navigation is done by landmarks.
Soundscapes use field recordings from Canada's North, and the wildlife mostly leaves you alone.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I'm actually asking about this one
lenses.headline: 'No wolves' is my headline feature.
lenses.body: I've been kicked out of every survival game the other two have made me try by an animal I didn't see coming. A game where I can gather firewood at my own pace without getting mauled is the first survival pitch I've ever been genuinely interested in. I'm still going to get lost without a minimap. But I'll do it in a good mood, which is a first for me and this genre.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: Reading the map is the strategy
lenses.headline: No compass turns landmarks into a real tool.
lenses.body: I'm suspicious of relaxing survival as a genre, because usually it means 'we removed the challenge.' Here the challenge is just a different one. It's spatial memory, moon cycles, and reading which biome is doing what this month. If the moon actually changes routes and resources in meaningful ways, that's a system I want to learn. If it's cosmetic, this becomes wallpaper.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A survival loop that fits at the end of a long day.
lenses.body: I want games I can play when I'm already tired, and this looks purpose-built for that. Field recordings and gentler wildlife are exactly the vibe. My only concern is long-term goals. Without a threat pushing you forward, the game needs milestones or the calm eventually becomes doing chores in a forest. If those hold up, I'm keeping it installed all winter.

bestFor: Survival fans who want the survival, not the constant near-death
Players who navigate by memory and don't need a mini-arrow
Anyone who ends the day wanting a quiet forest and a purpose
watchFor: Orientation options when there's genuinely no map to fall back on
Long-term goals once you've got food, fire, and a roof
Whether the shifting moon actually changes the game or is atmosphere

title: Fractured Blooms
deck: A cozy life sim about restoring a house, growing crops, and slowly realizing the day is not actually ending.
verdictTitle: Cozy chores weaponized by a time loop.
dadTake: Cozy farming, but Tuesday is broken and possibly watching.
verdict: Fractured Blooms is doing the exact kind of tonal ambush we love in principle and worry about in practice. Life-sim comfort like house repair, gardening, cooking, and caring for people, all inside a time loop that turns each ordinary task into a slowly building question. Serenity Forge has a track record of committing to a mood. If the loop actually changes what a chore means, this is one of the show's more interesting pitches. If it doesn't, it's cozy with an asterisk.
overview: Angie restores a neglected house, grows crops, cooks meals, and looks after the people inside. That is the entire opening ten minutes and it's genuinely inviting. You can see the cozy game inside. Then the day loops. Then it loops again. Whatever comfort was in that first day starts working differently, and the game becomes an unnerving question about which chores you're really doing and for whom. The studio describes it as inspired by a true story, which is a phrase you don't drop lightly.

The whole thing rides on the loop being more than a gimmick. If Tuesday resets exactly the same every time, comfort turns to homework and dread turns to a jump scare. If the reset changes what a repeated task means (same garden, different implication) that's a real trick, and the cozy-turned-uneasy shape earns its rent. Care will matter here. So will pacing. We're pulling for the good version.
facts: The daily loop covers house restoration, farming, cooking, and caregiving.
A time loop turns the cozy chore loop into the story structure.
The studio describes the project as inspired by a true story.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Familiar chores get me in the door.
lenses.body: A cozy shape is one I'll open on a Sunday afternoon without asking questions. What I don't want is a sudden gearshift into content that ambushes me halfway through the second chapter. If the studio's honest about the tone from the box art, I'm here for it. If it plays coy and then punches me in the sternum, I'm closing it and going back to my farming game.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Repeated days need to grow the plan.
lenses.body: A time loop is only interesting if what I learn on Monday changes what I do on the next Monday. I want information to be the real resource: knowing which pot boils over, which person walks past at 4pm, which choice unlocks a conversation next cycle. If it's the same day rendered with different lighting, the format falls apart. If it's cumulative, I'm playing the whole thing in one weekend.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: This is not a background game.
lenses.body: Life sims usually get to be a second-screen activity for me. This one doesn't. The whole point is paying attention to what changes between loops, and I know that going in. I'm ready to give it a real evening. My job is working out whether the payoff earns that attention. If the game handles the material with care, I'll finish it.

bestFor: Life-sim players who want the cozy stuff to actually mean something
Narrative fans who like learning through repetition
Players who don't need a warning that a game will make them feel things

Whether each loop changes enough to justify running it again
The true-story framing being handled with care

title: Moros Protocol
deck: A memoryless soldier wakes up on a haunted spaceship that reshuffles itself every run and is full of guns from 1997.
verdictTitle: Roguelite retro FPS with an actual look.
dadTake: The ship is haunted, the guns are loud, and bedtime was an hour ago.
verdict: Moros Protocol is the kind of pitch that gets all three of us leaning forward. Retro FPS crunch (chunky pixel textures, low-poly corridors) inside a roguelite that reshuffles the ship between runs. Combine that with augments and found weapons that actually reshape a loadout and you've got a genuinely good hook. It launched during the show, per the store page, which turns anticipation into 'when do we buy it.'
overview: The Orpheus is dead in space, its lights are on, and something on it isn't happy to see you. You wake up without your memory, which is a video-game problem so old it comes with its own retirement plan. The visual language is late-90s FPS by way of a very deliberate art director: crunchy pixel textures, low-poly geometry, corridors that look like a haunted level from a game you owned on a demo disc. That look is doing a lot of the pitch on its own.

Under it is a roguelite. The Orpheus reshuffles its corridors between runs, weapons are found rather than assumed, and augments change what a loadout can even attempt. That's the ingredient that separates it from nostalgic score chases. If augments only bump damage up a bit, it's a shooter with a checkpoint problem. If they actually change how a room gets cleared (mobility build here, sniper build there) we're all installing it the same night.
facts: The Orpheus reshuffles its corridor layout between runs, per the studio.
The look is a specific combo of low-poly geometry and crunchy pixel textures.
Weapons and augments together shape each run's loadout.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I need the game to not laugh at me
lenses.headline: Retro speed only works if failure is fast.
lenses.body: I haven't beaten a Doom-anything since Doom II, and this one looks meaner. What I need is enemies I can read at a glance and difficulty options that let me keep pushing without redoing the same three rooms fourteen times. If I've got to memorize corridor patterns to survive, I'm out inside a night. If a run stays interesting on the first attempt, I'll do a few more.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: Augments have to change my plans
lenses.headline: The loadout is the reason to keep running.
lenses.body: I respect the retro FPS layer, but the roguelite is where I live. I want an augment that flips my priorities. One that turns me from a slow tank into a mobility build, or makes a specific weapon suddenly the only correct choice. If the augment tree is +damage, +ammo, +health, I'll play once and move on. If a run's identity shifts by pickup, I've got a priorities spreadsheet by run three.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Short bursts, big volume; that's my exact evening.
lenses.body: A run-based FPS is basically designed for the window between the kids being asleep and me passing out on the couch. My main worry is boss checkpoint policy. If the loop is 'die at the boss, restart the whole ship,' I'm playing it twice and shelving it. If the game respects that I've only got forty minutes, this is a serious rotation candidate.

bestFor: Retro FPS fans who want procedural teeth on their nostalgia
Roguelite players who prefer aim over deck building
Anyone who reads 'derelict warship' and immediately opens the store page
watchFor: Whether early rooms feel new after a few runs
Difficulty and accessibility for players outside the retro FPS crowd
How much a single augment can actually change a run

title: Voidsayer
deck: A dark monster-tamer with a hundred-plus creatures, gear on every one, and a world already losing to the Abyss.
verdictTitle: Monster-taming with the lights turned down.
dadTake: Catch monsters, fight oblivion, try to remember which dad named the frog Terry.
verdict: Voidsayer is the darker, meaner cousin of the monster-tamer we all associate with elementary school. A hundred-plus tameable creatures, gear on top, evolution on top of that, and a world that isn't waiting for you to catch up. The tone alone is enough to make us curious. Whether it stays interesting depends on the roster having actual role differences, not a hundred copies of the same fire dog.
overview: Watching the trailer, the first thing you notice is the mood. The Abyss is eating the world. You are not, in this game, cheerfully collecting friends. You are recruiting soldiers for a fight the world is already losing. That is a solid premise. It's the kind of setup that makes a hundred-plus creature roster feel like a purpose instead of a checklist. The question is how many of those creatures actually feel different in a fight.

Under the tone is a genuinely deep tamer. Gear on every monster. Evolution paths on top of that. Procedural events and challenges across an interconnected map so you can't just memorize a single dominant team. That's a good frame; it turns team-building into a real, changing problem. Our only worry is the grind. If evolving and gearing three teams for three encounter types requires a spreadsheet and an evening we don't have, this becomes a game we admire from a distance.
facts: The roster runs to more than 100 tameable monsters, per the studio.
Monsters can equip gear and go through evolutions.
Procedural events and challenges vary the interconnected world map.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: A hundred is a lot of names
lenses.headline: Roster size is a promise and a threat.
lenses.body: I'm fine catching monsters. I'm not fine reading a menu of gear stats on a hundred of them. What I want is a filter that says 'this is who you should use for the next thing' and then lets me get on with it. If the game hands me roles and recommendations early, I can enjoy the collection. If it dumps a spreadsheet on me, I'll pick five monsters and never touch the rest.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Roster construction should punish universal squads.
lenses.body: This is my catnip. I want encounters that break a lazy party: a boss that ignores your one killer strategy, an area whose weather flips your damage type, a procedural event that penalizes the exact combo you've been leaning on. If the game actually forces roster rebuilds, gear and evolution turn into real tools. If it doesn't, a small set of monsters solve everything and the hundred is decoration.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A darker tone alone can carry a long campaign.
lenses.body: Most monster-tamers still read like a Saturday morning cartoon, and this one doesn't. That mood is enough to get me interested. What I want next is procedural events that actually stay memorable. If every random encounter is the same three problems, the campaign goes flat. If a run gives me three or four moments worth texting the other two about, I'll finish the whole thing.

bestFor: Monster-tamer fans who want gear and evolution to be real levers
RPG players comfortable rebuilding a party for a new problem
Anyone who thinks the genre could use a lot less sunshine
watchFor: Menu clarity when your roster crosses into three digits
Grinding needed to swap in an alternate team
Whether procedural events give you memorable stories, not just alternate stats

title: Letter Lost
deck: You work in a post office where room and board are included, leaving is not encouraged, and the employee handbook keeps a suspiciously friendly face.
verdictTitle: The employee handbook is the monster.
dadTake: Neither rain nor snow nor implied cult will stop this delivery.
verdict: Letter Lost has the best kind of horror hook: one where the scariest sentence in the trailer is a workplace policy. Sort mail. Live at the post office. Do not leave. The whole thing is going to work if the paperwork itself becomes evidence, if a return address is suddenly wrong, if a shift ends and the light hasn't changed. The mail loop has to be genuinely satisfying for the horror to bite. That's the whole game.
overview: Wistvale Post Office. Kharnym Isle. You stamp, sort, and deliver. Room and board are provided, which is mentioned three times in the first minute of the trailer in a tone that gets slightly less friendly each time. If you have ever worked in a job where the HR pamphlet was oddly emphatic about company loyalty, you already understand the game. The horror isn't a monster. It's the phrase 'mandatory room and board' delivered with a smile.

The mechanical loop is post office work. Stamp, sort, deliver. That's it, and that has to be the pleasure. A game like this only works if the routine is comfortable enough that the wrong envelope, the wrong route, the wrong postmark becomes a specific gut punch. The design ask is that the mail itself becomes evidence: that being good at your job is how you notice the job is wrong. If it lands, this is one of the smartest horror pitches at the show.
facts: The work loop is stamping, sorting, and delivering mail, per the studio.
Employees receive mandatory room and board on-site.
Friendly corporate language is used to conceal restrictive rules.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Doing a task calms me down enough to notice the horror.
lenses.body: I don't want a chase sequence. I want a job. Sorting mail is exactly the kind of thing my brain accepts as relaxing while the actual game unnerves me underneath. I'll play a shift, notice one thing that feels off, and text the other two about it. That's a good sign. If the horror escalates to running, I'm passing the controller and going to get a drink.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Sorting has to teach me the rules.
lenses.body: A workplace horror only pays off if the work is the puzzle. I want a return address I can question, an internal memo that contradicts yesterday's, a route that quietly gets shorter. If the letters carry information I can piece together, this is a genuinely smart game. If the mystery's happening in cutscenes while I stamp envelopes, it's two disconnected things.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Contained horror with a routine to hold onto.
lenses.body: A closed setting and a job to do is a horror shape I'll actually finish. I can picture playing this in one long Saturday-night sitting, quietly getting more uneasy. My only concern is variety. If a shift is the same envelopes and the same route for seven hours, the routine numbs the fear. New letters, new anomalies, new small changes have to keep coming.

bestFor: Horror fans who prefer psychological pressure to jump scares
Anyone who has ever read an HR pamphlet with real suspicion
Puzzle players who like their evidence hidden in ordinary paperwork
watchFor: The mail loop staying interesting on the fifth shift
How rule contradictions are surfaced without breaking clarity
Whether the mystery gets a resolution or just an atmosphere

title: Sky of Tides
deck: Nine floating realms hanging over a molten sun, nine fully voiced episodes, and a protagonist deciding who she gets to be in each one.
verdictTitle: A narrative RPG on a genuinely broken world.
dadTake: The world literally broke into nine chunks. Great news for anyone who hates a normal map.
verdict: Sky of Tides has the two things a narrative RPG has to have: a world you want to walk around in and a shape you can commit to. Nine floating realms above a molten inner sun is the kind of setting most games hint at once and back away from. This one lives in it. Nine voiced episodes give it a runtime we can plan around. The whole thing works if the risk and discovery choices leave marks.
overview: The world is called numen9. It is nine floating realms above a molten inner sun, and if that sentence didn't already sell it to you, we can't help you. Rin D'Lorah is our protagonist. She travels between the realms, has real choices to make about who she is in each one, and (crucially) is fully voiced across all nine episodes. That episode structure is the reason we can actually imagine finishing this.

The system pitch is that dialogue, discovery, and risk choices all leave marks on Rin and on the realms she's moving through. That's the promise. The reality has to be that a choice made in episode two is still audible in episode seven. Most narrative RPGs quietly forget you shifted an alliance the moment the next arc begins. If Sky of Tides remembers, it's the kind of thing our group chat argues about for a month. If it doesn't, it's still a nice place to visit.
facts: The world numen9 is nine floating realms above a molten inner sun.
The story is told across nine fully voiced episodes.
Dialogue, discovery, and risk choices are described as leaving marks on Rin and the world.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: Voice-acting is a green light for me
lenses.headline: Episodes let me breathe.
lenses.body: I'm not going to sit down for a forty-hour campaign. I am happy to sit down for one voiced episode and work out whether I want a second. That episode shape is the reason I'll open the game at all. My one worry is lore density. If the first hour drops thirty proper nouns on me, I'll politely close the tab. If the first episode teaches me gently, I'm staying.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I want receipts on the choices
lenses.headline: A choice is only a choice if something breaks.
lenses.body: Narrative RPGs love saying 'your choices matter.' I love calling them on it. If picking a side in episode two closes a door in episode six, that's a real system. If picking a side changes one line of dialogue and everything else proceeds identically, the game's theater. I'll have worked out which one this is by episode three, and I'll tell the other two in unnecessary detail.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Nine chapters I can actually schedule.
lenses.body: Full-voiced episodes with clear breakpoints are exactly the RPG structure I stick with. I can play one on a Sunday, put it down for a week, come back and pick it up. My concern is whether the world holds together across the pauses. If each episode's memorable enough to text about, I finish the whole thing. If they blur, I lose the thread at chapter five.

bestFor: Narrative RPG fans who care about world first and stats second
Players who need genuine episode breaks to finish a story
Anyone who reads 'molten inner sun' and immediately wants to visit
watchFor: Terminology density in the first episode
Whether an early choice is still visible five episodes later
Pacing across nine chapters, with no soft middle

title: Adaptory
deck: Four crew members, one deserted planetoid, and a base whose plumbing keeps working whether you understand it or not.
verdictTitle: A colony sim where the air has physics.
dadTake: A colony sim where even the air has a spreadsheet.
verdict: Adaptory is doing the interesting thing colony sims usually shy away from: capping the labor pool. Four crew members forever. As the base grows, automation stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the entire plan. Layer in a physics and chemistry simulation that tracks temperature, density, phase changes, and every crew member's nose running when the CO2 scrubber breaks, and you've got a game with genuinely stakes-y decisions. This one could go either way. We're rooting for it.
overview: Four explorers. One planetoid. No rescue ship. That's the whole opening pitch, and it's got the kind of clean constraint we like. The crew doesn't grow. You never recruit a replacement. Every job someone is doing manually is a job that isn't happening somewhere else in the base. So the game is really about automating your way out of a labor crisis before your labor pool collapses under the weight of the paperwork.

The trick is that the simulation is doing real work. Temperature, density, viscosity, phase changes, and gravity all get modeled, which sounds like a threat until you realize it's also the point. Pipes matter. Rooms matter. A room being one degree too warm actually cascades. If the game keeps that readable without turning into a chemistry midterm, this is a great one. If the physics is only interesting when it's failing, we're all learning viscosity at 11pm on a Tuesday.
facts: Each game starts with four procedurally generated crew members, per the studio.
The simulation models gravity, temperature, density, viscosity, and phase changes.
The crew size stays fixed, which makes automation the actual survival plan.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: The crew is what I'll care about
lenses.headline: Four people beat five hundred.
lenses.body: Colony sims usually lose me because I don't remember which of the 47 people is dying. Four crew members with names I can actually track is the version I can play. My worry is the physics. If a phase change cascade needs me to understand what a phase change is, I'll shrug and let it happen. The game needs alerts that tell me what to fix, not why it broke.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Fixed crew makes every task a real cost.
lenses.body: This is my favorite kind of constraint. When there's no way to hire more hands, every manual chore costs something concrete, and automation stops being an efficiency toy and becomes the plan. I want a simulation that punishes procrastination: a boiler that'll actually explode if I ignore it, not a warning that resolves itself. If the physics has teeth, I'm already sketching an automation plan on the back of a receipt.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A big sim you have to actually sit with.
lenses.body: This isn't the game I open for twenty minutes. I know that going in. What I want is a campaign shape that gives me milestones: a specific goal each session, a visible bit of progress each week. Without that, physics-heavy sims collapse into maintenance. With it, this is the six-month project I bore the other two about at length.

bestFor: Colony-sim players who want the physics to actually behave like physics
Automation planners who like being told they can't just hire more people
Players who read 'phase changes' and get excited instead of confused
watchFor: Alerts and overlays when the simulation starts cascading
Early-game teaching for anyone who last studied thermodynamics in 1997
Campaign pacing once basic survival is on autopilot

title: Sashimi Slayer
deck: Rhythm parries against fish, three levels of it, and an open-source sword controller that turns your living room into a hazard zone.
verdictTitle: The sword is the hook. Timing is the whole game.
dadTake: We came for the sword controller. We stayed until our shoulders quit.
verdict: Sashimi Slayer is exactly the game we'd walk past at a show floor and immediately want to try. Rhythm parries, clean cuts, three levels of it, and an open-source sword controller that turns the whole thing into a performance. The trick is that the same timing has to satisfy on a standard controller for the game to have a life outside of PAX. If it does, this is a genuinely fun small game. If it doesn't, it's a great convention memory.
overview: You duel fish. Bring the sword down at the right moment, parry the right beat, and reduce a sashimi-adjacent aquatic threat to its component parts. Three levels, hand-drawn art, original music. The trailer is what happens when someone commits fully to a bit, and honestly we love it. If any of us had actual triceps left, we'd already own the controller.

The specific feature that makes us pay attention is that the sword controller is open source. Which means the hardware isn't just a novelty; it's a project you can build. That's a genuinely charming design choice. What the studio still has to prove is that the core loop reads just as well on a normal controller for anyone who isn't going to solder together a beam-based hilt. Three levels can support real replay if the enemy patterns push past memorization.
facts: Combat is built on rhythm-timed parries and cuts, per the studio.
The physical sword controller design is open source.
The game ships with three levels, hand-drawn art, and original music.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I liked the trailer, haven't checked the price yet
lenses.headline: Swinging at fish explains itself.
lenses.body: I get it in eight seconds. I don't need a rhythm-game tutorial to understand a sword. My only concern is whether it's fun with a normal controller, because I'm not building a peripheral in the garage. If the timing feels right on a gamepad, I'll play a level or two on a Sunday. If it demands the sword to work, I'm out.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Three levels is enough only if the patterns keep growing.
lenses.body: Rhythm games live and die on whether the top of the skill curve is real. Three levels can absolutely support a serious ceiling if late patterns require reading and reaction, not memorization. I want a scoring layer that rewards precision, not luck. If I can shave a hundredth of a second off a parry and see it show up in a number, I'm playing this for weeks.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A physical controller is a home run at get-togethers.
lenses.body: This is the game that gets pulled out at a barbecue, and everyone who tries it has fun for exactly one round. What I care about is whether it survives past that first round: whether the standard-controller mode has real content and real replay. If it does, this is a great small game I keep installed. If it doesn't, it's a memory from someone's living room.

bestFor: Arcade rhythm fans who like a visible score chase
Parties or events with room for someone actually swinging a sword
DIY tinkerers who read 'open-source controller' and are already sourcing parts
watchFor: How much content lives inside three levels
Whether standard controls feel as good as the sword
The hardware being available at all outside a show floor

title: No Stone Unturned
deck: A fully voiced British detective comedy that keeps a straight face while investigating the murder of a chicken.
verdictTitle: A chicken murder with actual casework underneath.
dadTake: A chicken is dead. Three dads are already emotionally overinvested.
verdict: No Stone Unturned has a joke premise sitting on top of a genuinely structural detective game. Three linked cases from fairy tales, jokes, and children's stories all feed into A Murder Most Fowl, the chicken murder that gives the game its name. Ten-plus hours, fully voiced. The whole thing works if the humor sharpens observation instead of getting in the way of the actual deduction. If it does, this is a delight. If it doesn't, it's a comedy album with a magnifying glass.
overview: The premise is that a chicken has been murdered. The case, per the studio, is called A Murder Most Fowl. All three of us laughed exactly once at that name, immediately, out of self-respect. Underneath the pun is the actual game: three smaller cases inspired by fairy tales, jokes, and children's stories, each feeding into the central mystery. It is more detective than gag, which is a genuinely good sign for a comedy game.

The pitch is more than ten hours of story with a fully voice-acted cast. British humor is the tone. What we can't tell from the trailer is whether the deduction actually works: whether a stalled case has a hint system that helps, whether a solved case feels earned, whether the humor is doing the heavy lifting or the mystery is. The good version is that the jokes make you pay closer attention. The bad version is that every clue is a setup for a punchline.
facts: Three linked cases from fairy tales, jokes, and children's stories feed into the chicken murder.
The game is fully voice-acted.
Official materials describe more than ten hours of story.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Comedy softens the pressure of being wrong.
lenses.body: I'm genuinely bad at adventure games. I solve nothing. What keeps me playing is when the game's funny about it. A voiced cast making a joke about my terrible theory is a much better failure state than a wrong-answer chime. My one worry is a case stalling. If I'm stuck for twenty minutes without a nudge, I close the game and forget it exists.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: A funny game still needs consistent evidence.
lenses.body: I'm fine with a comedy tone. What I refuse to accept is a whodunnit that hides the answer behind arbitrary logic and then punches me for being reasonable. I want evidence that adds up, suspects who behave like people, and a solution that'd still make sense with the jokes removed. If the game clears that bar, the humor is a bonus. If not, no amount of British charm will save it.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A ten-hour voiced adventure is exactly a Saturday night.
lenses.body: Detective games with real voice acting are my favorite couch pick, because someone can sit next to me and yell theories. I can already picture the spouse-and-dad accusation sessions over the chicken murder. Ten hours is a runtime I can plan around. My concern is comedy repetition. If the same three joke shapes carry the whole thing, hour eight feels tired.

bestFor: Adventure fans who want their comedy voiced, not just written
Couples and small groups who love yelling theories at each other
Anyone who unironically enjoys British humor and storybook parody
watchFor: How generous the hint system is when a case stalls
Whether solutions feel deduced, not delivered
Comedy staying fresh at hour eight of ten
reviewBasis: Not a hands-on impression. This is us reacting to No Stone Unturned's Steam page and its PAX Rising Showcase slot on the official PAX West 2025 Steam event page.

title: Hank: Drowning On Dry Land
deck: A poisoned time-traveling vigilante drowns in spilled beer and takes a half-hour trip through his own subconscious to sort it out.
verdictTitle: Thirty minutes, fully committed to weird.
dadTake: Half an hour of cartoon noir, poison, and a very good reason to hydrate.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Hank has one of our favourite pitches this year: thirty minutes, one clear premise, no attempt to become a franchise. A poisoned vigilante crawling through his own subconscious set to a dark Saturday-morning cartoon is a whole idea. Whether it lands depends entirely on the ending.
overview: Hank is a time-traveling vigilante and he has been poisoned, and yes, his death involves spilled beer. That is the second sentence of the elevator pitch and we already respect it. The escape route runs through his own subconscious instead of a crime scene, which is either a stroke of confidence or a way to keep the art budget down. We haven't played it — we're writing off the store page — but the tone is doing plenty.

The whole thing targets roughly thirty minutes and it's framed like a dark Saturday-morning cartoon. That length is the point, not a shortcoming: a complete idea told once, on a Tuesday night, between dishes and bedtime. It also means tone, pacing and a proper ending have to carry it, because there is nowhere for the game to hide.
facts: The lead is a poisoned time-traveling vigilante trying to survive by walking around his own subconscious.
The visual tone is a dark Saturday-morning cartoon and it is committing to that.
Official runtime is roughly thirty minutes; this is one sitting, on purpose.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Thirty minutes is the correct length for a Tuesday.
lenses.body: I routinely start narrative games and abandon them at hour three. A game that ends before I can lose interest is a very generous thing to design. I need clear interactions and story beats that mean something without a wiki, and I'll almost certainly finish it. That's the highest praise I hand out.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: There's no campaign to optimise, and I'm fine with that.
lenses.body: I respect a game that doesn't ask me to spreadsheet it. Hank is structure, symbolism and pacing, not mastery, and I'm willing to enjoy it as an interactive short instead of an RPG in a trench coat. Whether it earns its half hour comes down to whether the imagery still means something after the credits roll.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A complete idea in the gap between bigger games.
lenses.body: My favourite thing in the world is a game that ends. Between two forty-hour campaigns, Hank is the ideal 8pm-to-8:30pm object. The cartoon-noir framing and unusual death make it easy to remember later, which is more than most short games manage. If the ending lands, I'll be nagging the other two to play it for months.

title: Table Tactics: physics-driven tabletop battles
deck: Forget health bars. You win by using arrows, marbles, fireballs and traps to physically knock the other side's miniatures off the table.
verdictTitle: Miniatures strategy where gravity does the damage.
dadTake: Finally, a strategy game where knocking things over counts as planning.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Table Tactics replaces invisible arithmetic with visible consequences, and that's a real design idea. Weight, shape, position and momentum decide whether a miniature stays upright, giving every move the clarity of a tabletop stunt and the possibility of an unexpected chain reaction. The Descent guy called it before the trailer ended.
overview: The board is a tabletop covered in collectible miniatures. Archers, catapults, mages, traps, marbles and other things that shouldn't be legal push instead of subtract; they apply actual force until something falls over. That's the whole win condition, and we love it. We haven't played it — we're reading the store page during lunch — and one of us is already sketching angle-of-attack diagrams.

Because weight and shape matter, building a roster is partly about physical properties, which is a lovely sentence. Coins earned through play buy and trade miniatures, so the physics puzzle sits on top of a collection layer that gives you a reason to keep prying open packs. It's the first game in ages we've all agreed to try, sight unseen.
facts: You win by knocking the other side's miniatures over, not by draining an HP bar.
Unit weight, shape, position, and applied force all matter to the outcome.
Coins support buying and trading miniatures to build your own roster.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I watched it once and got it
lenses.headline: Falling over is the clearest damage number in games.
lenses.body: I have never once understood a hit-point calculation, and now I don't have to. You aim, you push, the thing falls or it doesn't. That's a whole game explained in ten seconds. A lucky ricochet is going to be one of the funniest things I see all year, provided the aiming controls don't fight me.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I'm drawing angles in the air
lenses.headline: Physics makes positioning matter twice over.
lenses.body: I've been asking for this since roughly forever. A unit's tactical role and its physical body both belong in the plan, and the game rewards setup, angle, force and roster construction without hiding the result behind a spreadsheet. If it holds up, the other two aren't going to hear about anything else from me for a month.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: This is going to generate arguments.
lenses.body: I clocked it immediately: visible outcomes make the game easy to watch, easy to shout about, and easy to remember afterwards. Provided turns stay brisk, Table Tactics could work as both a solo strategy commitment and a reliable pass-the-controller party pick. I'm already saying words like 'Wednesday.'

title: Arcane Eats
deck: Ingredient cards, enchanted cooktops, and impatient customers turn dinner service into a compact turn-by-turn strategy problem.
verdictTitle: A deckbuilder where dinner service is the boss.
dadTake: The dinner rush now has spells and cards, and still no clean spoons.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Arcane Eats gives card play a physical process, which is a rarer thing than it sounds. Ingredients occupy cooktops, tools modify meals, and customers create actual timing pressure. The theme isn't pasted over the deckbuilder; it changes how cards occupy the board and when they become useful.
overview: Every parent in the group chat perked up at 'the dinner service is the boss fight.' That is not a subtle hook and we don't need it to be. Ingredient cards move onto enchanted cooktops instead of resolving as abstract attacks, and energy, timing, tools and customer demands compete for attention across a turn. We haven't opened it — this is off the store page — but the specificity is doing plenty.

The result is part deckbuilder, part service puzzle. A good meal isn't only about the strongest combo; it also has to reach the right customer before patience runs out, which is a very fair test of how any evening actually goes. What the trailer promises is that the kitchen tools aren't cosmetic and every run's problem is a slightly different diner from hell.
facts: Ingredient cards are played onto enchanted cooktops that hold them for time.
Magical kitchen tools modify meals and the cards feeding them.
Customer patience is part of every turn's puzzle, not scenery.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Cooking makes abstract card timing easier to read.
lenses.body: I've bounced off every deckbuilder that expects me to track eight resources. Cooking, at least, I understand from real life: ingredients need time, customers won't wait, spoons run out. The tooltips still have to keep the magical exceptions from swallowing that basic clarity, but the theme's doing the heaviest lifting a theme can do.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Cooktop capacity creates the real decisions.
lenses.body: I'm delighted by cards that become occupied ingredients on a board with capacity limits. Sequencing and layout suddenly matter as much as the deck itself, which isn't how deckbuilders usually work. The best decks should solve different service problems in different ways rather than converge on one efficient recipe. If they do, this stays installed on my machine.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A compact service loop is easy to come back to.
lenses.body: I like a game I can pick up between meetings and put down without regret. The familiar deckbuilder rhythm benefits from a theme that visibly changes the board every turn. Run length and customer variety will decide whether it survives the third week or becomes 'that one thing we tried once.'

title: Draco and the Seven Scales
deck: Top-down dungeons, sea routes, rival captains, and pixel-art piracy where the map you pick actually matters.
verdictTitle: A pirate map that rewards the long route.
dadTake: Pirates, dragons, and a map we will absolutely hold upside down.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Draco and the Seven Scales makes a strong case for putting the ship back into pirate adventure. Different sea routes open different dungeons, items and puzzles, which gives travel a strategic point instead of turning it into loading screens. If the two halves genuinely feed each other, this could be the throwback pick we all quietly wanted.
overview: Draco is a pirate captain trying to save what matters most to him, which is a solid amount of stakes for a pixel-art adventure. The game alternates between top-down exploration on foot and travel by ship across a large world, and the trailer is confident enough about it that we spent a whole coffee break arguing which half we're more excited about. We haven't played it. We're picturing it.

The pitch that got us was route choice. Different passages lead to different dungeons, puzzles and items, so the sea between islands isn't scenery. Rival captains, armadas and sea monsters make the choice pay off or hurt, depending. That's a lot of moving parts, and whether they lock together or drift depends on whether the map keeps meaningful options open past hour six.
facts: Exploration alternates between on-foot top-down adventuring and sailing between islands.
Different sea routes unlock distinct dungeons, items and puzzles.
Boss threats include rival captains, armadas, and honest-to-goodness sea monsters.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I'll find the treasure by accident
lenses.headline: Familiar top-down language means I don't need a manual.
lenses.body: I've played enough top-down adventures to recognise a door. Movement, dungeons and bosses are easy to understand, which means the ship layer needs to add possibility without turning basic getting-around into homework. If I can pick a route and just go, I'm going. If I have to consult a chart, I'm not.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I want routes with a memory
lenses.headline: Navigation choices need to actually stick.
lenses.body: I'm watching one thing: whether the route I pick changes what I see later. Multiple sea routes are worth something when they gate resources, equipment and future options in ways that persist. If every path eventually becomes mandatory, the map is just a checklist, and I'll say so at length.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A strong genre shape with one useful new idea.
lenses.body: I like classic top-down adventure and I don't need it reinvented. Pixel-art dungeons are familiar territory, but sailing that actually means something is exactly the sort of small change that keeps this from feeling like a game I already played in 2011. The balance between land and sea is going to decide the whole thing.

title: Beatdown City Survivors
deck: Zombie survival becomes an immersive-sim toy box where puddles, gas, cars and knife-slippers all count as tactical options.
verdictTitle: A systems-first survivors game with a mean toy box.
dadTake: The city has problems. Your solution is mostly uppercuts and puddles.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Beatdown City Survivors is most convincing when it treats the city as part of the loadout. Electrifying puddles and detonating gas promise better decisions than circling a horde, and weapon crafting gives the run structure a gleefully scrappy identity. Whether the systems stay readable when the screen fills up is the whole game.
overview: The elevator pitch is a survivors-like with an immersive-sim brain, which is not a sentence we expected to write this year. Varied characters drop into a sandbox city full of zombies and mutants where environmental hazards chain together: puddles, electricity, gas, and cars all interact. We haven't played it — this is off the store page — and the systemic promise alone is more interesting than most survivors trailers.

Crafted weapons push the improvisation into cheerful nonsense: knife-slippers, fireworks bazookas, the sort of thing that sounds like a group-chat joke that survived to production. The roster also extends beyond humans into animals and other unusual survivors, which is a very good sign for a game that wants to be systemic instead of grim. If runs earn their punchlines, we're keeping it.

Crafting supports deliberately absurd weapons and synergies — knife-slippers are canon.
The recruitable survivor roster includes humans, animals and other unusual fighters.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I'll start a fire by accident
lenses.headline: The sandbox should teach through obvious cause and effect.
lenses.body: I don't read builds. I do understand that cars explode and puddles conduct electricity, partly from games and partly from a couple of memorable childhood moments. lenses.name: The Tactician

lenses.body: I love the idea that positioning matters because environmental combinations do. Character abilities and crafting should reward setting up a chain — puddle here, gas over there, spark from the correct direction — instead of only scaling damage. If runs all converge on one obvious best combo, I'll be very polite about being disappointed.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The comedy works because the systems back it up.
lenses.body: Silly weapons make for good trailer clips, but my actual reason to come back is finding another interaction I didn't know existed. That's the hook I'd reuse, and it holds up across short evening sessions provided runs reach the interesting choices quickly instead of making me grind through a warmup phase.

title: Terrible Lizards
deck: A dead car and a decaying Route 66 dinosaur attraction turn a 1992 road stop into a horror movie you can't drive out of.
verdictTitle: Roadside Americana with teeth.
dadTake: Road trip rule one: never trust the dinosaur-shaped tourist trap.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Terrible Lizards starts from a location horror games have barely touched: a sun-faded tourist trap built around fake dinosaurs. The missing-child mystery gives us a reason to explore, and 1992 is a smart date because it takes away the exits modern technology usually creates. This is our most 'oh no, and yes' pitch of the week.
overview: The car dies outside Dalton's Dinos, a deteriorating Route 66 attraction in New Mexico. It's 1992, a child is missing, and the creatures stalking the property are more dangerous than the fibreglass statues around them suggest. That's already three of our favourite horror ingredients — bad decade, worse place, real reason to walk further in — and we haven't even opened the game.

The scale is the smartest part of the pitch. It's a contained attraction, an investigation and a chase, not another sprawling apocalypse. That means the location itself is the game's strongest asset, and the trailer is confident enough in the setting that it doesn't try to sell you on the world beyond the parking lot. Which is where every good horror movie stays.
facts: The story is set in 1992: no phones, no rideshares, no easy escape.
Dalton's Dinos is a deserted Route 66 dinosaur attraction in New Mexico.
You're investigating a missing-child case while creatures actively hunt you.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I'll try because the mystery has a shape
lenses.headline: A clear mystery pulls me in where pure survival can't.
lenses.body: I don't play survival horror because the loop punishes me just for existing. A specific mystery gives every scary corridor a purpose, and that's exactly the reason I keep going. Whether I stay depends on generous checkpoints and chases that tell me where safety actually is, because I will absolutely stop if the game punishes me for learning.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I want the monsters to have rules
lenses.headline: The attraction needs mechanics worth learning.
lenses.body: I only respect a memorable monster when its behaviour can be studied and used against it. If every encounter is a scripted sprint, the location carries more weight than the play, which is fine for one playthrough and not a game I replay. I want the fibreglass dinosaurs to have opinions.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The setting sells a focused, seasonal horror night.
lenses.body: A contained roadside attraction is easy to pitch to the other two and different enough that I'll remember it afterwards. I've already got it earmarked for a specific late-October evening once the kids are down. The ideal version stays tight instead of stretching the premise until the dinosaurs stop being scary and start being scenery.

Fans of analog-era stories where you can't call for help
Groups who want one focused seasonal playthrough
