title: Rogue Eclipse
deck: Fast starfighter combat, destructible battlefields, and enormous enemies aim to make even your worst run look spectacular.
verdictTitle: Starfighter spectacle built for another run.
dadTake: Space is vast, beautiful, and apparently full of things that need exploding.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Rogue Eclipse understands the thing most space roguelikes forget: the flying itself has to feel dangerous and fast. Destructible environments and behemoth-scale enemies give its run structure a strong visual reason to exist, and the Arabesque Futurism aesthetic saves it from looking like every other grey military sci-fi. Our concern is the same one we always have with roguelikes at our age.
overview: You're a pilot fighting for humanity's future through repeated arcade-style starfighter runs. That's a sentence we've read a lot, but the trailer sells the specific version well: fights escalate from fighter skirmishes to bumping into an enemy machine roughly the size of a small country. We haven't played it — this is off the store page — and the scale alone is doing sales.

Destructible environments widen the fight, and the visual direction pulls from Arabesque Futurism, which is a rare sentence in a spaceship trailer. The target is speed and spectacle without giving up the build decisions a roguelike lives on. Whether it earns another attempt is the whole test: a beautiful death is only fun the first three times.
facts: Arcade starfighter controls are paired with a repeated roguelike run structure.
Battlefields include destructible environments and enemy behemoths.
The visual world draws on Arabesque Futurism, and it's actually distinctive.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The controls decide whether I get invited.
lenses.body: I've never once enjoyed an arcade space game where I lost track of which way is up. Speed is only exciting if I can still tell where I'm pointing. Strong aim assistance and clear objectives would keep the spectacle available without turning every run into thirty confused seconds. I'll pick up a good arcade shooter. I'm not going to fight the camera.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Blowing things up should change routes, not just particles.
lenses.body: I have an opinion about destructible environments: they're valuable when they change routes, expose weak points, or create cover. Ship upgrades need the same tactical specificity. Give me a new gun that changes how I fight, not a percentage bump to a stat I've already forgotten. Real trade-offs will convince me. Nothing else will.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A clean run length would keep this in rotation.
lenses.body: Space combat and boss scale are easy to come back to, which is exactly why I'm nervous. Roguelikes eat evenings. I want a run to end at a satisfying moment, whether I won or died, so I can walk away without feeling like I owe it another attempt. Otherwise this becomes a weeknight problem.

Roguelike players drawn to visible build progression
Anyone tired of grey military sci-fi aesthetics
watchFor: Reading a fight at high speed without losing your orientation

title: RollerGirl
deck: A broken car, a pair of rollerblades, and a playlist turn a small-town summer into an unusually personal adventure.
verdictTitle: A small-town mixtape with wheels.
dadTake: A broken car, good music, and zero desire to call roadside assistance.
verdict: We haven't played it, but RollerGirl stands out by making music taste part of how the world reads its protagonist. The adventure will live or die on the writing, but its blend of movement, odd jobs, romance and playlist choices gives a familiar summer story a real point of view. It's not aimed at us. That's fine.
overview: Naomi is sixteen, her car has died, and getting around town now means rollerblades. That inconvenience is the door into a slice-of-life adventure built from conversations, odd jobs, romance and a small-town mystery. We haven't played a minute — we're reading the store page — and look, none of us are the target audience for this one, but the specificity of the pitch is doing plenty of work.

Songs are collectible, playlists are editable, and music choices actually change how the world responds. The 2000s-inspired soundtrack isn't just atmosphere; it's one of the main ways the player defines who Naomi is. That's a genuinely fresh mechanic for a genre where 'choice' usually means picking a nicer dialogue option, and it's the reason this one stuck in the group chat.
facts: Playlist choices change how characters and the world react to Naomi.
Collected songs expand the player's available playlists.
The setting mixes rollerblade traversal, odd jobs, romance and a small-town mystery.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I'm fine with a story game
lenses.headline: Movement and conversation are a low-drama way in.
lenses.body: I don't want a combat vocabulary. Conversation and rollerblading is exactly the sort of low-pressure adventure I'll open on a Sunday morning. The important test is whether skating actually feels good enough that traveling between conversations stays pleasant, because if it becomes an errand I will absolutely put the phone down and go weed the garden.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I want the playlist to hit back
lenses.headline: The playlist needs consequences, not just flavour.
lenses.body: I'm politely watching this one from a distance. Music-driven reactions can be a meaningful social system if the choices create trade-offs and reveal character. Without that, collecting tracks is a decorative checklist I'm never going to finish. If a bad playlist really shuts a door on me, I'm more interested than I'd admit out loud.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Specificity is doing the heavy lifting.
lenses.body: The small-town scale and 2000s identity give RollerGirl a mood I respect. It's a change of pace for players who want a focused story between larger releases, and the pitch is honest enough about who it's for that I'm going to recommend it to a handful of people I know before I ever open it myself.

title: Blocks for Babies
deck: Stack blocks in 2D, blast them apart in 3D, then build a roguelite run around the collision between both halves.
verdictTitle: Two genres slam into each other on purpose.
dadTake: Tetris got a shotgun. We have follow-up questions.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Blocks for Babies has a pitch that survives the elevator ride: stack the board, jump into it, shoot the mess you made. The deciding factor is whether upgrades turn that contrast into strategy instead of asking players to alternate between two disconnected minigames. If they do, this is the wildest party demo of the year.
overview: A run switches between arcade block-stacking and first-person shooting, which is one of those sentences we had to read twice. Clearing lines shapes the 2D board; entering it in 3D lets you destroy blocks directly with weapons. We haven't opened it — this is off the store page — but the group chat took roughly forty-five seconds to reach 'okay, when.'

Items, weapons and upgrades are designed to create cross-mode synergies, and bosses test whether the player understands both rule sets. That is the entire game, mechanically: a roguelite built around a mechanical punchline that either deepens or doesn't. We're rooting for it to deepen, because the alternative is a very good demo and a short third hour.
facts: Runs alternate between 2D block-stacking and 3D first-person combat.
Weapons, items and upgrades are designed to create cross-mode synergies.
Boss encounters test mastery of stacking and shooting together, not separately.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The concept explains itself before the title does.
lenses.body: I understand blocks. I understand shooting. Combining the two takes me about eight seconds to grasp and slightly longer to laugh at, which makes the first minute completely painless. The roguelite upgrade layer gets more demanding later, so the game has to earn my second hour on more than the opening gag.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I want the two halves to fuse
lenses.headline: The best runs should start on the stacking screen.
lenses.body: I'll only stay for the version where block placement creates opportunities for the combat phase — where my 2D setup is the reason a 3D room is winnable. If upgrades only raise damage numbers, the two-mode structure loses its reason to exist. This mechanic is either a whole game or a very clever demo.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: This is built for one-more-run handoffs.
lenses.body: Short, visible mistakes and an unusual premise make Blocks for Babies easy to pass around, and I've already flagged it as a game-night surprise. Whether it lasts depends on bosses and build variety keeping the joke from wearing thin. If it becomes 'switch screens for damage,' everyone's going to figure that out fast.

title: Never's End
deck: Possession-based party building gives this open-world tactics game a genuinely different answer to the usual roster problem.
verdictTitle: A tactics sandbox with possession at its centre.
dadTake: Possession: cheaper than recruiting, somehow worse for HR.
verdict: We haven't played it, but Never's End has the kind of central mechanic that can carry an entire campaign: your immortal spirit survives, but the bodies carrying it don't have to. If its weather, terrain, settlements and swappable hosts stay understandable when the battlefield gets busy, this is a top-of-the-year tactics game. The Descent guy has already booked a weekend.
overview: Humanity is almost gone, the Never is spreading, and you're an undying warrior spirit embodied in living silver. That's a lot of scene-setting for a tactics game, and we're here for it. Instead of recruiting a fixed party, you possess townsfolk and drag their abilities into turn-based battles. We haven't played it — we're writing off the store page — and the group chat has been sending each other 'wait, so —' texts for two days.

The open world adds settlements, temples and technology around a combat model that accounts for wind, water, weather and terrain. That combination makes Never's End look less like a chain of puzzle maps and more like a real campaign that produces stories worth telling later. The catch, obviously, is that a stack of interacting systems only stays interesting if you can read what any one of them is doing at a glance.
facts: Possession turns townsfolk into a flexible party-building system with real weight.
Wind, water, weather and terrain are simulated tactical factors, not scenery.
Settlements, temples and technology connect combat to an open-world campaign.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: A great hook still needs a gentle first hour.
lenses.body: I absolutely understand possessing a new host. That part's intuitive on its face. The risk is the stack of elemental, environmental and settlement systems landing on me before I know which decisions actually matter. If the game teaches me one thing at a time, I'll stay. If it opens with a screen full of weather icons, I'm closing it.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: This is the tactics game I want
lenses.headline: The roster is a resource, not a collection screen.
lenses.body: I've been complaining for years that tactics games all give you a fixed cast. A party I can rebuild through possession creates real adaptation. Add weather and terrain, and there are several ways to reward planning beyond raw damage, which is the exact stuff I was going to build a spreadsheet about anyway. I'm in.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The campaign pitch is stronger than any single battle.
lenses.body: Open-world consequences and changing hosts could make Never's End a game worth discussing between sessions, provided the simulation doesn't turn every encounter into a fifteen-minute setup phase. I'm genuinely optimistic here, which I rarely am about tactics games. I want the world to keep changing between sessions, and each battle to end before bedtime.

title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
deck: Turn-based RPG where every dodge is a reflex check, which is a lot to ask of men our age and yet.
verdictTitle: The best surprise of 2025.
dadTake: Finally, a JRPG that also wants you to have Souls reflexes. Great.
verdict: Clair Obscur is the best RPG surprise we've had in years. It looks like a painting, it plays like a rhythm game hiding inside a turn-based one, and it commits to a real story with real stakes. If we'd known a small French studio was cooking this we'd have cleared April ahead of time. Just play it.
overview: Expedition 33 opens on a doomed city, a big number, and a small crew of people volunteering to fix it, and inside fifteen minutes it's very clear this isn't going to be a gentle Saturday afternoon. The world is Belle Époque France run through a pastel filter and then set on fire, and every fight asks you to sit still and pick a move and then, treacherously, dodge in real time. We were not ready for that in Chapter One and we were less ready by Chapter Three.

The trick that makes this work is that turn-based combat gets a live-action layer bolted on top. You queue your action like any RPG, then you have to actually parry or dodge whatever the enemy throws back. It's beautiful and mean and it lands, because the animations are so precise you can read them. Bring reading glasses.
facts: Turn-based combat that adds real-time parry and dodge checks to every round.
The world is inspired by Belle Époque France, which means striking clothes and worse politics.
First game from Sandfall Interactive, which we're pretending to have known about all along.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I liked the parry rhythm more than the party menu.
lenses.body: I normally hard-pass on any game with a stat screen. Clair Obscur got me because the fights themselves are basically a two-note rhythm game, and I can do a two-note rhythm game. I let one of the other two build the party and just showed up to press the dodge button on time. I was suspiciously good at it.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: A turn-based system with real-time enforcement is my happy place.
lenses.body: I clocked that every character's kit is a small optimisation puzzle and immediately made a chart. Enemies telegraph their windups so precisely that I can plan three turns ahead and still parry the counter. I said the word 'clean' out loud. From me that's a five-star review, and I don't hand those out.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: It's a proper long RPG, and it earns every hour.
lenses.body: I was worried it'd be all vibes and no game. It isn't. There's a real story with a real ending and characters I actually cared about by the mid-game, which isn't something I say lightly. Save often, dodge always, and don't try to rush this one. It's better when you let it breathe.

bestFor: RPG folks who wish combat wasn't a menu you fell asleep in
Anyone who loved Persona but wanted more Bloodborne in their turn order
Dads who need proof a debut studio can still ambush the year
watchFor: The parry timing is unforgiving until you learn to read a windup
There is real story here and real death; it isn't a cosy hangout
You will spend one late night arguing about your favourite party member
reviewBasis: Played to the credits on PC by two of us across several weeks, mostly on school nights when the kids were asleep and the parry timing was mostly not.

title: Blue Prince
deck: A puzzle roguelike about drafting rooms into a mansion, which is basically Zillow with a body count and a locked door.
verdictTitle: The best notebook we've filled in years.
dadTake: Real estate has never made us this happy or this confused.
verdict: Blue Prince is the puzzle game that took over our group chat for a full month. It looks polite and then it eats your brain in the nicest possible way, one room at a time. Committing to it means committing to a physical notebook, and honestly that's part of the deal we signed up for.
overview: Every morning at Mt. Holly you wake up, you pick a door, and you place a room. The mansion redraws itself, you find a clue about a bathtub you didn't know existed, and then the day ends and everything resets. We spent our first week losing badly and pretending it wasn't personal. Then one of us cracked and now there's a shared spreadsheet none of the wives are allowed to see.

What makes it work is that everything is a puzzle inside a puzzle. The room draft feels like a light strategy game and then you realise the mansion has an actual mystery underneath it, and that mystery cares about details you noted on day three and forgot about by day nine. The game trusts you to keep up, which is flattering until you don't.
facts: Every morning redraws Mt. Holly from a fresh draft of rooms, so no two mansions are the same.
There's a mystery underneath the mystery, and it's the kind that rewards a real paper notebook.
Absolutely a single-player game, despite spawning at least three private chats in our house.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The mansion doesn't want me, and I agree.
lenses.body: I opened Blue Prince, drew a hallway that led to nothing, and closed Blue Prince. On night two I tried again with a beer and the same thing happened. I'm not the target audience for a game that asks me to write things down. I am, however, the target audience for laughing at the other two writing things down, and I've been eating well.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The best drafting-and-notes game in years.
lenses.body: I haven't been this happy since I first discovered pen-and-paper mysteries. Blue Prince is a drafting game inside a deduction game inside a mansion that keeps reshuffling itself, and I treat it like a job with better hours. I was chasing Room 46 while my eggs went cold. I'd do it again.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: It's a marathon, and worth every hour if you're in the mood.
lenses.body: A single day at Mt. Holly is a bite-sized run, which is friendly for a tired brain. The whole mystery is not bite-sized, and that's fair. I knocked off a couple of days a night for weeks and never resented the pace. If you can't stand keeping notes in a real notebook you'll have a bad time, but if you can, this is the best puzzle game we've played all year.

bestFor: Anyone who owns at least one graph-paper notebook they're proud of
Puzzle solvers who want a mystery big enough to text a friend about
People whose brains are itching for a game to bully them nicely
watchFor: It really does want you to take notes; no notes, no dice
The full mystery is a long haul, not a weekend
You will start describing your actual house in terms of doors and gems
reviewBasis: Played over about a month on PC by two of us, comparing notes in a shared doc that has since become embarrassing to look at. The third dropped in occasionally to laugh.

title: Split Fiction
deck: Two writers get yeeted into their own stories and the only fix is playing swap-the-controller with your best friend.
verdictTitle: Hazelight did it again.
dadTake: Turns out the best fantasy setting is 'someone else has to be player two.'
verdict: Split Fiction is a co-op adventure built to be played with exactly one other person on the couch, which is a heroic assumption for our lives, but boy is it worth clearing an evening for. It swaps genres every twenty minutes and never quite runs out of ideas. If you have someone to play it with, cancel your plans.
overview: We spent our first session with two of us on the couch, one dad hovering behind us with a beer, and inside forty minutes we'd been dragons, gunships, and something we couldn't describe out loud without laughing. Hazelight makes co-op games that assume you and your partner enjoy each other's company, which is either lovely or a red flag depending on the marriage.

The whole thing is built on constant reinvention. Each set-piece hands you two different tools and asks the two of you to solve one problem, and the answers get sillier as they get more ambitious. You can play remotely, but the game is engineered for a shared sofa and a shared groan when one of you drops the wrong glowing thing off the wrong glowing ledge.
facts: Two-player only, and every set-piece is designed around a shared couch or a shared voice call.
Chops between wildly different sci-fi and fantasy scenarios, and doesn't reuse a mechanic if it can invent a new one.
From the studio that made It Takes Two, so you already know what your kids will find you doing at 10pm.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I was the second player and I stayed the second player.
lenses.body: I normally bail at the first tutorial pop-up. I got through Split Fiction because it never once asked me to remember anything from twenty minutes ago. Whatever tool the game handed me this room, that was the tool for this room. I also refused to swap seats even once, which the other two say is how you can tell I liked it.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: Not Descent, but I made peace
lenses.headline: A co-op game whose puzzles actually need two brains.
lenses.body: I was ready to be annoyed and instead caught myself running spreadsheets for a physics puzzle that lasted five minutes. Every scene asks the two of you to solve a slightly different problem, and I love being useful. The gag is that my optimal solution and their chaotic one usually meet halfway with laughs, and I'm slowly learning to accept that outcome.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: It's a whole weekend of couch time if you can carve one out.
lenses.body: A meaty co-op that respects your marriage and your bedtime, in chapters you can bail out of cleanly. I'd rather do this with a real person than any online lobby, and it's the first game in a while all three of us actually cleared. Bring snacks. Bring patience for at least one 'you go left, no MY left.'

bestFor: Anyone with one specific person they want to play games with
Couples who can survive the phrase 'no, YOUR left'
People who miss the era when a game just kept throwing new ideas at you
watchFor: It really is two players only, so if your co-op partner cancels you're stuck
The tonal whiplash between genres is the whole point, but it is whiplash
You will lose an evening to a mini-game that has no business being that good
reviewBasis: Played to completion by two of us on the couch across three long evenings, with the third eating chips and directing traffic like a very tall referee.

title: UFO 50
deck: Fifty fake games from a fake 8-bit console, and about a dozen of them are better than the real games from the same era.
verdictTitle: Fifty games. A shocking number of hits.
dadTake: It's like our childhood, if our childhood had also been proofread.
verdict: UFO 50 is the kind of thing you'd assume was a gimmick if the people behind it hadn't made Spelunky. It's fifty full games, most of them properly designed, several of them among the best small games of the year. It's an absurd amount of stuff for the money and a genuine argument about what the 8-bit era could have been.
overview: You boot the front-end, it looks like a piece of hardware you would have owned in 1984, and you double-click a game called Barbuta. Barbuta is hard. Barbuta is also great. Then you try one called Bushido Ball and it turns out you love volleyball with a katana. Six hours later you have opinions about eight of the fifty games and you have not left the sofa.

The real trick is how many of the fifty are actually good. There are shmups, RPGs, roguelikes, sports games, puzzle games, and a handful of things that don't fit any genre. They share a made-up publisher's history and a fake console spec sheet, and the shared limits give the collection a personality that a big themed anthology usually can't muster. It's a museum you can play.
facts: It's fifty complete games sharing a fictional 8-bit-era console and publisher history.
The games span genres from shmups to RPGs to sports to puzzle to real-time strategy.
It's from Mossmouth, the studio behind Spelunky, and it shows in the design bones.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I latched onto one game and never left
lenses.headline: I play exactly one of the fifty and refuse all the others.
lenses.body: I found Bushido Ball, decided it was my personality now, and I've played nothing else for weeks. I won't try Grimstone. I don't care about Mortol. When people ask me what UFO 50 is, I say 'volleyball, but Japanese'. I'm technically correct. The best kind of correct.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: I wrote a ranking. Rewrote the ranking. Compared it to three online rankings.
lenses.body: I've got a full ranking with justifications. My top pick is a specific RPG we won't spoil, my bottom pick is a shmup I think unfairly reused its final boss, and my middle third is 'the ones nobody's talking about that are actually great'. I'm now writing a small essay about the collection's fake history. Nobody has tried to stop me and I'm choosing to read that as encouragement.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Even if half of them are duds, that's twenty-five good games.
lenses.body: I play it two or three games at a time and treat each session like a little sampler. Fair warning: the difficulty on a lot of them is genuinely 80s-hard, and a few will bounce anyone who isn't up for saving a lot. But at this price, for this many things, and this much design care, I can't think of a better deal we bought this year.

bestFor: Anyone with a fondness for the 8-bit era but not a lot of patience for the real thing
Group chats that need endless new game recommendations for the price of one
People who like an anthology with a story sitting quietly underneath it
watchFor: Some of the fifty are genuinely tough in the vintage way
You will play three, love one, and forget the others until later
The meta layer around the fake publisher is easy to miss and worth chasing
reviewBasis: All three of us have dipped in and out on PC across a few months, one of us is chasing full-clears. Facts checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Black Myth: Wukong
deck: You are the Monkey King, several bosses do not seem to know this, and you have to explain it to them one at a time.
verdictTitle: Beautiful, brutal, occasionally overlong.
dadTake: Finally caught up with what our children have been reading in books all this time.
verdict: Black Myth: Wukong is one of the most beautiful action games we've played and it's also more of a Souls than the marketing wanted to admit. The combat is heavy, the bosses are the whole show, and the mythology it draws on is a genuine delight. It's a bit long and a bit uneven in the middle, but the highs are stratospheric.
overview: You fight a wolf general, a giant spider, a bear the size of a temple, and every single one of them has a personal grievance with you. The Journey to the West source material gives Black Myth an art direction our library hasn't seen matched this year. Also, you can turn into different things. This never stops being funny.

Under the visuals is Souls-adjacent action combat that leans on staff stances, a stamina bar, and a handful of transformations and spells that recharge slowly. Bosses are where the game lives and dies — a couple are top-of-the-year, a couple over-repeat their patterns. The exploration is more linear than the trailers implied, but the boss-to-boss pace and the constant visual invention carry it further than that should.
facts: It's an action RPG drawn from the Chinese classic Journey to the West.
Combat runs on three staff stances, a stamina bar, and transformations that briefly turn you into other creatures.
Bosses are the whole spine of the game and there are a lot of them.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I got past the wolf and no further
lenses.headline: Souls-like difficulty has finally caught up with me.
lenses.body: I don't play Souls games. I gave this one a go on the strength of the trailers, made it to the first big wolf boss, died a lot, then respectfully closed the game. That wolf is my final boss, spiritually, and I'm happy to hear about the rest of the game from the other two at dinner. A perfectly reasonable Souls debut.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: The bosses are the game and I agree
lenses.headline: Staff stance timing is the whole meta and I've optimised it.
lenses.body: I tried all three staff stances, picked one, and never went back. My main note is that the middle chapters lean a bit hard on repeated enemy types and the level design gets a little corridor-shaped, but the boss encounters are worth the whole ticket. I'm still yelling about the tiger boss two months later, and nobody's worked out how to make me stop.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A long one, but the highs are worth the full sitting.
lenses.body: I finished it across about six weeks on PC and I think the pacing wobbles in the middle. I can also name four boss fights I'll remember for years, which is more than most action games this year gave me. If you don't already love Souls, this won't convert you, but if you're on the fence about mythology, come for the mythology.

bestFor: Fans of Souls-likes who want a different mythology to fight through
People who like a game that runs on 'and then a bigger monkey appeared'
Anyone who wants to look at the prettiest bosses of the year
watchFor: The middle chapters can drag and repeat enemies
Difficulty spikes are a real thing and there's no easy mode
PC performance can wobble on older hardware
reviewBasis: Two of us finished it on PC, one bounced at the first major boss and hasn't returned. Facts double-checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: ANIMAL WELL
deck: A tiny animal wanders through a labyrinth full of secrets, cats, and one large ostrich we are still afraid of.
verdictTitle: The map is the actual puzzle.
dadTake: First game where 'get out of the well' is a valid life goal.
verdict: ANIMAL WELL is a metroidvania where the platforming isn't really the point — the map is the puzzle, and the map keeps re-explaining itself. It's short by that genre's standards, densely secret, and the vibes are the best thing all three of us encountered this year. Some of the animals are not okay. That is not a spoiler.
overview: The screen is dark, there's a chirping noise, and something the size of a small horse just walked past the door you were about to leave through. That's about the first ten minutes. ANIMAL WELL is unsettling in a way we didn't quite expect from an eight-bit metroidvania, and every screen is doing something quietly weird — pipes going somewhere they shouldn't, animals doing more than they should, cats watching.

The tools you get aren't guns, they're gadgets — a bubble wand, a slinky, a frisbee — and each one unlocks whole new layers of the map you'd already walked past. The main game runs about eight hours, and then there's a rabbit hole underneath it that could eat the rest of your year. The pixel art is doing things we didn't know pixel art could do. The atmosphere is the whole meal.
facts: Everything you see fits into a single interconnected map and there are no cutscenes.
The tools are gadgets, not weapons, and the game is largely non-violent.
There is a whole layer of secret post-credits puzzles that we are nowhere near solving.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Loved the atmosphere. Left when a bird was mean to me.
lenses.body: I got three hours in, told the other two I loved the vibe, hit a puzzle involving a bubble and a specific ledge, and calmly closed the game. I now watch other people play it on YouTube and I consider this a healthy relationship. Which it is. Not every game has to fit every dad, and this one really wanted me to think.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: The full map is in my notebook
lenses.headline: I'm on a deeper layer. I won't say which one.
lenses.body: I'm deep in the post-credits content and I refuse to explain what I've found. All I'll say is that the game is more of a puzzle box than a platformer, that a specific gadget interaction genuinely broke me for a night, and that you should not look up any solutions or a specific animal will 'have lore'. I'm enjoying this too much.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Best-vibes game of the year. Not close.
lenses.body: I beat the main game in a long weekend and I haven't stopped thinking about it. Fair warning, the game doesn't hold your hand at all and you'll need to enjoy being lost as a texture. I also think the eight-hour main path is the correct length, and if you're not the type to chase every secret you'll still leave feeling like you got a whole game.

bestFor: Anyone who wants a metroidvania where combat isn't the point
Puzzle fans who like being genuinely stuck
People who miss playing games without a map marker screaming at them
watchFor: No hand-holding whatsoever, and you'll get lost at least twice
The secret content is the whole point and can be intimidating
Some of the animals are horrid. That's not a spoiler.
reviewBasis: Two of us finished the main game on PC, one is chasing post-credits secrets, one bounced happily. Facts checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Balatro
deck: Poker, but every hand you play warps time and every Joker card ruins your relationship with maths.
verdictTitle: The pause menu is a coping mechanism.
dadTake: Turns out we've been playing the wrong poker for thirty years.
verdict: Balatro is the most 'one more run' any of us has ever felt for a solo game. It looks like a screensaver, it plays like a slot machine wired to a spreadsheet, and by hour three you'll be seeing multipliers when you close your eyes. It's brilliant. Do not start it on a school night.
overview: You play a hand of poker. It scores 240. You buy a Joker. Your next hand scores 8,900. You start laughing, quietly, into your hands, at half past midnight. That is our shared review. Two of us have finished the game and one of us cannot stop starting new decks, and none of us is sure who's winning.

Under the hypnosis is a really careful design. Every Joker is a rule change, every deck has different constraints, and the boss blinds force you to actually vary your play. It's the perfect shape for a portable roguelike: quick runs, deep meta, no story to keep track of. The soundtrack is one hypnotic loop that we now hear in the supermarket.
facts: You're playing poker hands, but every Joker card can rewrite what a hand means and does.
Boss blinds impose weird constraints that make your best strategy suddenly the worst one.
It's the work of a single developer under the name LocalThunk.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I learnt the poker hands from Balatro
lenses.headline: I genuinely thought a straight flush was a Balatro invention.
lenses.body: I didn't know the hands going in and I don't fully know them now, but I understand multipliers and I understand greed, and those are the two required skills. I've got a favourite Joker I refuse to explain and I only ever play high card decks. The game does not care. It just keeps rewarding me.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: There is a mathematically correct move and it is 'buy the mult'.
lenses.body: I mapped the Joker interactions on a whiteboard. Then I discovered that half the fun is watching a stupid build overperform. Now I run joke decks on purpose and still hit high antes more consistently than the other two. My current thesis: Balatro is a stealth systems-design masterclass and everyone owes it to themselves to read the wiki once.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Runs are short. Sessions are anything but.
lenses.body: Individual hands take a minute. A full run takes about half an hour. You can do a run in a single sitting, and then you don't. I've put more hours into this than any other game this year and I could not tell you when. My one honest note: if you're prone to 'just one more' behaviour, this is the worst possible game and also the best possible game.

bestFor: Roguelike fans who have never once looked at a poker book
Anyone with a commute or a baby that naps unpredictably
Spreadsheet people who want a spreadsheet that fights back
watchFor: You will lose several evenings and blame the game correctly
Late runs can drag if you get a bad Joker shop opening
The main song will haunt you for the rest of the year
reviewBasis: All three of us have played it on PC across the year, two of us have won runs on higher stakes. Facts checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: HELLDIVERS™ 2
deck: You fight for democracy in the future by dropping large ordnance on your friends. Mostly on purpose.
verdictTitle: Managed democracy, unmanaged laughter.
dadTake: The only game where 'friendly fire' is a personality trait.
verdict: HELLDIVERS 2 is the funniest co-op shooter any of us have played since Left 4 Dead. Missions are the perfect thirty to forty minutes, the stratagems are stupid in the best way, and the difference between 'we succeeded' and 'we killed each other' is one badly-thrown grenade. We'd immediately re-buy it on any platform we owned.
overview: One of us threw an orbital laser to solve a bug nest and killed all three of us in the same move. We laughed for a full minute. The mission failed. We started another one. That's the pitch. HELLDIVERS 2 is a game about calling in enormous ordnance and mostly hitting yourself, and it's built precisely for people who cannot take themselves seriously.

Under the physics comedy is a really good third-person shooter. Guns feel weighty, the stratagems open up a real toolkit of orbitals and support weapons and turrets, and difficulty scales so hard that Helldive missions become full-on tactical operations. The galactic war meta gives you a reason to log in, without ever guilt-tripping you when you don't. That last bit is the one we care about.
facts: Four-player co-op with proximity chat, dropped in via literal escape pod.
Stratagems are called down with directional inputs and they will kill you if you type wrong.
The war state changes based on what all players collectively do that week.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: Reliable friendly-fire artist, and that's me
lenses.headline: I learnt to run and shout, and that's most of the game.
lenses.body: I pick a machine gun, point it away from the other two on request, and miss that request approximately half the time. Somehow I'm now the group's best flag-defender because I refuse to move and things die around me. I have not once opened the loadout screen and I keep getting promoted anyway. The universe rewards commitment.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: The stratagem loadout is a real one
lenses.headline: Optimising the mid-mission call-in order. Absolutely my lane.
lenses.body: I have a spreadsheet. Of course I do. The mid-mission economy of when to burn a resupply, when to hold your Eagle strafing runs, and how to sequence stratagems around a heavy nest is exactly my kind of maths. I'm quietly convinced this is the first co-op shooter since 1999 that respects positioning, and honestly, the other two agree with me.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Missions end when they say they'll end. Blessed.
lenses.body: Forty-minute cap, hard extract, done. That's the whole reason it's stuck in our rotation. I can start a Helldive at nine and be in bed by ten, which is the correct shape of a Friday. My only asterisk: bring headphones because the proximity chat is half the joke, and don't play it solo, because it becomes a completely different, worse game.

bestFor: Groups who laugh when they die
Anyone whose ideal shooter is 'John Wick, dumb friends'
People who want a live service that doesn't need daily maintenance
watchFor: Solo play is technically supported and emotionally punishing
Server issues can flare, though they've calmed since launch
You will start yelling stratagem codes in your sleep
reviewBasis: Three-player co-op sessions on weeknights on PC across roughly four months. Facts verified against the game's official Steam listing.

title: COCOON
deck: A small beetle carries a world on its back into a bigger world. Two hours later you're crying about topology.
verdictTitle: Every puzzle earns its little 'oh'.
dadTake: Nested puzzles, nested naps. We finished them both.
verdict: COCOON is the kind of puzzle game where you spend forty minutes stuck, one thing clicks, and the whole level rearranges itself in your head like a magic trick. It's short, dialogue-free, and every mechanic makes you feel like a genius when you crack it. Easy recommendation for anyone who liked LIMBO or INSIDE and wants the third one in that DNA.
overview: You are a bug. You walk up to an orb the size of your bug body and you pick it up and, inside the orb, there is a whole world. You walk that world into another orb. That's the whole hook. Two hours in it starts stacking them and you can feel your brain making sounds it hasn't made since university.

The rest is genuinely clever level design and lovely, muted art direction. There are boss fights, of a sort — patterned, puzzle-shaped ones — and the game teaches every mechanic wordlessly so you never once feel talked down to. It runs about six hours, which is exactly the right length. Every puzzle earns its 'oh' and none of them wear out their welcome.
facts: It's from Jeppe Carlsen, the lead gameplay designer on LIMBO and INSIDE, and it feels like it.
There is no dialogue, no HUD, and no on-screen prompts, and it still explains itself perfectly.
You can beat it in a weekend and think about it for a month.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I never once opened a menu, because there aren't any.
lenses.body: This is my ideal setup. No text. No tooltips. You just walk somewhere and something happens. I got through the first two worlds in a sitting, got stuck for an hour, refused help, and eventually solved it out loud while making dinner. It's the first puzzle game I've finished since Portal, and I wouldn't stop telling the other two about it.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The topology is the puzzle. I'm in heaven.
lenses.body: I drew a diagram. A real one, on real paper. I'm currently trying to articulate whether the fourth orb is a subset or a peer of the third and it's making me happier than any game this year. My only note is that a couple of puzzles are more parse-the-visual than think-the-thought, but I forgave it. Because it's beautiful.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Six hours, no filler, no season pass. What a relief.
lenses.body: I played it over three evenings and then spent a fourth one talking about it. It sits perfectly in the slot where you want something that isn't a live service and isn't seventy hours long. My only real caveat is that the boss fights, while charming, are the weakest bits, and you'll want to save mid-puzzle just in case a phone call happens.

bestFor: LIMBO and INSIDE fans who trust the whole team
Anyone who wants a puzzle game that respects a busy month
People who like to be a bug
watchFor: There's no hint system, and you will be stuck for real at some point
The boss fights are the least strong part, though still fine
It ends. You'll wish it didn't.
reviewBasis: Two of us cleared it on PC across a weekend, the third took about a week between commutes. Facts double-checked against the game's official Steam page.

title: Baldur's Gate 3
deck: A hundred hours, a mind flayer parasite, and companions who somehow become the second most complicated thing in your inventory.
verdictTitle: The RPG our whole marriages survived.
dadTake: Rolled a nat 20 on the sentence 'I'll just try it for an hour'.
verdict: Baldur's Gate 3 is the biggest RPG any of us has played since we were young enough to have time to play RPGs, and it earns every single hour. The turn-based combat is honest D&D, the writing is genuinely funny, and the choices matter in a way modern RPGs mostly pretend at. It is the closest thing to a religious commitment we can recommend.
overview: Astarion asks to bite your neck approximately six hours in and one of us said yes purely to see what happened, which turned out to be a fully motion-captured conversation with consequences we were still paying off in Act 3. This is the entire game. You do a small stupid thing, and thirty hours later a bard sings a song about it in a tavern. It's ridiculous. It's the point.

Under the fanfic energy is a real, hard, honest tactical RPG. Positioning matters. Elevation matters. Grease matters embarrassingly a lot. Each fight is a puzzle you can approach through spells, stealth, shove-off-a-cliff, or, memorably in Act 2, chucking a lit oil barrel at a boss's feet. That the co-op works at all is a small miracle. That it works this well is genuinely uncanny.
facts: It's a fully turn-based D&D 5e RPG with dice rolls exposed for every skill check.
The origin companions each have their own recorded backstories and can be played as the protagonist.
Two of us hit around a hundred hours before finishing Act 1 without cheesing anything.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I bounced at the character screen, then came back for Karlach.
lenses.body: I got four hours in, could not remember what a saving throw was, and quit. Then a clip of Karlach hitting an Absolute cultist in the face with a hammer hit our group chat and I came back. Now I play a barbarian who solves every conversation with intimidation and every combat with rage. I have no idea what the tadpole plot is. I'm having a great time.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Turns out I've had a control wizard in me this whole time.
lenses.body: I read the rules. All of them. I rolled a control wizard, memorised the difficulty class table by Act 2, and now the group's most reliable strategy is 'let me cast Hunger of Hadar'. My only complaint is that the endgame lets you break the encounter maths in half, which I did, on purpose, and then got mad the boss died in one turn.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: The one that ate our year
lenses.headline: It's genuinely too big and we're grateful.
lenses.body: A hundred hours in and I was still finding side quests I'd missed. I'll also warn anyone reading that the last chunk of Act 3 has some rough edges and a very heavy final week of decisions, and that saving before every conversation is a lifestyle. Even so: nothing else this year came close, and I'll be back for a full evil run when the kids leave for college.

bestFor: Anyone with a D&D group that hasn't met since 2019
People who want a co-op RPG that survives a scheduling disaster
Fans of the sentence 'let me just check one more thing before we long rest'
watchFor: Act 3 is enormous and can wobble on the hardware side
One of your companions will make you cry and you will not see it coming
You will lose an entire evening to choosing a hairstyle. Budget accordingly.
reviewBasis: Two of us finished it on PC across roughly six months, one solo and one three-player co-op run. Facts confirmed via the game's official Steam page.

title: DAVE THE DIVER
deck: During the day you fish in a mysterious hole. At night you run a sushi restaurant. Both are somehow the same story.
verdictTitle: Cozy in the mornings, unhinged by midnight.
dadTake: Finally, a job simulator where the boss is a giant squid and it's fine.
verdict: Dave the Diver is at least four games in a trenchcoat and every single one of them is charming. You spearfish in the mornings, run a restaurant at night, and every few in-game days a boss fight or a farm sub-plot shows up and you laugh, again. It's the coziest game any of us has bounced through in years.
overview: You are a man called Dave, you have a wetsuit and a personality, and your best friend Bancho runs the sushi bar you supply. Then a whale asks you to help. Then you are farming rice. Then it's a rhythm mini-game about food prep. We kept expecting it to run out of ideas, and it kept refusing to.

The real trick is how the two halves feed each other. Better weapons let you catch better fish which unlock better menu items which fund better weapons, and you're always one dive away from paying off the new dining chairs. It looks like a phone game and plays like something a lot bigger. The pixel art holds up when things get weird, and things get very weird.
facts: You dive by day and run the sushi restaurant by night, and both loops are full games.
The Blue Hole changes layout each morning, so no two supply runs go the same way.
There is a farm. There is not a good reason for the farm. It rules.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The one where I beat a boss and then made everyone dinner.
lenses.body: Cozy games are my lane and I never want to leave it. I got fully hooked on the restaurant side, obsessed over the menu, and refused to sleep until I'd unlocked the wasabi. When the other two asked how the story was going I said 'there's a story?' and then took a screenshot of a plate of sea urchin. That's the review.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Optimising a nine-seat evening rush. Absolutely my lane.
lenses.body: I was suspicious for about forty minutes and then I did the maths on the harpoon upgrades. Now I have opinions about which harpoon carries which fish, and I can price a nine-seat evening rush better than anyone else here. I'd like to lodge one complaint: the boss fights, while good, don't quite justify the ammo I keep burning. I'm fine. I'm fine.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The one I play after the kids are asleep and life has been long.
lenses.body: Sessions are self-contained. A dive, a service, off to bed. It's the game that fills the spot Stardew used to and it's a nicer looking one. If you're starting it, know that the mid-game pace slows a bit when the story goes big, but by then you're too fond of Bancho to leave. It's a really easy one for me to recommend.

bestFor: Anyone who wants a cozy game that still has a plot
Restaurant simulator fans who also enjoy stabbing eels
People who miss the point of the tutorial and are having a great time anyway
watchFor: The mid-game story pushes hard and the pacing wobbles for a few hours
Boss fights can spike in difficulty in a very not-cozy way
You will crave sushi. That's not a bug.
reviewBasis: Two of us saw the credits on PC, one of us hit around ten hours across a fortnight. Facts checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Resident Evil 4
deck: Leon Kennedy escorts the president's daughter through a village where nobody speaks the same language and everyone owns a scythe.
verdictTitle: Still the greatest bad first date.
dadTake: Turns out marriage counselling was Leon rescuing Ashley the whole time.
verdict: The Resident Evil 4 remake takes a game two of us already thought was untouchable and finds a way to make it better. Leon controls like a proper action hero, the parry adds a whole new rhythm, and the village opening is still the best hour in survival horror. If you didn't play the original, this is the version to start with. If you did, this is somehow still worth it.
overview: There is a moment early on where a mob of villagers surrounds a farmhouse, one of them is holding a chainsaw, and Leon calmly rolls under a table. Two of us have played that sequence a dozen times over twenty years and we still had to pause and breathe. The remake completely nails the pacing of the village while giving it a texture the original couldn't afford.

The parry is the big new toy and it changes everything. Suddenly the knife isn't just a knife, it's a get-out-of-Ganado free card, and Leon feels dangerous in a way he didn't in 2005. The merchant is back, Ashley is a real person this time, and the shooting galleries are still the funniest side content in the series. It's the rare remake that respects the original enough to actually change things.
facts: The village is set in an unnamed part of rural Spain and it is genuinely, correctly frightening.
The parry works on almost everything including axes, pitchforks and the occasional bit of horror-movie physics.
Ashley is no longer a health bar with legs and it improves every scene she's in.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I held on tighter than expected
lenses.headline: The stress of the village broke me. I came back for the castle.
lenses.body: I died five times at the farmhouse fight and put the game down for a fortnight. Then curiosity got me. Once the shotgun showed up I stopped panicking and started planning, and by the end I was calmly popping legs and reloading like a man who watches gun content on YouTube. Which I now do, apparently.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Optimal upgrade routes, aggressive parries, zero pity for Ashley.
lenses.body: I treated the whole game as an inventory-management puzzle and had spare grenades by Chapter 4. My actual thesis is that parrying a chainsaw is the closest thing modern shooters have to a real skill check, and the other two tell me watching me do it back-to-back at Professional difficulty was educational. I also refuse to sell the handcannon.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A twenty-hour action game that never stops finding new toys.
lenses.body: The pacing is the actual miracle. Village, castle, island — every act has a new hook and it never once felt like padding. I beat it across about three weeks of school-night sessions and every session ended at a satisfying stopping point. If more AAA games understood that we sometimes have to close the game at nine forty-five, we'd finish more of them.

bestFor: Anyone who missed the original because they were busy having children in 2005
People who want a horror game with more shotguns than jump scares
Fans of the merchant, and let's be honest, that's everyone
watchFor: The village opening is genuinely stressful and does not ease you in
Ashley sections still exist and one of them is a lot
You will start doing the merchant's laugh in real life
reviewBasis: All three of us finished it on PC on Standard, one of us went back for a Hardcore run. Details verified against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Pizza Tower
deck: A sweating Italian man runs at Mach 3 through cheese-themed hell to protect his failing pizza business. We love him.
verdictTitle: Peppino is our new life coach.
dadTake: Best cardio we've done in a decade and we didn't have to leave the couch.
verdict: Pizza Tower is 90s cartoon cocaine in game form. The movement snaps in a way we haven't felt since the Genesis, the pixel art is on some ungovernable next level, and by hour four all three of us were making the escape screams. If you can handle a game that never stops yelling, it's an easy recommendation.
overview: Peppino Spaghetti sprints across a level flapping his arms like he's been personally attacked by a wasp, and this is the game's neutral state. Then a laser eyeball starts chasing him and he goes even faster. It's the funniest use of pixel art any of us has seen in years and the animation frames alone are worth the money.

Under the visual noise there's a really good platformer. Every level is a run to the top, then a timed escape back down, and the whole thing scores you on speed and combo chains. Wall jumps, super jumps, shoulder charges, taunts — none of it feels like homework and all of it feeds into the same 'go faster' loop. It's the rare score-attack game we actually re-ran on purpose.
facts: Every level ends with a timed escape sequence that you sprint back through the geometry you just explored.
The pixel art is the work of a very small team and it shows in a way that's incredibly flattering to them.
Peppino has more animation frames than most AAA protagonists and about a hundred of them are just 'panicking'.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I got one P rank and I won't shut up
lenses.headline: Even I was doing sick combos by the second level.
lenses.body: I usually watch Sonic and ask who Dr. Robotnik is. Not here. Within twenty minutes I'd learnt the shoulder charge, forgotten what the buttons were called, and cleared a whole floor without looking at the screen properly. Apparently my face when I pulled off the escape run for the first time was the best thing the other two saw all month.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I read it as a routing puzzle
lenses.headline: The escape run is a subway map. My whole language.
lenses.body: The escape route is a puzzle you memorise, which is my exact love language. I got the highest scores in the group by treating each level like a subway map, plotting where to sprint and where to shoulder-charge. My only complaint is that the game rewards commitment more than precision, which I consider a moral failing. I was, by all accounts, insufferable about it for a week.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A game about panic that respects your session length.
lenses.body: Levels are five to ten minutes each and you can stop between any of them, which is a miracle for us. It's the loudest game in our library and we can only play it while the kids are asleep or the neighbours are on holiday, but the actual sessions are dad-sized. I beat a boss with twenty minutes left before bed and it made my whole week.

bestFor: Anyone whose favourite Wario Land is 'the one with the transformations'
Score-attack fans who hate being made to feel stupid about it
Group chats that need a new source of screenshots of a sweaty man
watchFor: You will need headphones and a household that's tolerant of screaming
P ranks are their own hobby and none of us have the wrists
The final act pushes the platforming hard enough that the Casual bounced
reviewBasis: Two of us cleared the main game on PC over the course of a month, one of us hit around six hours before life won. Facts checked against the game's official Steam page.

title: Vampire Survivors
deck: You do not move your attacks. You do move a small purple wizard, and thirty minutes later the sun comes up and everything on screen dies.
verdictTitle: Five euros. Ninety hours. Terms and conditions apply.
dadTake: It's a screensaver that hands out achievements. Best five euros I ever spent by accident.
verdict: Vampire Survivors is the best five euros a dad can spend. You don't aim and you don't attack; the game handles both. You just walk, dodge, and pick upgrades, and every run is thirty minutes to sunrise. What starts as a curiosity ends as a full brain-off wind-down machine that will still lead to shouting when your Bloody Tear evolves. Do not download it before a work night.
overview: You are a small pixel person on a large brown field. Bats show up. Then more bats. Then bats with skeletons in them. At no point do you aim; your weapons swing automatically, and your only job is to walk in circles picking up gems while trying not to die. Thirty minutes in, the entire screen is a lightshow, the sound is a horror, and the numbers going up are the numbers going up.

The design trick is that every weapon has an evolved form that requires a specific passive item at max level, and the fun is discovering those combinations. You'll go from confused to godlike in the space of a fifteen-minute run. And then you'll play the same map with a different character. And then you'll unlock the next stage. And then it's midnight.
facts: An auto-attack survivor game where you only control movement and level-up choices.
Runs are capped at thirty minutes, ending in a genuine boss-rush sunrise.
Every weapon has an evolution unlocked by pairing it with a specific passive item.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I've played more of this than anyone and I can't explain why
lenses.headline: I put it on for ten minutes and it took my weekend.
lenses.body: I'm the guy who plays four games a year. I've got 140 hours on Vampire Survivors. I don't know how. I call it 'the runaround game' and I put it on the second I sit down. There's no menu depth for me to complain about because I don't open menus. My only critique is that my screen gets 'quite busy' near the end, which I'm told is the entire point.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: It's Cookie Clicker with a plot
lenses.headline: I'm fine with that, and I've got a build spreadsheet.
lenses.body: I sniffed at it for a week and then wrote a fourteen-tab spreadsheet on weapon evolutions. I have an opinion on Peachone versus Ebony Wings. I'm running arcanas I'd very much like you to hear about. My serious critique is that the meta-progression can trivialise runs after a while. I am still playing runs after a while.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: The five-euro one I actually keep installed
lenses.headline: Perfect for a tired hour and terrible for a healthy sleep schedule.
lenses.body: It's the only game I'll play in bed. Thirty-minute runs, no live pressure, no session anxiety, and a satisfying number-go-up loop that resets nightly. I wish it were harder to say 'one more run' at 11pm, but that's an us problem, not a game problem. For the price of a coffee it's an obscene amount of game.

bestFor: People whose gaming windows are exactly thirty minutes long
Anyone who wants number-go-up without any twitch reflexes
Broke dads. Legitimately, five euros
watchFor: You will genuinely lose sleep to it, and the game will not apologise
The screen gets loud and busy. Photosensitivity warning, seriously
There is no story here and none pretending. You're on the wrong shelf if you want one
reviewBasis: Between the three of us we have somewhere in the region of two hundred hours on PC across roughly a year. We are not proud. We are not stopping.

title: Cult of the Lamb
deck: A cute little lamb starts a religion, and the religion is that you should really be looking after your compost bins.
verdictTitle: Charming. Also a spreadsheet in fleece.
dadTake: My cult expanded rapidly once I introduced dental.
verdict: Cult of the Lamb marries a roguelite dungeon-crawler to a village management sim. The village half is great, the dungeon half is fine, and the doctrine of 'these two loops feed each other' is what carries it. It's a game about cleaning up after true believers who won't stop pooping in the church. Which is a review in itself.
overview: You are a lamb. You die. A giant demon god called The One Who Waits offers you a bargain: he'll keep you alive, you have to build a cult in his name. Two hours later you're managing bathroom schedules for six wolves, a lizard, and a very disappointed frog. The art is Cuphead-cute, the tone is Adventure Time meets Wickerman, and the game is entirely aware of how funny that is.

The core loop is dungeon runs to gather resources and followers, then base management back at the compound to feed, sleep and radicalise them. The dungeon side is a serviceable roguelite; the base side is where the game lives, with rituals, buildings, and the fastest slide from wholesome to unholy in recent memory. If you love cosies with a mean streak, this is calibrated for you.
facts: A hybrid of a roguelite dungeon-crawler and a base-building village sim.
Followers age, get sick, and require your attention or leave the flock.
Doctrine choices unlock unique rituals and, honestly, a lot of the humour.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I kept the lamb, ditched the dungeons
lenses.headline: I wanted farming and I got farming with a knife.
lenses.body: I was in it for the animals and the cottagecore. I was less in it for the third combat run of the day. I got about eight hours in, at which point my cult had five levels of tents, and I stopped. The village sim is very good. I just wish there was more of it and fewer knives.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: The two loops feed each other and I love that
lenses.headline: This is what a good hybrid looks like, and I'm now taking questions.
lenses.body: I mapped the dungeon-to-village conversion rates on a napkin. I worked out which follower traits stack for which rituals. I beat the second bishop with an axe build and then made a spreadsheet about it. My only complaint is that the roguelite side has fewer weapon families than I'd like, which is a compliment. The rest of the design is exactly my thing.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: The one I cleared and moved on from
lenses.headline: Fifteen hours, four bosses, one cult, job done.
lenses.body: I finished the main story arc in about fifteen hours and stopped. The updates since launch have added stuff, but I have a life. As a one-and-done it's charming, it has a proper ending, and it never overstays. I also have a follower named after my real dog, and I won't let anyone excommunicate him.

bestFor: Fans of Stardew who want a mean streak in their cosy
People with a favourite pet name they can put on a sheep
Anyone who likes cult humour and doesn't take it too seriously
watchFor: The dungeon half is fine, but you'll notice it isn't the point
Late-game village management can lean heavy on chores
Your followers will die and you will be more upset than you expected
reviewBasis: Two of us reached the main ending on PC in roughly fifteen hours each; the third stayed at the village and never went back to the dungeons.

sources.label: Cult of the Lamb on Steam

title: Stray
deck: A cat runs around a decayed neon city and knocks paint cans off shelves. Somehow this is not enough for us.
verdictTitle: Short, gorgeous, mostly a mood.
dadTake: The first game where I checked on the kids because a cartoon cat looked sad.
verdict: Stray is a short atmospheric adventure about a cat in a cyberpunk city. As a mood piece it's genuinely beautiful and none of us regretted the six hours. As a game it's a fairly simple linear puzzle-adventure with some light stealth. Play it in one sitting, on a lazy Saturday, and don't come in expecting anything more clever than a very good cat.
overview: A cat falls through a hole in a wall and lands in a cyberpunk city where all the humans have been replaced by little robots in beanies. The cat is a very good cat. It miaows. It knocks stuff off shelves. It runs across pipes and up sofa arms and all three of us watched our own cats side-eye us during the playthrough. If you're immune to that, most of Stray does not have a plan B.

As gameplay it's a chapter-based linear adventure with light stealth and light platforming. Jumps are contextual, so you press a button and the cat goes where the cat should go. That sounds like a compromise but it's actually the mercy of the design. Where it goes short is that the puzzles are simple and the stealth is basic. What it gives you back is a hand-crafted city that we would live in.
facts: A cat-first adventure across a linear neon city with light stealth.
Contextual jumping means you never miss a jump, but never choose one either.
Runs about six hours, which is what an evening and a Saturday morning is.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The rarest positive review I can give.
lenses.body: I'm the guy who's finished four games in ten years. I finished Stray. I didn't complain about the mechanics because there aren't any to complain about. I said 'that's a nice game' and put it down, and if you knew me you'd understand that's a rave. Also my real cat sat on my lap for the last hour. Story checks out.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: There's no depth here and I'm fine with that
lenses.headline: A vibes game, I'm mid on the vibes, and the city carried it.
lenses.body: I was ready to be sniffy. Instead I sat down for one session, finished it, and made a note about how well the vertical level design works once you take away the ability to fail a jump. I want the world to know I'd have preferred an actual traversal skill tree. I also can't stop showing the other two my screenshot of the cat curled up under a lamp.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Short, complete, no seasons and no season pass.
lenses.body: Six hours and it rolls credits. No live service, no daily login, no NG+. I played it on a rainy Saturday with a mug of tea and had a lovely time. Would I pay full price? Probably not. Was it worth every minute? Yes. Sometimes that's all a game has to be, and I'm grateful for it.

bestFor: Cat people, obviously
Anyone who wants a beautiful thing to finish in one long sitting
Playdate-friendly co-watching with kids who like sad robots
watchFor: It is genuinely short. Buy on that assumption, not despite it
Puzzles are mild and stealth is basic. Not why you're here
You will miss the cat for a week afterwards
reviewBasis: All three of us finished it in single sessions on PC, roughly six hours each. Nobody replayed.

title: Neon White
deck: A speedrun FPS where every gun is a card, and every card is either a jump or a bullet, and never both without regret.
verdictTitle: It's a speedrun game about being late to heaven.
dadTake: First shooter that made a middle-aged man voluntarily replay a level. Terrifying.
verdict: Neon White is a first-person speedrunning platformer whose central idea is genuinely new: your gun is a card, and you can either shoot with it or discard it for a movement ability. Never both. Every level is a small puzzle about which of your six cards to fire and which to throw away. It is criminally addictive and also has a lot of anime dialogue you'll have to accept.
overview: Heaven has a demon problem. They've drafted an assassin called White to solve it, and he isn't hanging about. Every gun he picks up doubles as a movement move: the pistol becomes a double jump, the shotgun becomes a dash, the rifle becomes a soar. The joke is that you always have to pick: kill this demon, or use the gun to reach the next platform. Never both. The devils know.

The mechanic is elegant and the level design is exceptional. Every level is a puzzle you'll solve in a minute and chase for another thirty. There's a friends-times leaderboard that will absolutely eat your evening. The dialogue between the levels is bright, loud, and made for a younger crowd. You skip through it. The levels are the point.
facts: A first-person speedrun platformer where guns double as one-shot movement cards.
Each level is 30-90 seconds long, with gold and ace times to chase.
Friend leaderboards let you compare specific times per stage against people you know.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I got the first gold and left
lenses.headline: 'Try to beat the level' turned into 'I'm going to bed' quickly.
lenses.body: I liked the movement. I liked jumping about. What I didn't want was to redo the same level for the eighth time to shave 1.4 seconds off it. I got the first world's golds and dismounted. If this were called Neon Chill and had no timer I'd still be playing. As it is, it's not for me.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: The card discard economy is the whole game
lenses.headline: Cards as a resource and movement as a puzzle, and I'm in heaven.
lenses.body: I'd been asking for a game like this and refusing to believe it existed. Every stage is a hand management puzzle wearing a first-person shooter. Which gun do I fire, which do I throw away, which do I save for the last jump? I've got aces on the first world now, and strong opinions about mouse versus controller for it.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: Bite-sized. Perfect for the bad-back years.
lenses.headline: Ninety-second levels are what our lives look like.
lenses.body: The pitch is that any level is under two minutes. I can play three between putting the kids down and starting the laundry. The obvious weakness, the anime writing, is skippable. The obvious strength, how it feels to nail a run, is not. I won't finish it. I'll enjoy every session I do play.

bestFor: Speedrun brains who want the game to hand them the puzzle already
Anyone whose gaming windows are literally 90 seconds long
People who watch AGDQ and have opinions about IL rankings
watchFor: The dialogue is very much an acquired taste
On mouse and keyboard it feels perfect. On controller it feels almost as good
You will replay levels until 1am. This is not a suggestion
reviewBasis: Two of us cleared roughly a third of the main campaign across a fortnight on PC; the third got to the second world and switched to ace-hunting.

title: ELDEN RING
deck: FromSoftware's open world detour, complete with a horse called Torrent and a boss who's had four columns written about her.
verdictTitle: The one that got the dads back into FromSoft.
dadTake: First time we paused a boss fight for maths homework and came back to the same problem.
verdict: ELDEN RING is the game FromSoftware make when they finally have the time. Every corner has a boss, every corner has a lie, every corner has one more copper-plated statue with something better than it inside. It runs the risk of asking for too much of a life. It's still the most alive open world any of us has been in, and the co-op summoning is the best thing FromSoft have done for people over forty.
overview: You wake up in a place called the Chapel of Anticipation. Roughly ninety seconds later, a large gentleman on a large horse takes your head clean off. You wake up again, this time in a proper level, and someone gives you a horse of your own who can double-jump on gusts of wind. From that moment on, ELDEN RING is a game about riding towards a big thing on the horizon and finding out whether the big thing is a windmill or a dragon. Usually a dragon.

What makes it stick is that FromSoft's boss design finally has an escape hatch. Stuck on a wall? Ride past it. Do a legacy dungeon instead. Come back at level sixty with a bigger sword. The open world is a difficulty valve, and it turns twenty years of 'git gud' into something two working parents can actually finish. The bosses are still the point. But now the point respects your bedtime.
facts: An open world Souls-like from FromSoftware with the writing directed by George R.R. Martin.
Torrent, your horse, can double-jump on updrafts and eat spirit food.
Cooperative play via summoning signs. Yes, you can help each other with the horseback knight.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I died six times to Tree Sentinel and put it down for eight months
lenses.headline: Then I came back and became a Rivers of Blood merchant.
lenses.body: I'm the guy who has never finished a Souls game. This time I did. I respec'd into bleed, summoned any friendly ghost the game offered me, and didn't once feel bad about it. The 'ride around it' escape hatch saved me. So did the other two, three times, using the tarnished summoning ring. Apparently the best part was watching me talk about Godrick like he's a co-worker I'm still mad at.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Level design that gives me the shivers, and yes, I compared it to Descent.
lenses.body: I mapped every rune farm before the first legacy dungeon fell. I beat Malenia solo without Mimic Tear and posted the video in the group chat. I call Torrent 'Descent for people who can't fly' and the other two cannot make me stop. I'm insufferable when I'm right, and about ELDEN RING I'm right constantly.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: The one the group chat lived in for three months
lenses.headline: Two hundred hours across three of us, no complaints.
lenses.body: The genius bit is co-op. Bring in a mate for a boss you're stuck on, pay them back the following weekend. The game doesn't punish you for playing with your friends, and that's such a novelty. I do wish UI navigation on controller wasn't from 2011, and I'd appreciate more waypoints. Otherwise, one of the best three months of gaming our group chat has had.

bestFor: Souls veterans who wanted more room to breathe between the beatings
Souls tourists who bounced off Dark Souls and want an on-ramp
Anyone with a group chat that will summon them at 10pm
watchFor: Late game does repeat some earlier bosses in dungeons. It's fine, until it isn't.
UI on a controller is FromSoft-ancient. You'll learn to love it.
You may lose an entire spring to it, and possibly a summer too
reviewBasis: Roughly two hundred hours across three of us on PC, mostly co-op weeknights and solo cleanup on weekends; two of us finished the main campaign, the third is still in the Consecrated Snowfield.

title: Inscryption
deck: A card game where the cabin owner would rather you didn't leave, and the animals in your deck are getting mouthy.
verdictTitle: You can only play it once. Play it once.
dadTake: First deckbuilder where the deckbuilder wants to build you into the deck.
verdict: Inscryption is a card game about being in a cabin with a horror. Then it isn't. Then it isn't again. Any specific description is a spoiler. What we can say is that it's three distinct card games in one story, at least two of them are genuinely great, and the puzzling around the table is as good as the puzzling on it. Go in blind.
overview: You sit down at a table. The bloke across from you does not have a face. There is a stoat, and the stoat has notes. You play a couple of hands and lose, and then someone leaves a scalpel on the desk and suggests you might want to have a look around the cabin. This is roughly the point at which we started sending each other cryptic voice notes at 1am.

Mechanically it's a card game where every creature costs blood, and blood costs cards you already had on the board. That single decision structure ripples through everything: sacrifice, planning, which of your squirrels you love most. Then the game changes, and the mechanics change with it, and to say any more is to ruin the trick. It's a magic show. Do not read the reviews. Play the thing.
facts: A card game whose primary resource is sacrificing the creatures you already play.
Three distinct acts, each with a meaningfully different card system.
Meta-plot content unfolds via ARG-style discoveries during the game.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I beat act one and then had questions
lenses.headline: The cabin ruined a Wednesday and I thank it.
lenses.body: I don't usually play card games. I finished the first act because the horror man is charismatic. I don't know why the game keeps talking about a video store and I don't want to be told. I said 'is my computer okay?' out loud at one point, which is the highest compliment I can pay a work of art.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: The blood economy is a puzzle I love
lenses.headline: One resource, one board, and I cracked it open like a walnut.
lenses.body: The sacrifice loop had me from turn three. I'd worked out that stoats stack, that hoarders enable combos, that Leshy is looking at your hand and reading you back. I haven't been this happy with a card game economy since I got mad about Slay the Spire's Watcher. I'd like a comfier chair, but that one's on me.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: Twelve hours I'll never get back and don't want to
lenses.headline: You play it once and that's the deal.
lenses.body: About twelve hours, one long weekend. The story is the point, and the story doesn't rerun. I'm not doing NG+. I'm not touching Kaycee's Mod for months. I've told everyone in the group chat to buy it and then go silent, and that's a review in itself.

bestFor: Anyone who liked Slay the Spire but wants to be haunted by it
People who go into things blind and love it
Fans of Pony Island who've been asking Daniel Mullins for a big one
watchFor: Act two is the divisive one. He may or may not vibe with it
Do not, under any circumstances, watch a trailer
You can only play it once. Buy accordingly
