reviewBasis: All three of us played it to credits on PC across roughly a fortnight; discussions were held in a chat we now refuse to open.

title: DEATHLOOP
deck: A time loop assassin puzzle that treats you like a smart adult and then hands you a shotgun with googly eyes.
verdictTitle: Arkane at Arkane again.
dadTake: The only sim where 'I already know how tomorrow ends' is bragging, not depression.
verdict: DEATHLOOP is the Arkane immersive sim as a puzzle. You've got four times of day, four districts, and eight targets to kill in one loop. The joy is figuring out how. The wobble is that once you've solved it, the Julianna PvP invasion metagame is more of an idea than a scene. Worth playing anyway for the level design alone.
overview: You wake up on a beach in a nice jacket. You die. You wake up on the beach again. Someone called Julianna is on the radio being extremely rude to you. Colt has one day to kill eight targets across four maps, and if he can't get them all in a single loop, the loop resets and he has to figure out how to line them up. It's a puzzle box. A very stylish one.

What makes it work is that the map states genuinely change across morning, noon, afternoon and evening. A door that's locked in one is open in another. A target who's in one place at noon is at a party at night. You gather clues by playing badly, then plan a perfect loop with everything you've learned. When it clicks it's some of the smartest level design we've played since Dishonored 2, which is not an accident.
facts: Four maps, four times of day, eight visionaries to kill in a single loop.
Powers are 'infused' with residuum you collect from previous runs, so nothing is truly lost.
Julianna can be a real player invading your loop, or an AI if you'd rather sleep.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: The plan-a-day-of-murder game was too much planning for me
lenses.headline: I wanted a shooter and got a Rubik's cube with slabs.
lenses.body: I got maybe six hours in and started drifting. The problem is that DEATHLOOP wants you to hold a whole day of pieces in your head, and after work I don't have the head-room for that. I respected it. I want to be clear that I respected it. I also uninstalled it and put a hat on.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: This is what a real immersive sim looks like
lenses.headline: Four maps that talk to each other, and I drew a diagram.
lenses.body: I made a spreadsheet of which visionary is where at which time of day, colour-coded by lead. I solved the whole loop in my head before pulling a single trigger. Then I did it again, faster, without Reprise. I call that fun. The other two have quietly decided not to correct me. The level design is the closest thing to Dishonored 2 I've had in a decade.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: One glorious campaign, and a metagame I waved goodbye to.
lenses.body: I finished it in about twenty hours and then closed it forever. Not because it's bad, but because I'm done. The Julianna invasions are a great idea and a small part of the pie, and I was never going to be the guy who lived in them. As a one-and-done immersive sim it's easily worth the money, and the flick knife twist ending is genuinely great.

bestFor: Dishonored fans who wanted more Dishonored, please, thank you
Puzzle brains who want the puzzle to be 'plan a perfect day'
Anyone who reads investigation notes for fun in Skyrim
watchFor: The PvP invasion metagame is a small idea in a big frame
Colt won't shut up, and the constant chatter is a taste thing
On a controller some of the shooting feels a step behind the plan
reviewBasis: Two of us finished the main loop and rolled credits on PC, roughly twenty hours each; the third tried invasions for an afternoon and was fine with never doing so again.

title: Resident Evil Village
deck: Nine-foot vampire lady got the marketing, but this is really a fairy tale horror anthology in a coat.
verdictTitle: Tall lady, short opinions, big value.
dadTake: Finally an RE where the neck aches from looking up, not down at ammo counts.
verdict: Village is a fine sequel with four dramatically different setpieces stapled together by an Eastern European hamlet. When it's a haunted castle, it's brilliant. When it's a doll house, it's the best hour of horror we've had since Amnesia. When it's a factory, it's a factory. Worth every hour anyway.
overview: Ethan Winters gets his hands mangled again. There is a village. There is a lady who is nine feet tall and has become the entire personality of an internet. All three of us played it in first person on separate PCs and all three of us jumped in exactly the same place, which we now discuss on group chat like it's a shared trauma.

Structurally, it's four horror games with a shared spine. Castle Dimitrescu is a hide-and-seek mansion with a very tall stalker. House Beneviento is a psychological detour that would frighten a corpse. Moreau is a wet mini-boss run. Heisenberg's factory is a shooter. The variety is the pitch and also the wobble; you'll love at least two of them, and put up with one.
facts: First-person survival horror across four distinct 'lords' with different tones.
Runs on the RE Engine and is remarkably well-optimised on modest PCs.
Includes The Mercenaries arcade mode alongside the main campaign.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I made it to the doll and pressed pause forever
lenses.headline: I loved the castle. I did not love the doll house.
lenses.body: Halfway through Beneviento I took my headphones off, said 'no thank you', and didn't touch it again for a month. When I came back I was fine, and I finished it with the sound down. I'd like the record to show that the scariest thing I've ever heard in a video game came out of that mansion, and I want no medal for admitting it.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I counted the shots in every fight
lenses.headline: The economy is generous, and I took that as a challenge.
lenses.body: I immediately started running knife-only wherever I could. I kept a mental tally of Lei per encounter. I'm convinced the Duke's shop bends generosity into a puzzle you can pick apart. I'm right about that. I'm told I'm less right about the Heisenberg wave-defence bit, which I insist is a Descent room. Apparently it is not a Descent room.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Twelve hours, four flavours, and a proper credits roll.
lenses.body: I knocked it out over a long weekend and had no notes on pacing. The variety kept me awake, the runtime respected my back, and no chapter overstayed its welcome. I'd trade the factory for another Beneviento in a heartbeat, though I do understand why they can't make an entire game out of the Beneviento.

bestFor: Fans of RE4 who want more of what makes RE4 work
Anyone in the mood for genuinely varied horror across one weekend
People who wish their in-laws were nine feet tall and Romanian
watchFor: House Beneviento is not messing about, and you will know it when it starts
The story leans on RE7 lore in ways that a first-time player will have to google
Heisenberg's factory is the weakest hour, and it's a long hour
reviewBasis: Two of us finished the main campaign on PC across roughly twelve hours each; the third bailed after Beneviento and came back a month later.

title: It Takes Two
deck: The only game we've handed our partners a controller for and had them still speaking to us at the end.
verdictTitle: The co-op game they don't make anymore.
dadTake: Sold as marriage counselling. It's actually kart racing. Same thing, honestly.
verdict: It Takes Two is a two-player co-op adventure that changes what it is every twenty minutes. Platformer, shooter, boss rush, minigolf, tower defence, sometimes in the same level. There is no solo mode and there shouldn't be. Play it with the person you live with, on the sofa, at a sensible bedtime, and it's genuinely one of the best things any of us have ever finished together.
overview: You start as two puppets. Your daughter cries on you. A magic self-help book with a mediterranean accent shows up. What follows is roughly twelve hours of one of you shouting 'no, YOUR side, YOUR side' at the other, punctuated by boss fights against household objects that had no business being that scary. We laughed. We were also asked why we were laughing at 11pm.

The mechanic is that each of you has a different toolkit every level, and they only work when combined. One gets nails, the other gets a hammer. One gets fire, the other gets sap. It never repeats itself. Just when you're getting good at one thing, Josef Fares yanks it away and hands you a whole new pair of powers. It shouldn't work as often as it does.
facts: Two-player co-op only. There is no solo mode, and it's better for it.
Friend's Pass lets one copy invite a second player in for free.
Every level introduces a new pair of abilities and mostly retires them by the next.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I held the sticks correctly and everything
lenses.headline: The person who doesn't play games completed this with me.
lenses.body: My wife, who once described Mario Kart as 'the noisy one', finished this with me in three sittings. That's the point. The controls are simple enough that whichever half of a couple normally reads the instructions never has to. She got weirdly good at one boss I'd been dreading. I'm still processing that.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I wanted a mechanic to overthink and got twelve
lenses.headline: It refuses to let me settle in and I'm furious about it in a good way.
lenses.body: I had a whole plan for the first hour, and then the game handed me time-rewinding on a mouse. I kept expecting one core loop and got twelve small ones instead. This is not my usual thing. I've still ranked the boss fights, and I won't stop talking about the Rose's Room chapter, which coming from me is a compliment.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: The one I handed my partner
lenses.headline: Finishable at the rate real adults play at.
lenses.body: Twelve to fifteen hours, split across four evenings, no filler, no side content nagging at me. My marriage remained intact. The story is silly and the ending genuinely earns its swing. If you can get two adults on the same sofa on the same night in the same year, this is what you should be putting on.

bestFor: Couples with one gamer and one gamer-adjacent
Anyone who misses split-screen and forgives EA for the split-screen
Groups of two friends who need to prove they can still finish something together
watchFor: The dialogue leans hard on the therapy metaphor and lands where it lands
Zero solo option, so this genuinely needs a second human
Some late levels ask more of the platforming than we'd remembered
reviewBasis: Played to completion by two of us on separate PC sessions with our respective spouses on the sofa, roughly a week each.

title: Valheim
deck: A viking survival game where hour one is a pretty walk and hour five is your mate weeping over a lost longship.
verdictTitle: Log heavy. Vibes heavier.
dadTake: My back hurts and my longship sank. Ten out of ten viking authenticity.
verdict: Valheim is a survival game with a real spine. The bosses are worth beating, the biomes are worth crossing, and the moment your first proper longhouse comes together is genuinely one of the best things we've done in a co-op game since the pandemic. It's also long. If you don't like chopping wood, do not build a viking hall in Valheim; the maths does not work in your favour.
overview: You wake up on a beach with a stick. Ten minutes later you're chopping a tree and it's peaceful. Two hours later a tree is chopping you back because you didn't notice you were logging near a troll cave, and now the troll is trundling towards your half-built hut with what can only be described as focused intent.

What makes it stick is that every biome hides one specific resource you need for the next biome, and there's no way to skip the queue. The Elder makes swamp keys. The swamp gives you iron. Iron lets you survive the mountains. It's a chain of survival puzzles disguised as a Norse camping trip, and until you build a proper Karve and start doing real trade runs across the ocean, none of it clicks.
facts: 1-10 player co-op with procedurally generated worlds you can share between servers.
Every biome gates a specific resource you'll need for the biome after it.
Yes, you really do have to sail. There is no fast-travel for iron.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The vibes are lovely right up until it wants me to be organised.
lenses.body: The first fifteen hours I loved. Chopping wood, building a nice porch, admiring the sunset over the ocean. Then the swamp happened, I lost my hard-won iron in a leech pond, and I put it down. The problem isn't that Valheim is hard, it's that my lunch break isn't long enough for the walk back to my corpse.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The tech tree is a real tree and I've already trimmed it.
lenses.body: I've had spreadsheets going since the second biome. I track bronze-to-iron conversion rates. I have opinions on which honey stations should be inside the walls versus behind them. Everything I love about survival games is here: real progression, gear that matters, and enough Norse mythology to keep me distracted between wood runs.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Great once a week, catastrophic every night.
lenses.body: The session length is honest. A build night is two hours, a boss night is three, and a sailing expedition is 'better cancel morning'. I love it and I can't play it more than weekends. If your co-op group can commit to a weekly boat, Valheim rewards you. If it can't, someone will always be five biomes behind.

bestFor: Groups that can commit to a regular sailing night
Anyone who's played Minecraft and thought 'this needs more Odin'
Woodworking dads with time to spare
watchFor: The swamp will find your worst weakness and press on it
Iron logistics is a second job you did not apply for
Corpse runs across an ocean at 2am will test friendships
reviewBasis: Roughly a hundred hours across a two-person weeknight server on PC, plus a shorter solo run for the early biomes. Details checked against the game's Steam listing.

title: Hades
deck: Zagreus, prince of the underworld, on the sixty-third attempt to visit the surface and yell at his dad.
verdictTitle: Supergiant's masterpiece. Yes, we said it.
dadTake: It's a game about screaming at your father, and unlike our teenage years, this time it's productive.
verdict: Hades is the game we hand people who say they don't like roguelikes. Every run tells a story, every death moves the plot forward, and the combat is stylish enough to carry an evening on its own. It's a rare confluence of writing, art, music and design where each one is doing the heavy lifting for the others. It's also one of the funniest games any of us has played.
overview: You're Zagreus. Your dad, Hades, runs the underworld and is, on a personal level, a piece of work. You'd like to leave. To leave, you have to fight your way up through four increasingly annoyed regions, take a boon from Zeus, Aphrodite, Ares or whoever's on the phone at the moment, and probably die at the last boss. Then you come back home, get shouted at by Hades, and try again. The next attempt starts about eight seconds later.

The core loop is that death is the only way to progress the story. Every run you fail unlocks new dialogue, new relationships, new upgrades from the mirror in your bedroom, and new pact conditions for the next attempt. Six weapons — sword, spear, shield, bow, fists, rail — each with wildly different Aspects, keep the combat fresh over dozens of runs. And every character in the underworld remembers what you said to them last.
facts: There are six weapons, each with several Aspects that meaningfully change how they play.
The story unfolds specifically through failed runs — you cannot skip it by being good.
Dying is roughly a ten-second inconvenience before you're back at the door.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I picked the shield and never left.
lenses.headline: The rare roguelike that never made me feel bad.
lenses.body: I grabbed the shield on my first run, liked how it made me basically invincible if I got the block timing right, and never once tried another weapon. I've beaten the last boss. I have no idea who Skelly is. I romanced nobody. I had a wonderful time. That's the whole point of Hades — it lets me do that without ever making me feel like I did it wrong.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The purest boon-stacking build game in the genre.
lenses.body: I read the codex. I learned which duo boons need which pairings. I've got opinions about Aspect of Guan Yu on the spear at high Heat. I beat the game on the sword first, then the spear, then every other weapon, then started the pact conditions, and I'd like you to know that Zeus's chain lightning breaks the game in the right hands. I'm not wrong. I'm also insufferable. Both true.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The perfect this-week-and-next-week game.
lenses.body: A run takes twenty to forty minutes, and there's always something new to unlock or somebody new to talk to when I die. I picked it up for a fortnight over a summer, put an hour in most evenings, and finished the credits with a stupid grin. It's the rare roguelike that rewards putting it down, because when I came back the story remembered where I was.

bestFor: People who bounced off other roguelikes and thought it was them
Anyone who's ever wanted to yell at their dad but has been quite well brought up
Fans of the Supergiant back catalogue who trust them at this point
watchFor: The credits are the middle of the game, not the end
You will absolutely start a run 'just for the mirror upgrades' and lose ninety minutes
Skelly cares about you and it's fine, don't overthink it
reviewBasis: Two of us played it to a full credits roll on PC across a few weeks; the third's still working on his first past-run to the surface. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Deep Rock Galactic
deck: Four dwarves, a Space Rig with a working keg, and the only shooter our whole group chat can log into without arguing.
verdictTitle: Best call from the group chat, every time.
dadTake: The last time three of us wore matching hats we were on holiday and lost.
verdict: Deep Rock Galactic is the game none of us has ever uninstalled. It runs coop missions that fit inside a weeknight, has four classes that need each other in ways most coop games only claim, and it has never once made any of us feel stupid for being tired. There's a keg on the Space Rig. There's a barrel-hoop mini-game. There's genuine friendship happening down there.
overview: The Space Rig is a small orbital canteen with a working bar, a jukebox, a promotion terminal, and, for reasons only Ghost Ship know, a hoop you can toss beer barrels into. This is where every mission begins and ends. Then you drop into a hole full of glowing rocks, alien bugs and one mineral you specifically forgot to mine, and forty minutes later you come back to that same bar and buy each other virtual drinks.

The mission types are what keeps it fresh — Salvage, Egg Hunt, Point Extraction, Escort Duty, On-Site Refining. Every one demands a slightly different plan and rewards a slightly different loadout. Combine that with four asymmetric classes — Driller, Engineer, Gunner, Scout — and every session ends up being a small, specific improvisation instead of a template. It's the coop equivalent of an old friendly pub. Every time you show up, it works.
facts: There are half a dozen mission types, each with its own tactical shape.
Seasonal content has been free since launch, which we do not take for granted.
Yes, there's a barrel-hoop mini-game on the Space Rig, and it is the most important part of the entire product.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I main the Engineer for the turrets.
lenses.headline: The class that lets me think for a second.
lenses.body: I picked Engineer on my first mission because turrets sounded easier than aiming, and I've never played anything else. I drop platforms on demand, I set up my sentries, and then I mine while the other two handle the swarm. The game counts that as helping — it is helping, actually — and I get to finish the mission feeling like I did my part. Which is genuinely rare in a shooter.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The four classes are four verbs and every one is load-bearing.
lenses.body: I've got opinions on optimal loadouts for Elite Deep Dives, arranged in my notes app. I can tell you which secondary is best for a Salvage mission at Hazard 5. I also insist Scout is a support class, which starts an argument every single evening, and I am, technically, correct. I usually play Driller because I like drawing walls.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The game that has outlasted every other coop hit we've bought.
lenses.body: I play maybe once a week, maybe once a fortnight, and it never feels rusty. There's no rank pressure, no season pass to keep up with, no menu shame when I log in after a month off. Missions are thirty to forty minutes, matchmaking finds you people who yell nice things at you, and you can drop out mid-mission if a kid appears. That's why it's still on my hard drive.

bestFor: Groups whose skill levels differ by 'wildly'
Anyone whose evenings end without notice
People who miss playing coop games with actual roles
watchFor: The early hours drop resources more slowly than the late game does
You will develop opinions about grunts, and they will affect your life
Playing solo is possible but you'll be doing it with a drone, and the drone does not tell jokes back
reviewBasis: Hundreds of missions across a few years on PC, mostly three-player on weeknights, with occasional heroic solo attempts. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: DOOM Eternal
deck: The chainsaw is your ammo pack, glory kills are your health kit, and the ice bomb is basically your granola bar.
verdictTitle: A metal album you can play.
dadTake: Our doctor said no juggling. We didn't tell him about the chainsaw part.
verdict: DOOM Eternal is the loudest, fastest, most gleefully complicated first-person shooter of its generation, and it does not care whether you keep up. It's a symphony of resource management dressed up as a demon-punching festival. Once you get the loop — chainsaw for ammo, glory kill for health, flame belch for armour — it's the best FPS combat since the original DOOM.
overview: You are the Slayer. You are on Earth. It has been overrun by demons who are, honestly, a bit whingy about it. You have a shotgun that shoots a hook, a chainsaw that respawns to give you ammo, a flamethrower on your shoulder that makes armour, and an ice bomb that freezes things. The tutorial hands you all of these in about twenty minutes, and then the game says, right, keep up.

The combat is a puzzle. Enemies drop specific things when killed specific ways. The chainsaw is your ammo economy. Glory kills are your health economy. Flame Belch is your armour economy. If you stand still you die, if you use the wrong weapon on the wrong demon you run out of shells, and if you get it right it's the most kinetic thing in the medium. It's not for everyone. It's very much for some of us.
facts: The combat loop is built around dropped resources — ammo from chainsaw, health from glory kills, armour from Flame Belch.
Every gun has meaningful secondary fire modes, and swapping between them mid-fight is the whole game.
There are platforming sections, and yes, some people would like to speak with id Software's manager about them.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The one shooter I genuinely wanted to keep playing.
lenses.body: I don't normally play first-person shooters. I put it on the easier difficulty, treated the chainsaw as my emotional support tool, and had the best time I've had with a shooter in a decade. I still don't use the ice bomb correctly. I'm pretty sure the Flame Belch is called something else. I finished it. I was proud of myself. The other two were proud of me too, and I've decided to just accept that.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The first FPS since the original that's actually about thinking.
lenses.body: I treat every combat arena as a systems puzzle. Which demon do I kill for what I need next? Which weapon gets me the drop? I built an actual mental flowchart and then ran the whole campaign on Ultra-Violence like it was my job. I want you to know the ballista is criminally underused. I'm not wrong.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: You cannot play it for four hours in a row and remain a person.
lenses.body: It's loud. It's fast. It's genuinely tiring. Ninety-minute sessions are the sweet spot; any longer and my hands ache and my neighbours know exactly which fight I'm in. I finished it in about six weeks of evenings, and I'd describe the last mission as a personal test I passed by two hit points. Which is exactly right.

bestFor: Anyone who wanted their shooter with genuine rules
People who miss when shooters were about movement and not cover
Dads whose kids are old enough to sleep through a chainsaw
watchFor: It's exhausting, and that's on purpose
The platforming is genuinely divisive
Marauders exist and we will not be discussing them further
reviewBasis: All three of us played through on PC, two on the middle difficulty and one on Ultra-Violence, mostly in ninety-minute weekend chunks. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Half-Life: Alyx
deck: The reason two of us finally bought VR headsets, and the reason we've spent the last few years occasionally staring at those headsets in the cupboard.
verdictTitle: Yes, buy the headset.
dadTake: The scariest thing in VR isn't the headcrabs, it's admitting to your wife how much the headset cost.
verdict: Half-Life: Alyx is Valve at their absolute best, and it's the only game any of us has willingly bought a headset for. The gravity gloves alone are worth the price of the ticket. It's genuinely spooky in places, mechanically brilliant throughout, and it is a shame you cannot play it any other way than in VR, because you should absolutely play it.
overview: You are Alyx Vance. You are somewhere in City 17. There's a Combine patrol nearby and you have to physically duck down to hide from it. Then you rummage through a drawer, physically, for pistol rounds. Then a headcrab lunges at you and you shoot it in the face and shout something that used to be your dad's phrase and now belongs to you.

The gravity gloves are the whole thing. You point at an object, flick your wrist, and it comes to your hand across a room. It sounds small. It is not small. Every puzzle, every combat encounter, every quiet corridor is built around this one verb, and it makes the entire game feel like you're doing magic. Add in the best physical gunplay in VR and a story that fits neatly into Half-Life canon, and you have a genuine masterpiece.
facts: It's VR only — no flat-screen mode is officially supported.
Set between Half-Life and Half-Life 2, you play as Alyx Vance.
The gravity gloves are the mobility, puzzle and inventory system all in one.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I was queasy in twenty minutes.
lenses.headline: The most I've ever played VR in one sitting.
lenses.body: I don't do VR. I get motion sick on a swivel chair. I put the headset on, played the first chapter for about half an hour, took the headset off looking pale, and said, and I'm quoting myself here, 'that was the most cinema anything's ever been for me.' I didn't finish it. I watched one of the others finish it. That counts.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The single best-designed VR mechanic to date.
lenses.body: I spent about forty minutes on the gravity gloves alone, flicking magazines into my hand from across rooms. I called it 'the first honest VR affordance,' which sounds insufferable and also is completely right. I then treated every combat encounter like a physics puzzle. I beat the Jeff sequence without ever making a sound. We are not discussing my high-school theatre background.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A masterpiece with an equipment tax.
lenses.body: It's around twelve hours long, sessions can be shorter than you'd think because your face gets sweaty, and the game demands a setup that not every household can support. I borrowed a headset for a fortnight, played it in ninety-minute stretches, and finished it on schedule. I then handed the headset back and haven't touched VR since. I also haven't stopped talking about it.

bestFor: Anyone who already owns a headset and is looking for the killer app
Half-Life fans who accepted years ago that Half-Life 3 wasn't happening
People who like puzzles they can physically pick up and turn around
watchFor: You need a VR headset and a room to swing your arms in without hitting a bookshelf
Jeff will find you, and you will need to be very quiet
Motion sickness is real, and if you're prone to it, no amount of gravity glove is going to fix that
reviewBasis: One of us finished it on PC with an Index over a couple of weeks; the second played about half through a borrowed headset; the third watched twelve hours of VR footage and had opinions anyway. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Ori and the Will of the Wisps
deck: The prettiest metroidvania in the drawer, and yes, we did cry in the first ten minutes, and yes, our kids saw.
verdictTitle: Devastating. Beautiful. Absolutely worth it.
dadTake: The only game where we've had to pause because our eyes were doing something.
verdict: Ori and the Will of the Wisps is the kind of platformer that makes you glad your kids left you alone for an hour. It's a genuine metroidvania with a proper combat system this time, some of the best-looking hand-drawn animation in any game, and a handful of chase sequences that will make you feel very old and very fast simultaneously.
overview: You are a small white forest spirit called Ori. You are extremely cute. The opening cutscene will cost you something, emotionally. Then the game hands you a jump, a dash, and a sword, and quietly reveals it's a full metroidvania with a big interconnected map and enough abilities to eventually let you traverse three vertical screens in a single flourish.

The combat is the real change from the first Ori. There's a sword, a hammer, a bow, and shard slots that let you tune your build like a light RPG. Boss fights have proper arenas. There are chase sequences that are effectively 3D platformer runs on 2D rails, and they are genuinely thrilling in a way that makes you forget you're a middle-aged man watching a spirit-fox jump.
facts: It's a proper metroidvania with an interconnected map, ability gates and shard-based build variety.
The soundtrack is orchestral and, at points, does not play fair with your feelings.
The chase sequences are timed platforming set pieces that are much harder than they look.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I got weepy in the first hour.
lenses.headline: The rare pretty game I finished on purpose.
lenses.body: I usually bounce off platformers by the second wall jump. Not this one. I finished it in a week, in ninety-minute chunks, and I was audibly happy about it. I mostly used the sword. I never learned the hammer. I absolutely nailed one of the chase sequences on the first try and then spent forty attempts on a jump the other two had done blind. That's me.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The Bash mechanic is genuinely one of the great platformer verbs.
lenses.body: I got weirdly analytical about Bash — the ability to grab a projectile mid-air, freeze time and launch yourself off it. It's a two-axis control puzzle in the middle of a platformer, and once I'd used it as an offensive move against a spike wall I wouldn't shut up about it. I compared it to a certain 1995 shareware classic within twelve minutes. You can guess which.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Long enough to be a game, short enough to finish.
lenses.body: It's about twelve to fifteen hours if you're not chasing every collectible, and you will not chase every collectible. I put an hour in most evenings for a couple of weeks and came out the other side genuinely moved. It's not a game I'll replay, and that's fine. Some games only need one honest go.

bestFor: Anyone with a fondness for hand-drawn animation and a functioning heart
Metroidvania fans who missed out on the first Ori
Dads who want to feel something without booking a therapist
watchFor: The chase sequences are harder than the rest of the game combined
You will die to spike geometry and blame the camera
The story will absolutely get you, and there's nothing you can do about it
reviewBasis: All three of us finished it on PC in one wave over a couple of weeks, mostly in evening sessions once kids were down. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

sources.label: Ori and the Will of the Wisps on Steam

title: Disco Elysium
deck: A hungover detective, one dead body in a tree, and twenty-four skills in your head that would all like a word.
verdictTitle: Read the game. Just read it.
dadTake: Finally, a game where the voices in our head are also credited as skills.
verdict: Disco Elysium is our reigning best-writing-in-a-video-game champion. It's a proper detective story, a proper political novel, and a proper character study, and the mechanics are all about talking, thinking and rolling dice with parts of your own personality. Nothing else feels like it. Nothing has really tried.
overview: You wake up on the floor of a hostel room you have destroyed. You have no memory. There is a corpse in a tree outside. Twenty-four different parts of your brain start talking to you — Empathy, Volition, Inland Empire, Electrochemistry — and immediately begin arguing about whether the tie strangling the ceiling fan is your friend. It absolutely is, by the way. It's a great tie.

The systems are all dialogue and dice. Every skill is a voice; every voice can pipe up with a check; every check succeeds or fails and changes the case. You can be a communist detective, a coked-up genius, a sad philosopher, or a legally responsible adult. The murder is real, the politics are pointed, and the writing is genuinely as good as any novel any of us read this year.
facts: There is essentially no combat — checks are made through skills, dice and dialogue trees.
Twenty-four skills, each of which is a voice in your protagonist's head.
The Final Cut adds full voice acting to a game that was already very talky.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The one time I read every line of dialogue in a game.
lenses.body: I don't normally read tooltips. I read every skill check, every internal monologue, every book my character narrated aloud to himself. I took eight in-game days to leave the hostel and considered it well spent. I also failed the necktie check on purpose because I liked how the tie kept talking. I was correct.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The skill system is a personality generator.
lenses.body: I built a fully specced Logic and Encyclopedia detective, hit every white check by savescumming, and then did a second run as a purely physical man who solved the case with his heart. I've got strong opinions about which skills are traps. I want you to know Shivers is not a trap. Shivers is, in my own words, 'the whole game once you get it.'

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The rare no-combat game we all finished.
lenses.body: It's roughly thirty hours long, it has essentially no combat, and I could play it in one-hour sessions without losing the thread because the game keeps track of who you're talking to and what they said last. I finished it. So did the other two, which is basically unheard of for anything with dialogue trees. That's the review.

bestFor: Anyone who used to read
People whose favourite bit of Fallout was talking to a mushroom
Dads who want a serious game they can play in short sittings
watchFor: There is a lot of reading, and we mean a lot
The politics are not a garnish; the game has actual opinions
You will fail an important check and it will actually make the story better
reviewBasis: All three of us finished it on PC over the winter of that year; two of us went back for a second run to see the different political vision quests. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice
deck: The FromSoftware game where the shoulder button is the whole game, and one of us hasn't been the same since.
verdictTitle: Learn the rhythm or leave the mountain.
dadTake: The good news is our reflexes were bad before Sekiro came out, so there's no downgrade.
verdict: Sekiro is the tightest thing FromSoftware has ever made, and also the one most likely to end your relationship with FromSoftware. It's a rhythm game about a sword fight. Once you get it, nothing else feels like it. Getting there takes a lot of dying, and there's no summon, no coop, no build variety to help you avoid the wall you're currently sitting in front of.
overview: You are a shinobi called Wolf. You have a katana, a grappling hook, and a very specific problem with a horse-mounted knight who wants to end you in the first hour. You will not level up your way past him. You will not summon a friend. You will parry his sword clashes with L1, and when you finally do, the sound the game makes is one of the great sounds in video games.

Deflection replaces the dodge roll. Posture replaces the health bar as the thing you're actually attacking. Bosses are duels, and duels are conversations, and the conversation goes clang clang clang clang thrust until one of you is dead. The rest is grappling around beautiful mountain temples, finding prosthetic tools, and eventually beating a man who is essentially the concept of samurai.
facts: Combat is built around deflection and posture rather than dodge-and-hit.
There's no multiplayer of any kind — you die alone, in the classic FromSoftware manner.
The grappling hook is the mobility system, and it makes every arena feel like a jungle gym.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I died six times to the horseman.
lenses.headline: The wall I could not climb, no matter how nicely the other two asked.
lenses.body: I met Gyoubu Oniwa, the horseback samurai in the first area, and lost roughly six times in a row. Then I put it down for eight months. I came back one Sunday afternoon out of guilt, beat Gyoubu on the second try, and then quit again immediately, satisfied. I call that a win. It kind of is.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The purest FromSoft has ever gone.
lenses.body: I clocked the rhythm-game bones about ninety minutes in and never played anything else for a month. I've read the Mikiri counter frame data. I can explain when to Mortal Blade, when to firecracker, and when to just shut up and deflect for eleven straight seconds. I beat Isshin in my lunch break and told everyone at work about it. Nobody cared. I didn't care that they didn't care.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Beautiful, brutal, and honestly a big ask.
lenses.body: This isn't a game you can dip in and out of. Sessions need to be long enough that the fingers wake up. Bosses need runbacks. Runbacks eat evenings. I got about two-thirds of the way through and shelved it during a busy work week, and every time I came back I had to reteach my hands the parry timing all over again. Beautiful game. Not one for the two-hour weekday window.

bestFor: Anyone who wanted Bloodborne but with a sword and no guns
People who like being humbled by pattern recognition
Dads whose kids sleep through the night
watchFor: There is genuinely no easy mode, and no summon rescue
The story is oblique in a way even by FromSoftware standards
You will absolutely spend an evening losing to a large old man who is technically your dad
reviewBasis: Two of us finished it on PC, one after roughly forty deaths to Genichiro alone; the third made it about two-thirds through before life took over. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

sources.label: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice on Steam

title: Devil May Cry 5
deck: Three demon hunters, a robotic arm called Devil Breaker, and a soundtrack that sounds like it wants a divorce.
verdictTitle: Style ranks. That's the pitch.
dadTake: The last time we got an SSS rank at anything, our kids were being born.
verdict: Devil May Cry 5 is Capcom at maximum swagger, and every one of us grinned at least once per mission. It gives you three completely different characters and a scoring system that grades your combat like a strict but fair PE teacher. It's not deep, exactly, but it's dense — every button does a thing, and the thing is cool.
overview: You are Nero. You have a robot arm called a Devil Breaker. It has punched things, then exploded, and then you have laughed. Then the game hands you V, a goth with a cane who summons a giant bird, a panther and a golem while reciting poetry. Then it hands you Dante and you realise you had no idea what button-mashing could look like.

The core loop is fights, style meter, next fight, style meter. Every character has a completely different toolkit — Nero's arms are consumable and swappable, V's animals do the work while he reads a book, and Dante has four styles and eight weapons and no discernible cooldown between any of them. Missions run twenty minutes or so, and the game rewards replaying them the way an old arcade cabinet did.
facts: Three playable characters, all with completely different combat systems.
Style ranks go from D up to SSS, and yes, they are addictive.
Runs on the RE Engine, which is why every strand of Dante's hair moves independently.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I got a C rank and was thrilled.
lenses.headline: The rare action game where mashing looks fine.
lenses.body: I played Nero. I picked whichever Devil Breaker was on the shelf. I got C ranks throughout and considered that a personal best. The important thing is that Nero looked incredibly cool during those C ranks, because DMC5 is built so even beginner-tier combos are big splashy things, and I genuinely enjoyed a genre I normally avoid on principle.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Three protagonists, three fully realised combat games in one box.
lenses.body: I immediately locked in on V. V does nothing directly — his familiars do the damage while he trots around the arena reading. It's, mechanically, position management with delayed inputs, and it's the most Descent-adjacent thing in a game about a demon in leather trousers. I then went back and rank-graded every mission on Dante, because of course I did.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The best way to remember why you loved action games.
lenses.body: Missions are short. Twenty, twenty-five minutes. Cutscenes cut. I can pick it up for an hour, hit two demons very hard and put it down feeling like a whole person. I didn't finish it in a straight line, and it didn't punish me for taking two months off between mission sixteen and mission seventeen.

bestFor: People who used to feed pounds into Sega cabinets
Anyone who wants a AAA game they can finish in bite-sized pieces
Dads who need to remember what fun looks like at high volume
watchFor: The story is nonsense in a way you will need to accept early
V is not everyone's cup of tea and that is fine
You will absolutely try to look up how to reach SSS rank and then feel old
reviewBasis: Two of us finished the campaign across a couple of months on PC; the third loved the Nero missions and drifted before Dante fully unlocked. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Slay the Spire
deck: A card game that cost about twenty-five dollars and, according to our screen time reports, twelve of our combined years.
verdictTitle: One more run. We swear.
dadTake: It's a deckbuilder. That's an actual sentence we say to our wives now.
verdict: Slay the Spire is the game we've collectively re-installed the most times over the past few years. It's genuinely small — you draw cards, play cards, do damage, don't die — and the depth comes from how sharply every relic and elite bends the run. Play it once and you'll understand every deckbuilder released since.
overview: Ironclad, a big man with a sword, walks into a spire. He has a Strike, a Defend, and roughly nine hundred bad decisions ahead of him. You pick the Strike. Then the elite fight rolls a boss relic and you're suddenly playing a completely different game, because your Strikes also heal now, or your Defends also stun. That's the whole trick.

The four characters play like four different games. Ironclad stacks strength and swings until things end. Silent poisons them from the inside. Defect stores energy into orbs that fire on their own. Watcher slips in and out of stances that do math you have to explain to your friends. Every run is roughly an hour, every choice is real, and the Ascension levels take a good game and turn it into a graduate course.
facts: Four playable characters, each with their own decks, relics and terrible ideas.
Twenty Ascension levels for people whose brains work incorrectly.
One of the games that basically invented the modern single-player deckbuilder subgenre.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I play Ironclad. Just Ironclad. Forever.
lenses.body: I picked the Ironclad on my first run, made a deck that basically does one thing well, and haven't once tried another character. I've beaten the Heart. I don't care that there are three other characters. I call them the wrong characters. My deck is called 'the good one.'

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I wrote it up on a spreadsheet.
lenses.headline: The purest math game masquerading as a card game.
lenses.body: I spent an evening working out expected damage curves for Silent's poison deck at Ascension 12 and had a genuinely religious moment when I realised strength synergy on Ironclad broke my own model. I've got a colour-coded list of relics ranked by 'do I take this if I already have Runic Pyramid.' Apparently I'm everyone's favourite person to lose to.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The perfect midweek game.
lenses.body: A run takes an hour, more or less. You can quit in the middle. Nobody's waiting for you. There's no season pass, no daily login, no online lobby. It's just a small, sharp game I can dip into after the kids are down and put down when my wife walks past. I've played hundreds of runs and I wouldn't describe any of them as wasted time.

bestFor: Anyone who thinks card games are for accountants and would like to be corrected
People whose evening ends when a small hand appears in the doorway
Fans of roguelikes who don't want their runs to take four hours
watchFor: You will lose runs to a spider in Act 1 and it will feel personal
Ascension 20 is not for the well-adjusted
You'll spend real hours on the character select screen, staring
reviewBasis: Hundreds of runs across all three of us on PC over several years, with occasional bouts on the Steam Deck. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Resident Evil 2
deck: The best-looking rain-slicked police station in games, plus a seven-foot man in a fedora who wants to have a word with you specifically.
verdictTitle: Yes. Still. Buy it now.
dadTake: Turns out the scariest thing at 45 is the footsteps of a very tall man in a hat.
verdict: Capcom took a 1998 tank-controls classic and rebuilt it into one of the best horror games any of us has finished. It's tight, it's mean, and it uses its budget like every dollar had a name. Two campaigns, both worth doing, and the second time through it's a different game because you know where the herbs live.
overview: You walk into a police station that is somehow also a mansion designed by a man who really liked chess pieces. The lights buzz. There's a body in the lobby that will absolutely stand back up. Somewhere upstairs a very quiet, very heavy man in a hat has just started walking, and he does not need to run, because you are the one with the ammo problem.

What makes this remake sing is that everything in your inventory is a decision. Grenades, boards, herbs, keys, the pistol you probably shouldn't have used, all fighting for the same handful of slots. Enemies don't stay dead unless you actually kill them, which for a zombie takes more shots than you have. Save rooms feel like coming up for air. It's horror as spreadsheet, and we mean that as a compliment.
facts: Both Leon and Claire have their own campaigns, and yes, you should play both.
It runs on the RE Engine, which is why the fog looks like fog and the shirts look like shirts.
Mr. X shows up partway through the police station and does not care about your item box logic.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I hid in a save room for an hour.
lenses.headline: The scariest game I've finished since our twenties.
lenses.body: I got about ninety minutes in, met Mr. X for the first time, and quit until the other two peer-pressured me back a week later. To my credit, I did finish it. I also spent the entire police station holding my breath, and every save room typewriter felt like a small win I was allowed to celebrate out loud.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Small inventory, a hundred decisions, no wrong answers, plenty of wrong answers.
lenses.body: I treated it like a resource puzzle from minute one. Grenades saved for the sewers, gunpowder combos worked out on paper, the shotgun kept in the box until it earned a slot. Then Mr. X kicked the door down and none of it mattered for about eleven minutes. I said, out loud, 'this is good design.'

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The kind of horror game we actually finish.
lenses.body: Eight to ten hours per campaign, roughly. I can knock out Leon over three evenings if the kids cooperate, then do Claire the next weekend and get a slightly different story for my trouble. It doesn't drag. It doesn't pad. It's the rare AAA game that respects that we have work in the morning.

bestFor: Anyone who wanted to feel this scared but forgot horror was allowed to be this scared
Fans of the 1998 original who are willing to admit the tank controls were rough
Dads who want a horror game that finishes in a week, not a season
watchFor: Mr. X is a real presence and he does not respect your podcast schedule
You will absolutely die because you tried to conserve shotgun shells
Some of the puzzles are still the same medallion nonsense as 1998, which we love, but
reviewBasis: Two of us finished both Leon and Claire on PC across a few weeks; the third bailed after the sewers and has been threatening to come back for a year. Details checked against the game's official Steam listing.

title: Return of the Obra Dinn
deck: A murder-mystery in 1-bit dithering where a magic pocket watch lets you re-live sixty deaths on a boat, and the boat is very upset with you.
verdictTitle: The best notebook you will ever fill in.
dadTake: Turns out I will happily take notes for a boat, but not a meeting.
verdict: Return of the Obra Dinn is one of the smartest games ever made and one of the least explained. It hands you a manifest of sixty crew members, a pocket watch that shows the exact moment of each death, and expects you to work out who was who. There's no combat, no puzzle to grind, no help. There is you and a chair and, if you're serious about it, actual paper.
overview: You are an insurance adjuster. You are the only insurance adjuster in a game, we think. That is already funnier than most stories start. Your job is to walk around the deck of a ghost ship, click on skeletons, watch the frozen moment of their deaths, and identify each corpse by voice, hat, tattoo, or the fact that the guy standing over him is definitely his brother. This is our idea of a proper Saturday.

The dithered 1-bit art is not just a stylistic call, it is the puzzle interface. You have to read faces, read patterns, read shadows. The Memento Mortem watch snaps you into a paused three-dimensional tableau you can walk through and inspect. The book of the manifest is your working notepad, the game validates identities in threes so you can't brute-force it, and the whole thing takes about eight to twelve hours. It is airtight.
facts: Every one of the sixty crew members can be identified from information gathered inside the game. No online lookups needed, no cheating required.
Solutions are checked in batches of three, so guessing is punished and reasoning is rewarded.
The 1-bit art style renders proper volumetric 3D scenes, which is a bizarre technical trick worth noticing.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: Filed as homework, not a game.
lenses.headline: I respect it from a healthy distance.
lenses.body: I got through the tutorial, wrote three names down, then noticed the pocket watch was flipping between accents and quietly closed the laptop. I'm not the target audience. I respect it from a distance. I told my wife it looked like a very expensive escape room, and I wasn't entirely wrong about that assessment.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I wore holes in a real notebook.
lenses.headline: Twenty-seven crew identified in a single sitting.
lenses.body: I printed off the manifest. I organised my notes by chapter. I identified twenty-seven crew in a single sitting and then couldn't sleep because I was still working out the topman with the tattoo. This is exactly the kind of game my brain was born for, and one of the few times the other two have been genuinely jealous of that brain.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.signal: One of the best twelve hours in games.
lenses.headline: You only get to solve it once, and that's fine.
lenses.body: I finished it over four evenings on PC and I reckon that's the correct scope. I also think it's the sort of game that only really works once, and that's fine by me. You get one honest solve and a story you'll bring up at dinner parties. That's more than most twelve-hour games manage in our house.

bestFor: Anyone who liked The Case of the Golden Idol and wants more brain-tickling
People who enjoy taking notes on a physical piece of paper
Solo evenings with a lamp, a beer, and no other tabs open
watchFor: No combat, no timers, no hand-holding. Some of you will bounce off the deduction loop.
The 1-bit look can strain tired eyes; the game has settings for that, use them
You will absolutely spoil it if you Google anything. Please don't.
reviewBasis: All three of us finished it on PC. Two took about ten hours each, the third took twenty and refused to look anything up, and we respect that.

sources.label: Return of the Obra Dinn on Steam

title: Dead Cells
deck: A 2D roguelite where you die a lot, respawn as a headless prisoner, and somehow finish evenings feeling productive about it.
verdictTitle: Twenty minutes at a time, forever.
dadTake: Every death teaches me something. Mostly that I should have parried.
verdict: Dead Cells is the roguelite we default to when nobody wants to commit to a save file. Runs last twenty to forty minutes, unlocks stick, and the combat is the sharpest 2D melee this side of Hollow Knight. It leans harder on twitch than some of its peers, so if you like your action turn-based, this won't convert you. If you like a good dash and a real parry, this is your new home.
overview: You are a green goo that stitches itself into a headless corpse and picks up a rusty sword. Then you die, and become a new green goo, and pick up a slightly better sword. Somewhere between the first and fiftieth run this stops being a joke and starts being a very tight little metroidvania that gives you permanent shortcuts, permanent gear, and permanent grievances against a specific type of archer.

Runs are linear-branching. You always start in Prisoner's Quarters, but which biome you pick next changes the weapons, mutations, and boss you'll see. Combat is a shield-and-dodge affair with a real parry window, dual-wielded weapons on the fly, and mutations that turn your build into small essays. There are a lot of DLC areas now, and the game is generous about letting you skip the ones you dislike. We approve.
facts: Every run generates a new castle from the same set of biomes, but the routes between biomes are your choice.
Permanent unlocks come from cells you spend at the Collector between biomes: die before you reach him and you lose that run's cells.
The base game has been updated for years with free content and paid expansions layered on top.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Twitch platforming with a fail state isn't my Wednesday.
lenses.body: I get to the first biome, die to a lancer, and blame the game. I'm not entirely wrong. I don't enjoy this one. I've tried. Twitchy platforming with a fail state after twenty minutes isn't my idea of a Wednesday. I'd like to note that the goo animation is very funny, and I stand by that observation.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: I can name every weapon by its scaling colour.
lenses.body: I can name every weapon by its scaling colour and I've got strong opinions about which mutation combos are broken this patch. I beat the four-boss-cell version and moved on to the fifth. I'm genuinely good at this, it's genuinely my kind of game, and the other two can't watch me play without feeling old.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The twenty-minute run is the perfect after-work format.
lenses.body: I play it in bursts. A run before bed, another after a work call, one on the couch while the kids are in the bath. The way runs slot into whatever twenty minutes you've got is the game's real trick. I haven't cleared the hardest difficulty and I don't care to. That's a functioning brain talking.

bestFor: Roguelite fans who want their runs shorter than Hades
Players who like a parry window they can actually feel
Solo evenings on the twenty-minute-slot economy
watchFor: Genuinely twitchy. A bad night for your hands is a bad night for this game.
The DLC list is long now, and the cost adds up if you buy in blind
Cell-difficulty scaling is unforgiving; the last two tiers are for a specific kind of gremlin
reviewBasis: Roughly two hundred runs between two of us on PC over a couple of years; the third put in about ten hours and quietly moved on.

title: Monster Hunter: World
deck: The game about hitting a lizard the size of a warehouse until it drops the exact shoulder plate you need for your slightly better pants.
verdictTitle: Hitting lizards is fine, actually.
dadTake: I now own a spreadsheet called Great Jagras Farming Route. Please send help.
verdict: Monster Hunter: World is the entry we tell people to start with, because it finally learned how to explain itself. The hunts are cinematic, the fourteen weapons play like fourteen different games, and the four-player co-op works even when one of us has to leave at exactly 9:47. Some of the menus still assume you've played six of these before. That's the tax.
overview: You are in a forest. A dinosaur the size of a hotel is standing in your way, and one of your friends has a horn instead of a sword. You spend twenty minutes learning its patterns, break its tail off with a great sword, and drag it back to base camp so a chef can turn it into steaks. This is the entire game, and it is somehow one of the best things our group has done together in a decade.

Fourteen weapons that play like fourteen different games, hunts that run twenty to forty minutes, and monsters that feel less like enemies and more like weather systems. There's a real ecology to it: apex predators knock lesser ones out of biomes, elder dragons rearrange terrain, and every big fight has phases you learn like a boxing match. It rewards a small commitment to reading its systems, and it punishes just about everything else.
facts: Fourteen weapon types, all mechanically distinct. Great sword, insect glaive, and hunting horn share basically nothing.
Multiplayer supports groups of up to four, with drop-in join once you've watched the mission's opening cutscene.
Palicoes are your solo companions and yes, they can wear tiny hats. This is important.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I made my cat wear a hat.
lenses.headline: Twenty hours with a sword and shield and no regrets.
lenses.body: I picked the sword-and-shield because it seemed forgiving, learned exactly one combo, and had a great time for the first twenty hours. Then the monsters grew bigger than my patience. I kept logging on for co-op nights though, because my palico's outfit is worth the drive. That's a completely legitimate reason to play, and I'll argue it with anyone.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The support role is the real main character.
lenses.body: I picked the horn, learned the note charts, and turned into a walking buff dispenser. I know the elemental weakness of every monster in the base game and I can tell you which fight is the Rathalos 'actually you're wrong' fight. I build sets. I post them in the group chat at midnight. The other two ignore me and they're better for it.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Sixty hours, main story done, endgame skipped.
lenses.body: I got about sixty hours in over a season, finished the main story, and didn't touch the endgame. That's the correct dose for most dads. The hunts land beautifully, the co-op sessions are exactly the right length, and the menus are the price of admission. I'd tell you to bring a friend, and to pick the same weapon.

bestFor: Groups of two to four who want hunt nights on a rotating schedule
Anyone who liked Dark Souls's boss-first design but wanted less dying
People who enjoy learning one weapon deeply and forever
watchFor: The menus and crafting UI are genuinely rough by modern standards
Solo is doable, but the game shines with a party of two or more
You will spend an evening on a Palico armour set. Everyone does. Accept it.
reviewBasis: Weekly four-player co-op for around three months on PC, plus one of us playing solo through the base story to check the campaign flow.

title: Subnautica
deck: A survival game about being alone in an ocean, and the specific noise you make when a Reaper Leviathan finds you the first time.
verdictTitle: The best game about being terrified underwater.
dadTake: First game to make me buy a bigger monitor. Then regret it, immediately.
verdict: Subnautica is the only survival game we've all finished, because it has an actual story and it respects your time. The base building is generous, the crafting is nested but sane, and the fear of the deep is completely earned. Some of us can't play it at all. Others can't play anything else. Both of these are correct responses.
overview: The escape pod hits the water. You surface. There is nothing on the horizon except a spectacularly on-fire spaceship and a very convincing sunset. You dip your head under and it is beautiful, and something down there sings a note you do not like. You don't know it yet, but that is the game telling you the ground floor is at about two hundred metres and there is no first floor.

The loop is proper survival: scan things, craft tools, build a base, make a bigger vehicle, go deeper. The Seamoth becomes the Cyclops becomes the PRAWN suit, and each unlock buys you access to a new biome that wants you dead in a specific new way. There are almost no guns. You mostly solve problems by running away. This is a survival game that understands its own horror.
facts: No procedural generation. The entire ocean is hand-built and hides the same secrets for everyone.
A full crafting and base-building tree, with power management, hull integrity, and modular subs.
There's a story, an actual ending, and a suggested critical path. Rare for the genre.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I would not enter deep water.
lenses.headline: I uninstalled after my first Reaper sighting.
lenses.body: I stayed in the Safe Shallows for about four hours, built a modest base, farmed peepers, and had a lovely time. Then I saw a Reaper on the horizon, uninstalled the game, and told my kids I'd read a bad review. That bad review was the other two. They wrote it for me at the kitchen table. I'm still not okay.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Silent running, thermal reactors, and one deeply organised sub.
lenses.body: I kitted the Cyclops with silent running, thermal reactors, and a sub-frame's worth of storage lockers. I drew my own map of the biomes. I caught myself using words like 'logistics chain' about a lifepod, and neither of the others stopped me. This is my exact genre, and I couldn't be happier about how it turned out.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Forty-five hours, well spent, no regrets.
lenses.body: I finished it over about forty-five hours on PC and I think it's the best-paced survival game I've played. Sessions bank cleanly, the fear is real but not gratuitous, and the ending is properly earned. I don't recommend it to friends who are afraid of the water, and everybody who's ever done a dive with me thanks me for that.

bestFor: Survival-curious players who bounce off crafting for its own sake
Anyone who liked FTL's 'you against the void' energy but wanted more scuba
Dads with a couple of hours after bedtime and nothing to prove
watchFor: Thalassophobia is not a joke here, and some of you should not play this
Performance can be rough in the late game, especially in the deepest biomes
You will hear the Reaper Leviathan noise in your dreams. That's the game working correctly.
reviewBasis: Two of us finished the main story on PC across around forty hours each; the third made it as far as the first Reaper and hasn't been back.

title: Celeste
deck: A precision platformer about climbing a mountain and having a panic attack that told two of us more about ourselves than any therapy app.
verdictTitle: The best air-dash in games. Also the kindest.
dadTake: The mountain wants you to be okay. The mountain also wants to kill you. Very balanced mountain.
verdict: Celeste is a precision platformer with real feelings, which is not a sentence we expected to type. The core movement is as tight as anything since Super Meat Boy, and the story about anxiety is genuinely moving without being twee about it. Assist mode makes it available to anyone. That is a big deal, and the game refuses to make you feel bad about using it.
overview: You are Madeline. You are climbing a mountain. A wispy purple version of you is trying to talk you out of it. Also the floor is spikes. Also there are strawberries, and you don't have to collect the strawberries, which is a stunning show of restraint from a game about precision platforming. This is the sort of game that gives you an option to be kind to yourself and completely means it.

Under the hood it's Maddy Thorson at their sharpest: a jump, a climb, and a single mid-air dash that recharges when you touch ground. That's the whole toolkit. Every screen is a self-contained puzzle with a checkpoint at the door, so death is basically free and instant retries mean you're only ever ten seconds from another attempt. The B-sides and C-sides are the real final boss, and yes, they broke us.
facts: Assist mode lets you slow the game down, add extra dashes, and turn off death, and the game refuses to make you feel bad about any of it.
Every death is instant-retry with a checkpoint per screen, so the loop is punishing without being punishing.
The B-side and C-side chapters are optional and roughly as hard as anything the genre has produced.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I finished it, in a first.
lenses.headline: First precision platformer I've ever seen credits on.
lenses.body: I turned on infinite dashes in chapter three and finished the whole main game. This is the first precision platformer I've ever seen credits on, and I'd like the record to reflect that. Then I told the other two the story hit me harder than I expected, and got quiet. It was a whole thing. Ten out of ten evening.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Wave-dashing has entered my vocabulary, permanently.
lenses.body: I turned assist mode off, cleared every B-side, and started chasing golden strawberries around the point most people would've moved on with their lives. I can lecture you on wave-dashing. I do. I'm convinced the movement tech alone puts this in the top ten of the decade, and nobody's going to argue me out of it.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A twelve-hour game that feels like a full meal.
lenses.body: I finished the main game over about twelve hours on PC and I reckon that's the correct scope. I liked that any given session could be twenty minutes and still feel complete, and that the story didn't force me to sit through a cutscene at 11pm. I've used it as a gateway drug on at least two friends the other two know about.

bestFor: Precision-platformer-curious players who've been scared off before
Anyone who thinks games can't do mental health without being embarrassing
Short-session players who want to feel finished
watchFor: Base Celeste is not long, and the extras are the meat if you want more
The soundtrack will follow you around for weeks whether you want it to or not
You will absolutely try wave-dashing in the kitchen and hurt yourself
reviewBasis: Two of us finished the main game and most of the B-sides on PC; one of us used assist mode without shame, one refused. The third finished it once and considers his Celeste career complete.

title: Cuphead
deck: A jazz-scored, hand-inked cartoon boss rush that will find and delete your last shred of hand-eye coordination.
verdictTitle: A masterpiece and a punishment. Same thing.
dadTake: We had to start doing actual wrist stretches to play a cartoon.
verdict: Cuphead is one of the most beautiful games ever made and also the reason two of us stopped playing together for a month. The boss rush structure is glorious in short bursts and merciless if you sit down to grind. If you like precision platformers and can accept dying to a Rube Goldberg machine, buy it. If not, watch a good YouTube run and thank us.
overview: The first time you see the potato-plant boss you'll laugh, take a screenshot, and send it to a friend. Around the tenth time you're staring at the potato because you cannot get past his second phase, and it is midnight, and you have a stand-up meeting in six hours. Cuphead does not care. Cuphead is a 1930s cartoon, and 1930s cartoons hated you.

Mechanically it's a run-and-gun boss rush with three hits per attempt, a parry that requires you to jump a second time on a pink object, and a super meter you build by shooting. Every boss is hand-drawn, cel-animated, and has three or four phases you have to memorise. There is no assist mode. There is a Simple difficulty, and it does not count for the last island. That's the deal.
facts: Every animation frame is hand-drawn on paper, in the style of Fleischer and early Disney shorts.
The soundtrack is original 1930s-style jazz, recorded live with a real band. It's not a filter.
Simple difficulty exists, but you need Regular clears to unlock the final island.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I cheerfully quit at Rumor Honeybottoms.
lenses.headline: Two islands in and out, no regrets.
lenses.body: I got to the bee, laughed at the sting animation, died fourteen times, and traded the controller for a beer. I came back and beat exactly one more boss on a different night. That's where my Cuphead ends, and where I insist it should end for every dad, which is the closest I've come to writing a review of anything.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: I know every parry window in the game.
lenses.body: I know every parry window in the game and I can list bosses in the order you should tackle them for the shop upgrades. I play with a lap-desk. I hum the level themes. I'm a menace but a joy, and this is exactly the kind of game my brain lives in when nobody's watching.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The forty-minute session is the correct dose.
lenses.body: I finished it on Regular over about fifteen hours because Cuphead sessions can be exactly forty minutes long, which is a huge point in its favour. I wouldn't recommend it to anyone whose hands hurt, or to anyone who doesn't already like precision platformers. I'd recommend it to everyone else, loudly, and I do.

bestFor: People who like Contra, Contra Hard Corps, and being humbled
Anyone with a soft spot for 1930s animation and jazz
Short-window players who want a discrete goal per session
watchFor: No assist mode, and Simple difficulty locks off the last island
Local co-op is available but arguably makes some bosses harder, not easier
Your kids will absolutely want to watch, and then they'll want to play
reviewBasis: Two of us finished it on Regular over the course of a year of on-and-off evenings on PC; the third quit at the honeybee and has stayed quit.

title: Divinity: Original Sin 2
deck: The four-player co-op RPG that let one of us set the other three on fire, on purpose, in the first town.
verdictTitle: The best local council election in RPGs.
dadTake: Every party meeting ends in arson. So does every real one, honestly.
verdict: Divinity: Original Sin 2 is the best four-player RPG we have ever run at the same table. Turn-based combat that reads the room, party members who can straight-up disagree with your dialogue choices, and a Fort Joy opening so dense you'll reroll a character just to see what you missed. It is a hundred-hour commitment. It is completely worth it.
overview: The first tutorial we all remember is one of us casting a rain spell on a corpse fire, which cooled the fire but flooded the corridor, which the enemy mage then electrified, which killed three of us and half of a merchant. That is how we learned about elemental combos. That is also how we learned who was going to be a problem for the whole campaign.

The turn-based combat is a physics puzzle. Ground surfaces stack: oil becomes fire becomes smoke becomes cursed fire, and every ability is a small lever you can push on that stack. Around it Larian have built a properly reactive world, with quest solutions that assume you'll try dumb things. Four-player co-op means the party can split, argue with itself, and vote against you in dialogue. Nothing has felt more like a real tabletop campaign.
facts: Fully cooperative for up to four players, each with their own character sheet and dialogue choices.
Combat surfaces persist and interact: oil, fire, water, electricity, poison, blood, cursed variants of all of the above, all stacking.
Origin characters have their own quests, so replaying with a different lead genuinely reshuffles the game.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I'd never touch this solo. In our party, I was gold.
lenses.body: I'd never touch this alone. In our four-player run I played a rogue, stole everything not nailed down, and once slept-arrowed an entire boss fight while the others did the actual work. I had a great time. So did they. I still couldn't tell you what Source is, and honestly, at this point, neither could a lot of players.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Necrofire is not just fire, apparently.
lenses.body: I turned the loading screens into lectures. I built a summoner-necromancer who kept undead armies on the field for eight-turn fights, and I laughed in a way that made the other two worry. This is the game that finally beat Descent as my default conversation-starter, which is a real sentence about a real man, and that man is me.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Get four dads on a weekly slot and it repays you tenfold.
lenses.body: Getting four dads into one campaign is like herding fireflies. We managed it for about six months and finished Act 2. I think that's a legitimate victory. The pacing rewards long sessions and yes it does drag in the third act, but the highs are the highest co-op RPG has produced for us since the previous Larian game.

bestFor: Groups of three or four who can lock in a weekly session
Players who miss Baldur's Gate 3 already and want to know where it came from
Anyone who has ever wanted to be the party's designated problem
watchFor: Act 3 has known pacing issues that even the Definitive Edition did not fully solve
Character build regret is real and respec-ing is doable but a chore
One player will absolutely become the arsonist, and it will always be the same person
reviewBasis: Weekly four-player co-op for around six months on PC, plus a solo run to see the origin content the campaign group missed.

title: Prey
deck: You are a scientist on a space station and every coffee cup might be a spider. That is the whole pitch, and we love it.
verdictTitle: System Shock's ghost is in the coffee cup.
dadTake: The mimic ate my in-game keys. And also, somehow, my real ones.
verdict: Prey is the closest we've had to a proper immersive sim in a decade, and it flew under most people's radar because Bethesda named it after a completely different game. Talos I is a hand-built puzzle you can approach through the vents, the crawlspaces, or by physically stacking chairs. If any of that sounds fun, buy it.
overview: You wake up on a space station. A coffee cup on the desk turns into a shrieking spider and lunges at your face. That is the first minute. From there it is your job to work out what the hell Talos I is, why your brother is on the intercom, and whether the chair in the corner is a chair. Answer: it might not be. Panic accordingly.

Under the mimic gag sits a proper Arkane playground. Neuromods buy powers, so you can be a hacker, a wrench-lugger, or eventually, a chair. The GLOO cannon glues enemies in place and doubles as a set of stairs, and every locked room has three ways in if you're patient. It's Deus Ex on a space station, and it's the only game the Tactician has ever called 'a decent effort'.
facts: Talos I is one interconnected station you learn like a house, with shortcuts that open up as you go.
Neuromods let you buy alien Typhon powers, which then flag you as a threat to the station's turrets. Choices matter.
The GLOO cannon is a legitimate traversal tool and possibly the best gadget in any 2010s shooter.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I attacked my own office chair.
lenses.headline: Genuinely tense in a way I wasn't ready for.
lenses.body: I shot a chair. Then a mug. Then a fire extinguisher, just to be safe. Somewhere around hour four I stopped panicking, and around hour eight I stopped playing, because the horror element wore me down. Fair call. The station is beautiful, but it's genuinely tense, and the sessions run long by my standards.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Free-form 3D level design I've been waiting for.
lenses.body: I clocked the free-form spatial design in about ten minutes and then wouldn't shut up about it. My exact words: 'verticality that actually means something, again.' I mapped out a wrench-only pacifist route on my second run because of course I did. This is the exact kind of thing my brain was built for.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The last stretch sags, but the middle sings.
lenses.body: I finished it once, on the recommended difficulty, and I think that's the correct dose. Talos I is a great place to get lost in, the mimics stay scary for longer than you'd expect, and the story lands.
