I do note that the last few hours drag a bit, and that saving before every door isn't paranoia, it's policy.

bestFor: Anyone who misses proper immersive sims and has ninety spare minutes at a time
People who like games that reward reading every email in every office
Dads who want a horror-adjacent game they can actually pause safely
watchFor: The opening hours are stingier with tools than the later game
The end stretch is weaker than the rest, which is a well-known complaint
You will inspect every coffee cup for the rest of your life
reviewBasis: Two of us finished it on PC, one across two full runs with different power builds. The third pushed through about eight hours and switched to something with less indoor lighting.

title: NieR:Automata™
deck: Robots with skirts, a fishing minigame with existential stakes, and an ending screen that asks if you would like to erase your save for a stranger.
verdictTitle: Finish it five times. Yes, really.
dadTake: First game that made me cry. And I have watched every Pixar movie in a hospital.
verdict: NieR: Automata is a game we still bring up at unrelated dinner parties. The combat is Platinum-slick, the story is a series of small gut punches, and there is no way around telling you the truth: you have to play it more than once for it to land. If that sounds like homework, this isn't the one. If it sounds like an offer, get in.
overview: You're a battle android in a skirt and a blindfold, fighting a giant machine that is somehow riding a rollercoaster. Nine hours later that same game is a top-down bullet hell, then a text adventure, then a boss fight that reads like a philosophy lecture with a health bar. Yoko Taro is doing something. We're not always sure what. We are always in.

The Platinum combat holds it together: light attack, heavy attack, dodge, a hovering pod that lays down suppressive fire. Under that sits the chip system, where every ability is a physical circuit board you slot into a limited grid, HUD elements included. Skip the map on purpose, unslot it, that's on you. It's the only game we know where the pause menu is part of the story.
facts: The full arc requires multiple playthroughs, each of which reframes the earlier ones. This is on purpose, not padding.
The score is by Keiichi Okabe and it is enormous. It has ended more than one of our long car rides in a good way.
Combat is Platinum-developed, so it feels closer to Bayonetta than to a traditional JRPG.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I got to Route B and made a face.
lenses.headline: The 'do the same game again' pitch didn't land at first.
lenses.body: I finished the first playthrough, got told the game hadn't really started yet, and made the face we all make about paperwork. I picked it up again a month later, hit route C, and admitted it was good, actually. I still can't tell you what the plot is. Neither can the other two, if we're honest.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Fusing chips to slot a bigger HP bar is a real move.
lenses.body: I treated the chip grid like a loadout puzzle and had a two-tab spreadsheet inside a week. Fuse chips to save slots, delete the HP bar to gain damage: this is my exact vocabulary now. I argue the top-down shooter sections are the sharpest part of the game, and one of the other two is starting to suspect I might be right.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The story earns every one of its five endings.
lenses.body: I went in expecting a hack-and-slash and came out staring at the wall. Sessions run long because you can't stop at a chapter break, and the fishing is a genuine trap for an evening. I recommend it to the exact friends who ask, and to nobody else. Which is, I think, the correct posture on this game.

bestFor: People who don't mind games with homework if the homework is good
Anyone who liked Bayonetta but wanted it to make them sad
Group chats that can handle 'let me explain ending E' at 11pm
watchFor: The PC version is famously fussy at launch and you'll want the community fixes
Route A ends before the game really starts, which is a divisive design call
There is fishing. You will lose an evening to it.
reviewBasis: Two of us reached ending E on PC across around forty hours each; the third stopped after Route A and needs to be gently coaxed back.

title: Hollow Knight
deck: A hand-drawn bug kingdom that quietly ruins your evening, six times, before you finally beat False Knight and text the group chat.
verdictTitle: Bugs, sad piano, and a map that fights back.
dadTake: We came for the bugs. Stayed for the emotional damage.
verdict: Hollow Knight is the game we all keep restarting, because nobody wants to admit they forgot where the second dream nail upgrade was. It's brutal in a very quiet way, gorgeous in a way that outlasted its screenshots, and the sort of thing you either sink ninety hours into or bounce off in the first cavern. All three happened here.
overview: You wake up in a windswept town called Dirtmouth, next to an old bug who looks like he has already given up on you. Then you drop into a hole. Somewhere below there's a kingdom of dead insects, a corrupted plague, and the exact same jumping puzzle three times in a row. Somehow this is charming. Somehow we all keep going back.

The genius is that you don't get a map from a menu. You find a mole cartographer sitting in the middle of a cave, and you buy quills off him. So the map lags one biome behind you, forever. Combat is nail-and-spell, dodging is a dash, healing takes a full second while a giant maggot chews on your ankle. It reads simple. It is not.
facts: Hallownest is one interconnected hand-drawn map, no random generation, all built by two people plus a small team.
Healing costs the same soul you use for spells, so every fight is a tiny budget crisis.
There's a fast-travel system, but you have to walk to every stagbeetle station first. Cruel.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I'm stuck at False Knight, forever.
lenses.body: I got as far as False Knight, died six times, and put it down for a year. Every time the other two mention it I say 'the one with the sad bug', nod, and start a different game. I'm not wrong to bounce. There's no assist mode, no difficulty toggle, and the map thing is a real ask on a work night.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.signal: I sat down and made a spreadsheet.
lenses.headline: Charm loadouts have entered the group chat.
lenses.body: I rebound every button, kept a text file of charm loadouts, and had opinions about shaman stone versus quick slash three hours in. I also finished it. Twice. The nail combat scratches my precision itch, and the wandering map system rewards the sort of brain that draws its own subway maps on napkins.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Fifty hours, done in twenty-minute slices.
lenses.body: I finished the main path, saw one of the endings, and quietly closed the game before Path of Pain existed to me. Correct move for a dad. Fifty hours is a huge ask, but the sessions bank well. You can play forty minutes, remember exactly where you are next time, and slot right back in. That's rare.

bestFor: Anyone who owns a comfortable controller and a working sense of grievance
People who like drawing their own maps in their heads
Solo evenings when the kids are finally asleep and you want to feel something
watchFor: No assist options and no difficulty toggle at all
The map system is genuinely part of the puzzle, which will annoy some of you
Charm synergy discussions will absolutely leak into your real conversations
reviewBasis: Two of us finished the main path on PC over roughly seventy hours combined; the third put in about four hours before politely returning to Stardew Valley.

title: DOOM
deck: You wake up, punch a demon, and don't stop punching demons until the credits and possibly your work Slack notifications go completely ignored.
verdictTitle: The rip and tear renaissance.
dadTake: I have not been this loud at midnight since the children were born.
verdict: DOOM (2016) is what happens when id decides shooters can be fun again. You move like a track star, you tear demons in half with your bare hands, and the whole game is scored by Mick Gordon at a volume that will get you divorced. It's the tightest single-player shooter any of us has played in a decade and we cannot recommend it more strongly.
overview: You start the game handcuffed to a slab. Ten seconds later you've smashed a zombie's head into the floor and picked up a shotgun off a corpse. The tutorial pop-up says something. You don't read it. Nobody reads it. You just start moving, and about fourteen hours later you will emerge blinking into daylight and realise the phrase 'work-life balance' meant something to you once. It's an assault. In a good way.

The core loop is the whole reason. Demons drop health only when you glory-kill them, ammo only when you chainsaw them, and armour only when you use the flame belch. The game is teaching you to keep moving, be aggressive, and never, ever hide behind cover. It's a great thirty-minute session game with a fantastic campaign attached, and yes, that music will live in your head rent-free forever.
facts: A hard reboot of the DOOM name that pretends the last two decades of shooter fashion never happened.
The core loop punishes cover and rewards aggression; glory kills refill health, chainsaws refill ammo.
The soundtrack is by Mick Gordon, which is why your subwoofer needs a breather between rooms.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: The shooter I actually finished. I didn't see it coming either.
lenses.body: I don't usually last two hours in a shooter campaign. I sat down with DOOM, held the shotgun, ran into a demon, and suddenly I was the one telling everybody else to pause because I wanted 'one more arena'. I don't fully understand the upgrade menus and I don't need to. I just move and shoot and grin.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Health from glory kills. Ammo from chainsaw. It's a whole doctrine.
lenses.body: I spotted the design straight away: the game teaches you to be aggressive by making cover a losing move and executions a healing move. The chainsaw as a resource valve is the elegant part. I also drew a Descent comparison inside the first thirty minutes, because momentum-based movement drags me back to 1995 no matter what genre we're in. I'm not wrong.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Perfectly cut into thirty-minute chunks. School-night gold.
lenses.body: The campaign breaks naturally into arenas that resolve in twenty to thirty minutes. I played it in bite-sized bursts on PC over two months and never once wished I had four uninterrupted hours. That's a rare thing in a modern shooter. I also keep the master volume at seventy percent, because my youngest can hear a fly two rooms over.

bestFor: Fans of the original DOOM who thought the genre had lost its way
Anyone who wants a shooter that respects thirty minutes at a time
Dads with a good pair of headphones and understanding neighbours
watchFor: The music will move your ribcage; be nice to sleepers upstairs
Some of the rune trials are annoying spikes in the flow
The upgrade menus are more than you'd expect from a game this fast
reviewBasis: One full campaign each on PC across a couple of months, plus revisits when we wanted to remember why we like shooters at all.

title: DARK SOULS™ III
deck: FromSoftware's greatest hits album, with all the parry timings and none of the mercy. We died a lot. On purpose.
verdictTitle: The one that finally clicked.
dadTake: The bonfire is now my emotional support furniture, thank you for asking.
verdict: Dark Souls III is FromSoftware refining every idea they'd been kicking around since the first game and packaging it in a tighter, faster, more coherent adventure. It's still cruel, it's still gorgeous, and it will still make you put the pad down at least once. But the level design is the best in the series, and the boss fights are the reason we still bring it up in the group chat five years later.
overview: You wake up in a graveyard. A guy in a huge hat is on fire nearby. Somewhere a king refuses to sit on his throne and that is somehow your problem, there are skeletons on every stairwell, and you are made of tissue paper. This is From's opening pitch. If you know, you know. If you don't, prepare to die a lot in service of eventually learning what a Havel is.

What separates the third one is the pace. Rolls are faster, weapons are more varied, the levels sprawl less than Dark Souls 1 but respect you more than Dark Souls 2. Boss fights are the best in the series, full stop. If you've bounced off Souls before, this is a better place to try again than the original. If you're already in, it's the one to keep on the drive forever.
facts: The third and, at time of release, final numbered Souls game before Elden Ring rethought the whole format.
Combat is faster than the first two Souls games; weapons have unique weapon arts this time out.
The two DLC entries, Ashes of Ariandel and The Ringed City, are extremely worth playing.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I died to the first knight so many times I uninstalled.
lenses.body: I got past the Iudex Gundyr fight, met the first proper knight on the High Wall, died six or seven times to a shield-and-halberd routine, and put it down for eight months. I came back the following winter, respecced into a strength build, and finished it with a lot of yelling. I'd never do it again. I also would.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Iframes on rolls. Poise thresholds. I know the numbers.
lenses.body: I've got a hardback binder of build notes. I can tell you which weapons R1 through what animations and which have hyperarmour on the swing. I run a straight sword and quickstep loop with an ashen estus split I keep refining. And yes, I do compare the level design in the High Wall to Descent's atrium levels, which the other two have agreed to accept as tribute at this point.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Two hours a week, one boss a month. It works.
lenses.body: I don't have five straight hours to grind through Lothric Castle. I treat the game like a puzzle you solve one bonfire at a time. I beat Nameless King three months after picking the game up and it was worth every session. This is the correct way for a busy adult to play a Souls game and I will fight you about it.

bestFor: Souls-curious dads who owe themselves one more try
Fans of tight combat over open worlds
Anyone who wants boss fights that stay with them for years
watchFor: The first three hours are the worst of the game; hang on
Poise is complicated; the internet will help you understand it
You will scream 'the tracking on that swing' out loud at least once
reviewBasis: One full clear on PC plus DLC by two of us; the third made it to Pontiff Sulyvahn and quietly closed the game for six months before finishing.

title: Firewatch
deck: You take a job in a fire lookout tower and spend four hours flirting with a woman you never see. Extremely early-nineties dad energy.
verdictTitle: Yes it's short. Yes it's worth it.
dadTake: The only game where your handheld radio has more character development than you.
verdict: Firewatch is a short, sad, funny walk through Wyoming with the best voice acting we heard that year. Nothing dramatic happens by triple-A standards, and everything dramatic happens by grown-adult standards. You'll finish it in an evening and think about it for a month. If you want a game to remember, not a game to grind, this is the pick.
overview: You're Henry. You're forty-something. Life gave you a very specific kind of bad news and you responded by taking a summer job as a fire lookout in a Wyoming forest, because that's the kind of person you are and also, honestly, the kind of people we absolutely understand. Your only real relationship is a woman on the other end of a walkie-talkie named Delilah, who is delightful and complicated and lies constantly.

It's a walking game, mostly. You get a map, a compass, radio prompts, and the freedom to reply in whichever tone you're feeling. Choices don't fork the story into a thousand endings; they colour Henry as a person, which is a smaller and more grown-up kind of consequence. The writing is a cut above almost anything else in the medium. Play it with headphones. Don't check reviews for the ending first.
facts: First-person narrative, no combat, roughly four hours long from start to end.
The whole game is a two-hander between Henry and Delilah over radio; the voice work is superb.
Made by Campo Santo, published by Panic; the first game either studio shipped.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I walked, I listened, and I shut up.
lenses.body: I'm the first to skip cutscenes in any other game. In Firewatch I sat there in silence for the full four hours with the good headphones on, ignored my phone, and admitted afterwards that Delilah made me miss my own dad. Then I made the other two promise never to mention it, and here I am, mentioning it. Sorry, me.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: I came in ready to complain about walking sims. I didn't.
lenses.body: I've got strong views on games where you can't die and a lot of them are wrong. Firewatch is the one that reset my priors. The map-and-compass system is a real mechanic, the choice-branching has authorial confidence, and the writing is better than my last three podcasts combined. Then I shut up, which never happens. It counted.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: One evening, one glass of red, one very good game.
lenses.body: I played it on a Friday night after my kids went to bed and finished it before midnight. I didn't move to check my phone once. That's the single highest praise I hand out to anything. Short doesn't mean small. Short means I can commit to it, and that turns out to be a great gift for a busy dad.

bestFor: Anyone with headphones and one free evening
Dads who miss physical paper maps
Fans of good dialogue and unreliable narrators
watchFor: It is genuinely short; that's the point, not a flaw
The ending divides people and always will
The map-and-compass system is the main mechanic; love it or you won't love this
reviewBasis: Two of us played it in a single sitting on PC; the third stretched it out over three evenings because his back hurt.

title: Stardew Valley
deck: You inherit a farm, plant some parsnips, and eight months later your wife is asking why you're crying at a pixel of a chicken.
verdictTitle: Turnips heal what capitalism broke.
dadTake: Marnie's animals cost more than my kid's actual college fund.
verdict: Stardew Valley is one man's love letter to Harvest Moon and it landed with the force of a full pumpkin harvest. It's calm, it's warm, it's endless. You will lose two hours making sprinkler layouts and not notice. We keep new save files running just in case one of us needs to escape reality for an evening. It works every single time.
overview: It's your first spring. You have twelve parsnip seeds, a beat-up tin watering can, and Grandpa's ghost is somehow judging you already. The mayor won't shut up about a chicken. Somewhere in town there's a purple-haired girl who has decided you're her problem now. This is the tone. If it sounds annoying, it isn't. If it sounds soothing, it very much is.

Under the calm sits a genuinely deep game. Crop planning has real optimisation, the mines have combat and randomised layouts, fishing has a mini-game half of us love and half of us despise. Marriage, kids, festivals, and the community centre give you long-form goals that don't nag at you. Play twenty minutes a night for a year and you'll still have things to find. It's the definition of a game that respects your time.
facts: Made almost entirely by one person, ConcernedApe, over roughly four years.
Runs on almost anything and supports co-op for up to four players.
There is no hard end; you can keep farming as long as the seasons keep turning.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: Fell in love with a chicken
lenses.headline: I named a chicken. I wept when it died. It didn't die.
lenses.body: I named the first hen Beatrice, panicked when she stopped laying, and spent forty minutes reading the wiki convinced she was ill. She was fine. She'd just been eating in a corner. I haven't opened the crafting menu in six months, but I can tell you every chicken's mood on a scale of one to ten.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Ancient fruit into kegs. It's an economy. I run it.
lenses.body: I found the ancient fruit and iridium sprinkler pipeline in my first Fall, set my greenhouse up for maximum keg throughput, and spent Winter maximising my profits from a single crop. I talk about starfruit in a way that would make a Wall Street trader nervous. I also did the math on Prismatic Shards, which I'm told is insufferable. I was right.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The genuine best wind-down game any of us owns.
lenses.body: Twenty minutes before bed and the entire day's stress melts off. I play a farm in the corner of my life the way some people knit. It doesn't ask me to be good at anything, it just gently gives me something to tend. I've got three farms across three platforms and I would like an Xbox save transfer, thank you.

bestFor: Anyone whose brain runs hot after work
People who owned a Game Boy Advance and remember Harvest Moon fondly
Dads on the verge of buying real chickens
watchFor: Year one is stingier than the loop eventually becomes
Fishing is a subject of religious debate at our house
You may accidentally become a Junimo economics scholar
reviewBasis: Two of us have multi-year saves on PC; the third has three separate 'just one more day' farms he refuses to abandon.

title: XCOM® 2
deck: Turn-based tactics where you name a soldier after your kid and then you have to look them in the eye when they miss a 95% shot.
verdictTitle: The best strategy sequel of the decade.
dadTake: The dice have been sent to review, and they have chosen violence.
verdict: XCOM 2 is what happens when Firaxis gets to make Enemy Unknown again with the safety off. Turn timers force you to commit, the resistance framing gives every mission stakes, and the game rewards the tacticians who read the whole tooltip and the casuals who just want to yell at a screen. It's a sequel that improves on every part of the original. Ironman it if you dare.
overview: You've named your Ranger after your seven-year-old. She's flanked, she has a 92% shot, she has a clean line of fire. She misses. She dies. You look at the ceiling for about ninety seconds. Then you close the save. Then you don't. This is XCOM 2, the game that turned all three of us into people who whisper 'come on Karen' at a monitor at 11pm on a work night.

What makes it work is the pressure. Turn timers mean you can't sit and overthink every move, the strategy layer piles on decisions you can't fully afford, and the class system rewards specialisation without forcing it. War of the Chosen builds on all of it, and the mod scene fixes the parts you didn't like. Also, the character customisation lets you have a soldier named Preston Garvey. Do with that what you will.
facts: Turn timers on many missions force fast, committed play instead of overwatch parking.
Soldiers are permadeath by default and character customisation makes it worse (or better).
The War of the Chosen expansion changes the campaign so thoroughly it's practically a sequel.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I named a soldier after my daughter. She died. I put the game away.
lenses.body: I got through the tutorial, made it to about the fourth mission, watched a Ranger named after my kid get one-shot by an ADVENT MEC, and quit for six months. When I came back I played on Rookie with the timers turned off and had a much better time. Sometimes you just want to punch aliens without the emotional damage. I respect that this is the game working.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: Reveal, position, alpha strike, extract. I run a doctrine.
lenses.body: I treat every mission like a chess opening. I know the Sword of Damocles line, I pre-call concealment breaks, and I will physically stand up if you overwatch when I told you to move. I also draw a comparison to Descent's degrees of freedom whenever I can, which isn't often in a grid-based game, and yet. I have notes.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: A campaign takes twenty hours and one crying toddler.
lenses.body: Missions are long, the strategy layer punishes bailouts, and Ironman doesn't care that someone spilled milk. I finished a Commander campaign over three months of unbroken Sunday evenings and I'd call it one of my best strategy runs. I also refuse to touch it now that my youngest is a light sleeper. I'm waiting for the kids to move out.

bestFor: Fans of turn-based tactics who can handle heartbreak
People who name characters after coworkers they don't like
Anyone with a working spreadsheet brain and a free weekend
watchFor: The base game is punishing early; War of the Chosen softens some of it
Timers stress some players; you can mod them out without shame
A single mission can eat your entire evening
reviewBasis: The Tactician ran a full Legend campaign on PC over a winter, the All-Rounder finished Commander over three months of Sunday evenings, and the Casual quietly played Rookie with timers off after his first team wipe.

title: Fallout 4
deck: You leave a vault, meet a dog, and immediately spend forty hours arguing about wall placement in a settlement nobody asked you to build.
verdictTitle: The dog is 10/10. We love it anyway.
dadTake: I came for the story. I stayed to make Preston Garvey suffer.
verdict: Fallout 4 is the Bethesda RPG most likely to be labelled 'flawed' by people who then poured 300 hours into it. The shooting is finally good, the settlement building is a rabbit hole with no bottom, and the writing is uneven in the way Bethesda writing has always been. We had a great time and also complained the whole way through. That's a Bethesda game.
overview: The dog's name is Dogmeat and he does not deserve any of this. You've stumbled out of a vault into Boston, someone has stolen your baby, and there's a robot butler with more emotional intelligence than any of the humans left standing. Somewhere in the first hour you'll find a settlement full of people who need your help, which will consume the next six weeks of your life. Preston has another one for you.

The gunplay is the best the series has ever had, VATS is still a joy when you want tactics without the pause menu, and settlement mode is either a whole second game or a chore depending on the day. The main story doesn't fully land, but the moment-to-moment loot-and-explore stuff is Bethesda at close to full strength. Also, the power armour finally feels like power armour and not like a slightly heavier shirt.
facts: Gunplay was tuned with input from id Software, so it feels far better than earlier Bethesda RPGs.
Settlement building is entirely optional and also somehow eight hours of your evening.
The dialogue wheel condenses your choices into four options and yes, that's the main complaint.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I never opened the perk chart and I finished the game.
lenses.body: I picked up whatever gun the ground offered, wore whatever the dead were wearing, and shot ghouls in the head for sixty hours until the credits rolled. I don't know what a settlement is. I'm aware of Preston Garvey only as 'the guy who won't shut up' and I think power armour is 'the good chair'. I liked it a lot.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: I respecced the whole build at level thirty. Twice.
lenses.body: I treat the SPECIAL system like a puzzle and I have a real opinion about which perks are traps. I also spent a full weekend on a settlement wall alignment that would make a city planner cry. Fallout 4 is Bethesda in prototype mode and I love that; it means the systems are pokeable and the mod scene is limitless. I run about twenty mods and refuse to name them.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: It plays better in ninety-minute chunks than we'd expected.
lenses.body: Because the settlement stuff can be closed at any time and the map is dense with short stories, it works as a school-night game if you avoid the main plot missions. I finished it slowly over a summer on PC, put the settlement systems down when they got too fiddly, and had a genuinely great time. I've also got a soft spot for Nick Valentine.

bestFor: Anyone who wanted a shooter with a real world to poke around in
People who peace out the second Preston starts talking
Dogmeat enthusiasts (all of us)
watchFor: The main story is not the reason to be here
Settlement mode will steal a week if you let it
You'll want mods eventually, and they exist
reviewBasis: Two of us finished the base campaign on PC around launch; the third came back years later with mods and never actually left.

title: Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes
deck: One dad stares at a bomb, two dads argue over a PDF, and everyone learns that saying 'the red one' out loud is not helpful.
verdictTitle: Marriage counselling with a countdown timer.
dadTake: We defused the bomb. The friendship? Less clear.
verdict: Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes is a party game that turns your dining room into an air traffic control tower and reveals which one of your friends should never be trusted with instructions. It's cheap, it's replayable, it's genuinely hilarious, and the manual is a print-and-clip nightmare in the best way. If you have three people who can talk over each other, you have a game night.
overview: One of us is holding a bomb. The other two are elbow-deep in a spiral-bound manual we printed at Kinko's, arguing about whether a wire is 'red' or 'burgundy'. The bomb is beeping. Someone is describing a Simon Says pattern in three different words. This is a real thing that happened, on a Thursday, with a baby monitor going in the next room. We did not get to the Venn diagram module in time.

The genius is that the fun comes from the miscommunication, not from being good at the game. You'll get better with time, but you'll also invent new ways to be bad at English. It plays with or without VR, works with any number of manual-readers, and rounds are short enough to fit into a school-night window that closes at ten. It's the game we boot up when we want to remember why we're friends.
facts: One player defuses the bomb; everyone else reads a manual they cannot see.
Bomb modules include wires, keypads, memory games and a Morse code puzzle that briefly ruined a friendship of ours.
It works flat on a monitor or in VR, and rounds run only a few minutes each.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: Great at wires, bad at Simon
lenses.headline: I'm the wire whisperer and Simon Says' natural enemy.
lenses.body: For reasons none of us understand, I can call wire colours out at speed under pressure. The Simon Says module, however, appears to be my kryptonite. We now assign roles at the top of each round so we can defuse the bomb before we defuse our own friendship. It works about half the time. The other half we all just yell 'blue'.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: I printed the manual and put it in a spiral binder.
lenses.body: I laminated the memory module page. Yes, laminated. I colour-coded the wire chart too. When I'm on defuse duty we win about ninety percent of the time; when I'm reading the manual we win as soon as I stop trying to skip pages. I'm the reason we own the game and also, honestly, the reason we still play it.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: Under an hour, no cards, no board, no rules argument.
lenses.body: Sessions run under an hour, rounds run a few minutes, and everyone gets to play every role. I rate it against Codenames and Just One and it's the only video game I'd say holds up in that company. My only complaint is that it doesn't scale up cleanly past four; but honestly, so what. It's meant for a couch.

bestFor: Groups who like communication under pressure without the shame of Trivial Pursuit
Anyone with a printer and a strong marriage
People who own a spiral binder for some reason
watchFor: The manual is the game and you must print it or accept doom
Late-game bombs will make you invent new swear words
Playing solo is technically possible and legally miserable
reviewBasis: Roughly a dozen game nights over the years on flat-screen PC, with a couple of VR sessions when one of us borrowed a headset from work.

sources.label: Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes on Steam

title: Undertale
deck: A tiny RPG about not killing monsters, which spent our entire group chat arguing whether Toriel is our mom now.
verdictTitle: Mercy is a mechanic and it hurts.
dadTake: I petted the dog. Then I petted the dog again. Then I lost my job.
verdict: Undertale is a small game with the confidence of a much bigger one. You can spare everything you meet, you can murder your way through, or you can find out that both options make the game legitimately upset with you. It's a JRPG built by one person that made grown dads misty-eyed at a fight against a goat, and we don't fully understand why it works either.
overview: You fall into a mountain, meet a goat lady who bakes you a pie, and are politely informed the whole underworld would like to kill you. Then a talking flower turns out to be a menace, and eight hours later you're weeping about a skeleton. We don't have a coherent way to describe this. It's just what happened. All three of us. On different weekends.

Combat is a bullet-hell dodge minigame layered over turn-based RPG choices, and every enemy has a non-lethal solution if you can figure out the correct compliment. The music is doing a lot of the emotional work, the writing is doing the rest, and the game remembers your choices in ways that will make you very careful about restarting. Or, if you're the Tactician, curious in a way that ruined a Saturday.
facts: Made largely by one person, Toby Fox, who also wrote the soundtrack and drew most of the sprites himself.
Combat blends bullet-hell dodging with turn-based menus, and every enemy has a non-violent option.
It plays in about six to eight hours on a single route, and the routes are extremely not the same.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: I was fine. Then Toriel showed up. I was not fine.
lenses.body: I didn't know I was signing up to be emotionally ambushed by a goat lady with a rolling pin. I beat the pacifist run over three evenings on PC, teared up twice, and I'm refusing to say which parts on the record. I'd like everyone to know I was 'just tired' during the boss fight. The other two weren't there for it, and somehow they still saw it.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: The game reads your save data and I had opinions about it.
lenses.body: I clocked what the game was doing with save data about ten minutes in and it became a whole thing at the kitchen table. I respect it, mechanically. I also think it's the most Descent-adjacent thing about the game, which is a hot take you can only get from a man with strong opinions about six degrees of freedom in a JRPG. That man is me.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: The rare short game we discussed for a month.
lenses.body: I finished it in a week of school-night sessions and then spent the next month making the other two discuss the ending in the group chat at increasingly unreasonable hours. It's short, it fits between kids' bedtimes, and it does more with six hours than most games manage with sixty. I put it in my top ten and I haven't budged since.

bestFor: People who loved Earthbound and haven't stopped talking about it
Anyone who wants to play something short that stays with them
Dads who need to be reminded to feel things
watchFor: The pixel art masks how much reading you're doing
The bullet-hell escalates in the back half and gets genuinely tough
You will absolutely spoil yourself if you Google the wrong word
reviewBasis: All three of us played the pacifist route on PC, one of us did the neutral run out of curiosity, and none of us have the stomach to do the third one.

title: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
deck: A hundred hours of witchering, arguing about baths with Ciri, and losing three consecutive evenings to a card game we all resent.
verdictTitle: Yes, it's the best RPG. Yes, still.
dadTake: Gwent stole more of my life than any of my children.
verdict: The Witcher 3 is the game we point to when someone asks whether the medium can do serious storytelling. It's also the game we accidentally spent forty hours playing card mini-games in. Both things being true is why it's still, ten years later, the RPG the rest are measured against. Play it. Take breaks. Don't feel bad about skipping to Skellige.
overview: You're standing in a swamp holding a sword bigger than your torso, watching a griffin eat a horse, and the game politely suggests that maybe you should also finish the herbalist's contract, do a witcher hunt, meet an emperor whose name you'll forget, and possibly bathe. Geralt is having a normal one. So are we, three hours past bedtime, still saying 'one more contract'.

The world does the heavy lifting. Every question mark on the map is at least a story, and every side quest was written by someone who wanted you to remember it. Combat is chunky and satisfying rather than technical, alchemy is optional in a way that suits a busy dad, and the choices land because the writing carries them. Also, Gwent. We are not talking about Gwent.
facts: The base game runs somewhere between forty and sixty hours if you're focused and roughly a hundred and change if you're a witcher tourist.
It ships with two large expansions, Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine, that are basically full RPGs on their own.
Gwent is entirely optional and half of us couldn't stop playing it anyway.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.headline: Roll toward the monster, roll away, roll into a tree.
lenses.body: I got to Velen, picked one sword, refused to swap to silver even when the game begged me, and just rolled at everything until it stopped moving. It worked more often than it should have. I'm still not sure what a Quen is and I don't want to be told. I finished the game with the Igni button unused.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: There is a build. I found the build. I explained it at length.
lenses.body: Sign build, mostly Igni, alchemy tree for the crit multiplier. I rerolled at level twelve to fix my character sheet and I haven't shut up about the Euphoria mutation since. The Witcher 3 is one of the rare places my tuning-fork brain and my story brain agree, and I'm told that's insufferable. Correct, but insufferable. Ask me about tears of the goddess sometime.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: It doesn't respect your evening. That's the price.
lenses.body: The world is enormous and the sidequests are actually good, which is a nightmare when your gaming window ends at 10:45. I finished it over ten months on PC, one contract at a time, and I still haven't started Blood and Wine because my kid takes swimming lessons on Saturdays. I say I'll get to it. I won't. Yet.

bestFor: People who missed The Witcher 3 the first time and would like to be smug about it now
Fans of world-building where every peasant has a name
Anyone with a hundred hours to bury
watchFor: The first four hours in White Orchard are the slowest part of the game
Gwent is a cognitohazard, treat it like a slot machine
You will start a Blood and Wine playthrough and forget the main plot
reviewBasis: Two of us cleared the main game and Blood and Wine on PC; the third quit at Skellige for a year and came back to finish it out of stubbornness.

sources.label: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt on Steam

title: Cities: Skylines
deck: The classic reply-guy dream: build a city, then rebuild it three times because you refuse to admit the roundabout was the problem.
verdictTitle: The traffic AI won. We lost.
dadTake: We didn't found a metropolis. We founded a very expensive intersection.
verdict: Cities: Skylines is what happened when SimCity took a decade off and Colossal Order politely stepped in with a working game. It's endlessly moddable, it's meditative on a Sunday afternoon, and it will destroy an evening faster than any of us can fetch a beer. Ten years on it's still the one we boot up when we want to feel competent and then very quickly not.
overview: You start with a stretch of grass, one road, and the confident belief that this time you're going to plan the highway before you plop the residential zones. Two hours later you have a hospital nobody can reach, sewage flowing into your reservoir, and forty-two garbage trucks pointed the wrong way down the same street. Welcome to mayor.

What actually makes it work is the traffic simulation. Every vehicle picks a route based on the network you built, which is a beautiful idea until you realise the vehicles have been to a different school than you. That, plus mods, plus DLC across roughly a decade, means you can sculpt one map for a hundred hours and still have places you haven't zoned. It rewards patience the way a jigsaw does.
facts: Traffic is simulated per-vehicle, which is why one bad exit ramp can grind your entire economy to a halt.
Mod support runs deep on PC and the community fixed problems that shipped with the base game.
You can play it entirely at 1x speed if you want to feel like a wise mayor with cheese and crackers.

lenses.name: The Casual
lenses.signal: I built one roundabout and left
lenses.headline: The stadium came first. So did the bankruptcy.
lenses.body: I plopped a stadium down in the first ten minutes because it looked cool, then ran out of money before the sewage plant. I'm not entirely convinced you can lose at Cities: Skylines, and yet, I have. Twice. I now maintain that my role is 'the aesthetics guy' while the other two handle infrastructure.

lenses.name: The Tactician
lenses.headline: I made a real spreadsheet. It was tabbed.
lenses.body: Traffic flow, tax rates, industry zoning ratios — I built the spreadsheet before I built the first block. Then I ran a lane math simulation in Excel while the game sat paused. I'm not the reason SimCity died, but I am the reason our shared save file has three underpasses labelled 'do not touch'. It's fine. It's mostly fine.

lenses.name: The All-Rounder
lenses.headline: One hour in, three have passed. Every time.
lenses.body: Cities: Skylines doesn't tell you it's midnight. It doesn't warn you that you've got work in the morning. It just quietly plays that ambient traffic hum while you tweak one intersection and suddenly it's tomorrow. I respect it deeply and I refuse to install it on my laptop before big meetings.

bestFor: Anyone who wants management sim without a UI screaming at them
